title: Abolitionism
summary: The interracial movement to end slavery in the United States, which grew from Quaker and revolutionary-era antislavery societies and gradual-emancipation laws into the radical demand for immediate emancipation in the 1830s, and which helped bring about the Thirteenth Amendment of 1865.

review.question: Why did the abolitionists of the 1830s reject colonization, which many earlier antislavery whites had supported?
review.answer: Free Black Americans opposed it, declaring at an 1831 convention that the United States was their home, and the writings of David Walker and James Forten persuaded William Lloyd Garrison that colonization was inherently racist, so the new movement demanded immediate emancipation and Black citizenship instead.

review.question: How did abolitionist women's work help launch the women's rights movement?
review.answer: Women such as the Grimké sisters lectured and petitioned against slavery and faced backlash for speaking in public; when the 1840 antislavery convention in London refused to seat women delegates, Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton returned determined to fight for women's rights and organized the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848.

review.question: How did abolitionists help bring about the Thirteenth Amendment?
review.answer: The Women's Loyal National League, led by Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, gathered nearly half a million signatures on emancipation petitions that Charles Sumner presented to the Senate from February 1864, and Sumner credited the league as the principal force behind the amendment, which the Senate passed in April 1864.

review.question: Why did the American Anti-Slavery Society split around 1840?
review.answer: Garrisonians held that the Constitution was proslavery and relied on moral suasion, while political abolitionists believed the Constitution could be used against slavery and formed the Liberty Party; the election of Abby Kelley to the society's business committee led Arthur Tappan and other conservatives to walk out.

timeline.event: Philadelphians, sixteen of the twenty-four of them Quakers, found the Society for the Relief of Free Negroes Unlawfully Held in Bondage, later the Pennsylvania Abolition Society.
Pennsylvania enacts the first state law for the gradual abolition of slavery.
Benjamin Franklin, as president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society, signs an antislavery petition to the First Congress, which tables it.
Delegates from abolition societies in six states meet in Philadelphia and agree to petition Congress against the slave trade.
The American Colonization Society is founded to resettle free Black Americans in Africa.
Samuel E. Cornish and John B. Russwurm found Freedom's Journal in New York.
David Walker publishes his Appeal to the Colored Citizens of the World.
William Lloyd Garrison founds The Liberator; a New York convention of free Black people rejects colonization.
Reformers from ten states found the American Anti-Slavery Society, pledged to immediate emancipation.
A Boston mob breaks up a meeting of the Boston Female Anti-Slavery Society and threatens Garrison's life.
The House adopts the gag rule, barring discussion of abolitionist petitions.
A mob in Illinois kills the abolitionist editor Elijah Lovejoy.
A mob burns Pennsylvania Hall in Philadelphia during the Anti-Slavery Convention of American Women.
The American Anti-Slavery Society splits over women's leadership and politics; the Liberty Party runs James G. Birney for president.
Frederick Douglass publishes his Narrative.
The Fugitive Slave Act penalizes Northerners who aid freedom seekers.
Senator Charles Sumner presents the first 100,000 signatures from the Women's Loyal National League's emancipation petition.
The House passes the Thirteenth Amendment, 119 to 56, after the Senate had passed it in April 1864.
The Thirteenth Amendment is ratified, abolishing slavery throughout the United States.

misconception.myth: Abolitionism was a popular Northern cause, led by white reformers on behalf of enslaved people.
misconception.fact: Abolitionists were a small minority whom most white Northerners disliked, and mobs attacked them in Boston, Philadelphia and Illinois; Black Americans, free and formerly enslaved, were central from the start, from the 1831 free Black convention and David Walker's Appeal to Frederick Douglass's lectures and writing.
misconception.why: Picturing a broadly antislavery North led by white allies hides how unpopular the movement was and erases Black activists who shaped its demands, such as the rejection of colonization.

title: Abraham Lincoln
summary: The 16th president of the United States (1861–1865), an Illinois lawyer and Republican who led the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, backed the Thirteenth Amendment, and was assassinated in April 1865.

review.question: Why did Lincoln win the presidency in 1860 with less than 40 percent of the popular vote?
review.answer: Four major candidates split the vote; Lincoln carried every free state, which gave him 180 of 303 electoral votes, a clear Electoral College majority, even though he was not on the ballot in much of the South.

review.question: How did the actions of enslaved people shape Lincoln's emancipation policy, according to historians such as Ira Berlin?
review.answer: By fleeing to Union lines and offering labor and military service, enslaved people forced Union officers, Congress and the president to decide their status; Lincoln, who had first favored gradual, compensated emancipation and colonization, moved toward the Emancipation Proclamation as that pressure grew.

review.question: Why do historians debate Lincoln's title of "Great Emancipator"?
review.answer: Some see his leadership as the decisive force that ended slavery, while others argue he was a reluctant emancipator and that enslaved people were the prime movers; the debate is about how to weigh presidential leadership against the agency of the enslaved.

timeline.event: Born near Hodgenville, Kentucky.
First elected to the Illinois legislature.
As a first-term Whig congressman, introduces the Spot Resolutions challenging the case for war with Mexico.
Gives the "House Divided" speech; later loses the Senate race to Stephen A. Douglas.
Elected 16th president with a majority of electoral votes from the free states.
Inaugurated after seven Southern states had seceded.
Thirty-eight Dakota men are hanged at Mankato after Lincoln commutes most of the death sentences.
The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect in areas in rebellion.
Delivers the Gettysburg Address.
Reelected president.
Shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre; dies the next morning.

misconception.myth: Lincoln dashed off the Gettysburg Address on the back of an envelope on the train to Gettysburg.
misconception.fact: Lincoln worked on the speech in the weeks before November 19, 1863; a Library of Congress copy begins in ink on Executive Mansion stationery written in Washington, and the drafts are in steady handwriting unlike a moving train's.
misconception.why: The envelope story turns a carefully revised speech into a lucky improvisation and hides how deliberately Lincoln shaped his public words.

title: Affordable Care Act
aliases: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
summary: The federal health care law signed by President Barack Obama on March 23, 2010, and amended a week later by the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act, which expanded coverage through subsidized private insurance exchanges, a broader Medicaid program, an individual coverage requirement and new rules for insurers, and which survived three major Supreme Court challenges.

review.question: Why did the Supreme Court uphold the individual mandate in NFIB v. Sebelius even though it rejected the Commerce Clause argument for it?
review.answer: The Court held that the penalty for going without insurance could be sustained as an exercise of Congress's power to levy taxes, so the mandate was constitutional on that basis even though it was not valid under the Commerce Clause or the Necessary and Proper Clause.

review.question: How did NFIB v. Sebelius change the Medicaid expansion?
review.answer: The Court found that threatening states with the loss of their existing Medicaid funds was coercive, and limited the remedy so that states could decline the expansion to adults with incomes up to 133 percent of the poverty level without losing their other Medicaid money, making the expansion optional.

review.question: Why did California v. Texas end without a ruling on whether the law was constitutional?
review.answer: Because Congress had set the penalty for going without coverage at $0, the Court found the plaintiffs could not show an injury traceable to the government enforcing that provision, so they lacked standing and the case was dismissed.

timeline.event: President Obama addresses a joint session of Congress to press for health care reform.
The Senate passes H.R. 3590, as amended, by 60 to 39.
The House agrees to the Senate amendments, 219 to 212, with no Republican votes in favor.
Obama signs the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act.
Obama signs the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act, which amends the new law.
In NFIB v. Sebelius the Supreme Court upholds the individual mandate as a tax but makes the Medicaid expansion optional for states.
The individual mandate, the exchanges with their premium tax credits and the ban on preexisting-condition exclusions for all ages take effect.
In King v. Burwell the Court, 6 to 3, holds that tax credits are available in states that use the federal exchange.
Obama vetoes the first repeal bill Congress sends him.
The penalty for going without coverage falls to $0 under the 2017 tax law.
In California v. Texas the Court, 7 to 2, dismisses a challenge to the law for lack of standing.

misconception.myth: Congress repealed the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate in 2017, and the Supreme Court later struck the law down.
misconception.fact: The 2017 tax law reduced the penalty for going without coverage to $0 from 2019 but left the coverage requirement in the statute, and in California v. Texas (2021) the Supreme Court dismissed the challenge for lack of standing, leaving the rest of the law in force.
misconception.why: Zeroing out the penalty was widely described as killing the mandate, and a lower court had ruled the whole law invalid before the Supreme Court reversed, so headlines from different stages of the fight blur together.

title: African Americans
summary: Americans with origins among the peoples of sub-Saharan Africa, most of them descended from Africans enslaved in North America and others from more recent Caribbean and African immigration; the 2020 census counted 46.9 million people who identified as Black alone or in combination with another race.

review.question: How did a relatively small number of African arrivals become one of the largest Black populations in the Americas?
review.answer: Only about 388,000 captive Africans landed in British North America and the United States, but in places like the Chesapeake the enslaved population became self-sustaining through births from about 1730, so the population grew by natural increase rather than continual imports.

review.question: Why did free Black Americans build their own churches and societies in the late 1700s?
review.answer: Facing segregation in white-led institutions (Richard Allen could lead only segregated services at St. George's in Philadelphia), they founded independent bodies such as the Free African Society (1787), Mother Bethel (1793) and the AME Church (1816), and mutual aid and fraternal groups that provided help, leadership and self-determination.

review.question: What pushed about six million Black Southerners to move north and west between 1910 and 1970?
review.answer: They sought to escape racial violence and Jim Crow oppression and to find economic and educational opportunity, and wartime labor shortages in both world wars opened industrial jobs in cities from Chicago and Detroit to Los Angeles and Oakland.

review.question: Why does the census give two different counts of the Black population in 2020?
review.answer: The "Black alone" count (41.1 million, 12.4 percent) includes only people who chose that single race, while "Black alone or in combination" (46.9 million, 14.2 percent) also includes people who reported Black together with one or more other races.

timeline.event: The privateer White Lion brings captive Africans from the kingdom of Ndongo to Old Point Comfort, Virginia.
Prince Hall establishes African Lodge No. 459 in Boston, the start of Black Freemasonry.
Richard Allen and Absalom Jones found the Free African Society in Philadelphia.
The African Methodist Episcopal Church is organized as an independent denomination, with Allen elected its bishop.
The African Institute, later Cheyney University, opens in Pennsylvania, the first HBCU.
The War Department creates the Bureau of Colored Troops; about 179,000 Black men go on to serve in the Union Army.
The Great Migration out of the South begins; about six million people move north and west by 1970.
The 2020 census counts 46.9 million people who identify as Black alone or in combination with another race.

misconception.myth: Most of the Africans carried across the Atlantic in the slave trade were taken to what became the United States.
misconception.fact: Of about 10.7 million Africans who survived the crossing, an estimated 388,000 (about 3.5 percent) landed in British North America and the United States; about 40 percent went to Brazil and about 35 percent to the non-Spanish Caribbean.
misconception.why: The U.S. Black population grew mainly through births rather than imports, so a comparatively small number of arrivals became a large population, which can make the United States seem the center of a trade that was mostly directed elsewhere.

title: American Civil War
summary: The war of 1861–1865 between the United States and eleven slaveholding Southern states that seceded to form the Confederacy; it preserved the Union and destroyed slavery at a cost of roughly 750,000 lives.

review.question: Why did Deep South states secede after the 1860 election, before Lincoln had taken office?
review.answer: They saw the victory of a party opposed to slavery's expansion as a threat to slavery itself. Mississippi's declaration said its position was thoroughly identified with slavery, and South Carolina's centered on Northern refusal to return fugitives from slavery.

review.question: How did enslaved people help turn a war for the Union into a war against slavery?
review.answer: By fleeing to Union lines from 1861 on, they forced the army and Congress to decide their status, which led to contraband policy, the Confiscation Acts, abolition in Washington, D.C., the Emancipation Proclamation, and the enlistment of about 179,000 Black soldiers.

review.question: Why do historians now cite about 750,000 deaths instead of the long-used 620,000?
review.answer: J. David Hacker compared census survival rates for 1860–1870 with the decades before and after, and the shortfall pointed to about 750,000 deaths (range 650,000–850,000), since earlier counts relied on incomplete military records.

timeline.event: A South Carolina convention votes 169 to 0 to secede after Abraham Lincoln's election.
Delegates from seven seceded states meet in Montgomery, Alabama, and choose Jefferson Davis as Confederate president.
Confederate forces fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor; it surrenders the next day and Lincoln calls for 75,000 volunteers.
At Fort Monroe, General Benjamin Butler begins receiving people fleeing slavery as "contraband of war."
Congress abolishes slavery in the District of Columbia.
The Battle of Antietam, the bloodiest single day in American history, gives Lincoln the victory he awaited to announce emancipation.
The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect in areas under Confederate control.
The War Department creates the Bureau of Colored Troops to organize Black regiments.
Pickett's Charge fails, ending the three-day Battle of Gettysburg.
Vicksburg surrenders to Ulysses S. Grant, splitting the Confederacy in two.
Congress grants Black soldiers pay equal to white soldiers, retroactively.
William T. Sherman's army captures Atlanta before marching to the sea.
Robert E. Lee surrenders the Army of Northern Virginia to Grant at Appomattox.

misconception.myth: The Civil War was fought over states' rights or tariffs, not slavery.
misconception.fact: The seceding states said otherwise at the time. Mississippi declared its position "thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery," South Carolina complained that Northern states would not enforce the Fugitive Slave Act, and Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens rested the new government on Black inequality. The only state right at stake was the right to protect slavery.
misconception.why: The postwar "Lost Cause" story recast secession as a defense of constitutional principle. Believing it hides what the war was about and why emancipation and the Reconstruction amendments followed from it.

title: American Revolutionary War
summary: The war of 1775–1783 in which thirteen British colonies, allied from 1778 with France and later joined in the wider war by Spain and the Dutch Republic, fought Great Britain and won recognition of the independence of the United States in the Treaty of Paris.

review.question: Why did the American victory at Saratoga matter far beyond the battlefield?
review.answer: It was the first surrender of a British army to another nation, and the news persuaded France's foreign minister to offer a formal alliance; the treaties signed in February 1778 brought French money, troops and ships and turned the rebellion into a global war.

review.question: Why did most Native nations side with Britain, and how did the war turn out for them?
review.answer: Nations such as the Shawnee, Creek, Cherokee and most of the Six Nations hoped a British victory would hold back settlers west of the Appalachians; American victory opened those lands to expansion, and even the Oneida, who fought for the Americans, lost villages in the war and saw promises to protect their lands go unenforced.

review.question: How did the war open paths to freedom for enslaved people, and why were those paths limited?
review.answer: British offers of freedom such as Dunmore's 1775 proclamation led tens of thousands to flee their enslavers, and some Black men won freedom by serving in American units; but many who reached British lines were still held by loyalists, and the evacuations of 1782–1783 carried some to freedom in Nova Scotia and others onward in slavery.

review.question: Why did the war not end immediately after Yorktown?
review.answer: Britain still held New York, Charleston and other posts with about 26,000 troops, frontier warfare continued, and peace required a change of government in London, preliminary articles in November 1782 and a final treaty in September 1783.

timeline.event: British regulars march to seize militia stores at Concord; fighting at Lexington, Concord's North Bridge and along the road back to Boston opens the war.
New England militia begin the siege of British-held Boston.
The Continental Congress votes to raise a Continental Army and the next day unanimously chooses George Washington to command it.
After losing New York, Washington crosses the Delaware and surprises the Hessian garrison at Trenton.
Oneida warriors fight beside New York militia at Oriskany as the Haudenosaunee Confederacy splits over the war.
John Burgoyne surrenders his army to Horatio Gates at Saratoga, New York.
American commissioners sign the Treaty of Alliance and the Treaty of Amity and Commerce with France.
Spain enters the war against Britain.
One of the principal Oneida villages is destroyed, a year after Oneida scouts guided the Clinton-Sullivan expedition against the British-allied Six Nations.
The French fleet under de Grasse turns back a British fleet at the Battle of the Capes, sealing off the Chesapeake.
Cornwallis's army surrenders to American and French forces at Yorktown, Virginia.
Lord North resigns as prime minister; the new British government opens peace talks in Paris.
British rangers and Native allies rout Kentucky militia at Blue Licks, ten months after Yorktown.
American and British commissioners sign preliminary articles of peace.
The British evacuate Charleston, South Carolina, taking loyalists and thousands of Black people with them.
The Treaty of Paris is signed, ending the war and recognizing American independence.
British forces leave New York City, their last stronghold in the United States.

misconception.myth: The Revolutionary War ended when Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown in October 1781.
misconception.fact: Britain still had about 26,000 troops in North America after Yorktown, fighting went on in the West and South into late 1782, the peace treaty was signed only on September 3, 1783, and the British did not leave New York City until November 25, 1783.
misconception.why: Yorktown was the last great battle in the East and broke Britain's will to keep fighting, so later histories let the surrender stand for the whole victory and forgot the two years of frontier war, evacuation and diplomacy that followed.

title: Articles of Confederation
aliases: Articles of Confederation and Perpetual Union
summary: The first written frame of national government for the United States, adopted by the Second Continental Congress on November 15, 1777, in force from Maryland's ratification on March 1, 1781, until the Constitution replaced it in 1789; it joined sovereign states in a league governed by a one-state, one-vote Congress with no power to tax.

review.question: Why did Congress under the Articles struggle to pay its bills, and what did that mean in practice?
review.answer: The Articles gave Congress no power to tax; it could only ask the state legislatures for money, and between 1781 and 1787 it received about $1.5 million of the $10 million it requested, leaving it unable to pay war debts or raise its own army, as Shays' Rebellion showed.

review.question: How did the dispute over western lands delay the Articles from taking effect?
review.answer: Ratification had to be unanimous, and states without western land claims, above all Maryland, refused to ratify until states such as Virginia gave up their claims; Maryland ratified only on March 1, 1781, after Virginia agreed to do so.

review.question: How did the Articles' clause on Indian affairs lead to conflict at Fort Stanwix in 1784?
review.answer: The Articles gave Congress power over affairs with Native peoples who were not members of any state, but New York claimed the Haudenosaunee as within its jurisdiction and held its own meeting, so Congress and the state competed for land cessions, and New York later sold land it had failed to obtain by treaty.

review.question: Why did the framers of the Articles deliberately create a weak central government?
review.answer: Many Americans feared losing power to a central body, as the earlier failure of the Albany Plan showed, so the Articles let each state keep its sovereignty and every power not expressly delegated, gave Congress no taxing power and no independent executive or courts, and required every state to agree to amendments.

timeline.event: After the Lee Resolution, the Second Continental Congress appoints a committee, one member per colony, to plan a confederation.
The committee, with John Dickinson as principal writer, presents its draft to Congress.
After debate sharpened by the British capture of Philadelphia, Congress adopts the Articles.
Congress sends the Articles to the states, all thirteen of which must ratify.
Virginia becomes the first state to ratify.
New Jersey ratifies after holding out over western land claims.
Delaware ratifies, leaving Maryland the last holdout.
Congress creates a Department of Foreign Affairs.
Maryland ratifies after Virginia agrees to give up its western claims; the Articles take effect.
Confederation commissioners impose the Treaty of Fort Stanwix on Haudenosaunee delegates while New York pursues its own negotiations.
Delegates from several states gather at the Annapolis Convention.
New York's refusal of the revised impost ends Congress's attempt to win a national tariff.
The Constitutional Convention meets in Philadelphia to revise the Articles and instead drafts a new constitution.
The Articles cease to be in force as government under the Constitution begins.

misconception.myth: The government under the Articles of Confederation accomplished nothing and was simply a failure.
misconception.fact: Despite having no power to tax, the Confederation Congress saw the Revolutionary War to its end with the 1783 Treaty of Paris, set up departments of Foreign Affairs, War, Marine and Treasury, and passed the Land Ordinances of 1784 and 1785 and the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, which created a process for admitting new states on equal terms with the original thirteen.
misconception.why: Because the Constitution replaced the Articles, the Confederation is often remembered only as the failed first draft, a view that overlooks lasting achievements and the real reasons people in the 1770s distrusted a strong central government.

title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: The Japanese carrier-air and midget-submarine attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet and military airfields on Oʻahu, Hawaiʻi, on the morning of Sunday, December 7, 1941, which killed 2,403 Americans and brought the United States into World War II.

review.question: Why did Japan decide to attack the U.S. fleet at Pearl Harbor?
review.answer: After Japan moved into French Indochina in 1941, the United States and Britain cut off its oil and Washington froze its assets. Japan's main aim was the oil of the Dutch East Indies, which meant fighting Britain and the United States; planners struck the Pacific Fleet to keep it from interfering while Japan seized Southeast Asia, hoping for a quick victory because they doubted they could win a long war.

review.question: How did the attack bring the United States into the war in Europe as well as the Pacific?
review.answer: Congress declared war only on Japan on December 8, 1941, but Japan's ally Germany then declared war on the United States on December 11, putting the country at war in both Europe and Asia.

review.question: Why did the attack fall short of crippling the United States in the long run?
review.answer: All three Pacific Fleet aircraft carriers were at sea, fuel storage and repair facilities survived, and many sunk or damaged ships were raised, repaired and returned to service; six months later U.S. carriers sank four Japanese carriers at Midway.

review.question: How did the attack affect Japanese Americans?
review.answer: The FBI immediately arrested people on prewar watch lists, and on February 19, 1942, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, which led to the mass removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans on the West Coast, about two-thirds of them U.S. citizens by birth.

timeline.event: Fighting at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing opens full-scale war between Japan and China, turning U.S. opinion toward China.
Japan signs the Tripartite Pact with Germany and Italy.
After Japanese forces move into French Indochina, the United States and Britain impose a full oil embargo and Washington freezes Japanese assets.
About 7:55 a.m. the first wave of 183 Japanese aircraft strikes Oʻahu; a second wave of 170 arrives about 8:50 a.m.; the attack lasts about 75 minutes.
Roosevelt addresses a joint session of Congress at 12:30 p.m.; Congress declares war on Japan, with one dissent, and he signs the declaration at 4 p.m.
Germany declares war on the United States.
Roosevelt signs Executive Order 9066, which leads to the mass incarceration of Japanese Americans on the West Coast.
Admiral Chester Nimitz presents the Navy Cross to Mess Attendant Doris Miller for his conduct aboard USS West Virginia during the attack.
A Joint Congressional Committee opens the eighth and most thorough investigation of the attack.
The USS Arizona Memorial, built over the sunken battleship, is officially dedicated.
Congress designates December 7 as National Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day.

misconception.myth: President Roosevelt knew in advance that Japan would strike Pearl Harbor and let it happen to bring the United States into the war.
misconception.fact: U.S. codebreakers were reading Japan's diplomatic messages (MAGIC), which tracked Tokyo's policy but did not reveal military plans; those travelled in Japanese Navy codes that largely resisted American cryptologists. Eight wartime and postwar investigations divided blame among the Hawaiʻi commanders and officials in Washington, but none established foreknowledge.
misconception.why: Responsibility was never settled to everyone's satisfaction, and for decades revisionist accounts defending the local commanders claimed that intelligence had been suppressed, keeping the story alive.

title: Betsy Ross flag myth
aliases: Betsy Ross and the first flag
summary: The popular story that Philadelphia upholsterer Betsy Ross designed and sewed the first Stars and Stripes at George Washington's request in 1776, a family tradition first made public by her grandson in 1870 that no contemporary document supports.

review.question: Why do historians doubt that Betsy Ross made the first flag at Washington's request in 1776?
review.answer: The story first appeared in 1870, almost a century later and 34 years after Ross died, and rests on family recollections from people who had not witnessed the events. No document records a congressional flag committee in 1776 or any dealing between Washington and Ross, and Congress did not adopt a flag until June 14, 1777. Even Canby's own research found no supporting documents.

review.question: How did a family story become a national legend between 1870 and 1909?
review.answer: Canby's 1870 paper was repeated by national journals by 1873, embellished in books such as Reigart's 1878 history, and dramatized in Charles Weisgerber's painting, which crowds saw at the 1893 Chicago fair and which was reproduced widely. The flag was becoming a revered symbol after the Civil War, and the 1909 book by Canby's relatives, school lessons and toys fixed the story in memory.

review.question: What does the documentary record actually show about Betsy Ross's work?
review.answer: She ran an upholstery business, was paid by the Pennsylvania State Navy Board in May 1777 for making ship's colours, and went on making flags for decades, including many under government contracts around the War of 1812. Historian Marla Miller calls her one of Philadelphia's most important flag makers of the Revolution, alongside others such as Rebecca Young, Margaret Manney and Sarah Barry.

timeline.event: Elizabeth Griscom, later known as Betsy Ross, is born in Gloucester City, New Jersey, and raised a Quaker.
She elopes with upholsterer John Ross and is expelled by the Quakers for marrying outside the meeting.
The Continental Union (Grand Union) flag, with British crosses in its canton, flies over Washington's camp in Massachusetts.
The Pennsylvania State Navy Board pays Ross for making ship's colours, her earliest documented flag work.
The Continental Congress resolves that the flag be thirteen red and white stripes and thirteen white stars on blue.
Francis Hopkinson asks Congress to pay him for designing the flag and other emblems; the claim is refused.
Betsy Ross dies in Philadelphia; her grandson William Canby is eleven years old.
William Canby reads a paper to the Historical Society of Pennsylvania telling the family story of the first flag.
Harper's Weekly and other national journals repeat the story as fact.
J. Franklin Reigart's book embellishes the tale, crediting Ross with originating the first flag.
Charles Weisgerber's painting of the scene draws crowds at the World's Columbian Exposition and is widely reproduced.
Canby's brother and nephew publish The Evolution of the American Flag, fixing the story in public memory.
President Woodrow Wilson proclaims a national Flag Day on June 14.

misconception.myth: George Washington asked Betsy Ross to design and sew the first Stars and Stripes in 1776, and she did, adding five-pointed stars in a circle.
misconception.fact: No contemporary document records the visit or credits Ross with the design. Congress adopted the flag only in June 1777, Francis Hopkinson claimed the design in 1780, and Ross's documented work is as one of several Philadelphia flag makers.
misconception.why: The story entered print in 1870 from family memory, then spread through a widely copied 1893 painting, school lessons and patriotic tourism because it offered a founding heroine for a newly revered symbol.

title: Blues
summary: A form of African American music that took shape in the rural South in the decades around 1900, built on work songs, field hollers and older Black musical traditions, which spread through sheet music, vaudeville and records, moved north with Black migrants to cities such as Chicago, and shaped later American popular music, including rock.

review.question: Why is it misleading to say that W. C. Handy invented the blues?
review.answer: Handy himself described hearing the blues from Black musicians in the Delta around 1903, before he played it; he wrote down and arranged fragments he heard from itinerant performers and published them, which made him the music's great popularizer rather than its creator.

review.question: How did the blues change when Mississippi musicians moved to Chicago?
review.answer: In the city they electrically amplified their instruments and added drums and horns, so the solo singer with a guitar became the blues band heard on labels such as Chess.

review.question: Why did Mamie Smith's 1920 recording of "Crazy Blues" matter to the music business?
review.answer: It was the first commercial vaudeville blues record by a Black singer, and in the following years "race records" — recordings by Black artists marketed mainly to Black buyers — grew into a business that sent scouts across the South and into northern cities to find blues talent.

timeline.event: An English traveler describes the music of enslaved people on a Georgia rice plantation, an early account of music that would later evolve into the blues.
Bandleader W. C. Handy settles in Clarksdale, Mississippi, and around this year hears a slide guitarist playing a blues at the Tutwiler railroad station.
Handy publishes "The Memphis Blues" and sells its rights for $100.
Handy publishes "St. Louis Blues," his best-known composition.
Mamie Smith records "Crazy Blues," the first commercial vaudeville blues record by a Black vocalist.
Bessie Smith makes her first recordings, beginning a 14-year recording career of more than 150 songs.
Ma Rainey records "See See Rider Blues" with Louis Armstrong and Fletcher Henderson.
Son House records for Paramount.
John and Alan Lomax first record Lead Belly while he is imprisoned in the Louisiana State Penitentiary.
Robert Johnson makes the first of his 1936–1937 recordings.
Alan Lomax records Muddy Waters for the Library of Congress.
Muddy Waters, now in Chicago, is recording for the Aristocrat label (later Chess).
Muddy Waters records Willie Dixon's "I'm Your Hoochie Coochie Man."
B.B. King records the album Live at the Regal at Chicago's Regal Theater.
The U.S. Senate marks the centennial of Handy's Tutwiler encounter by declaring 2003 the Year of the Blues.

misconception.myth: W. C. Handy, the "Father of the Blues," invented the blues.
misconception.fact: Handy was a trained bandleader who encountered the blues already being played by Black musicians in the Mississippi Delta around 1903 — a slide guitarist at the Tutwiler station and a string band in Cleveland, Mississippi — and only then worked it into his repertoire. He wrote down and combined fragments of melodies and lyrics he heard from itinerant performers, arranged them as published songs, and made the music a national craze; the "Father of the Blues" title, which he used for his 1941 autobiography, honored him as its popularizer.
misconception.why: Published sheet music, copyrights and an autobiography left a paper trail with Handy's name on it, while the unnamed rural musicians who created the music left almost no written record.

title: Brown v. Board of Education
aliases: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
summary: The unanimous 1954 U.S. Supreme Court decision holding that state laws segregating public schools by race violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, rejecting the "separate but equal" doctrine in public education.

review.question: Why did the NAACP's lawyers value the Kansas case even though Topeka's Black and white schools were roughly comparable in buildings and resources?
review.answer: Because the facilities were substantially comparable, the Kansas case forced the Court to decide whether segregation itself was unconstitutional rather than merely ordering states to equalize unequal schools, and it showed that school segregation was a national issue and not only a Southern one.

review.question: Why was the District of Columbia case, Bolling v. Sharpe, decided separately from the four state cases?
review.answer: The Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause restrains the states, not the federal government, so segregation in the federal capital had to be challenged under the Fifth Amendment instead.

review.question: How did the Court's approach to remedies allow segregation to continue for years after 1954?
review.answer: The 1954 ruling did not say how or when schools must desegregate; Brown II in 1955 left it to federal district courts to proceed "with all deliberate speed," and opponents used that vague standard to delay, admit only token numbers of Black students, pass new segregation laws, or, as in Prince Edward County, close public schools from 1959 to 1964.

timeline.event: Students led by 16-year-old Barbara Rose Johns walk out of the overcrowded Robert Russa Moton High School in Farmville, Virginia.
NAACP lawyers file Davis v. County School Board of Prince Edward County, later joined to Brown.
The Supreme Court hears the first arguments in the consolidated school cases.
Reargument begins on questions the Court posed, including the history of the Fourteenth Amendment and possible remedies.
The Court rules unanimously that segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause; Bolling v. Sharpe is decided the same day.
In Brown II the Court orders desegregation to proceed with all deliberate speed under federal district courts.
The Southern Manifesto denouncing the decision is introduced in Congress.
Prince Edward County, Virginia, cuts off public school funding rather than desegregate.
Prince Edward County's public schools reopen after the Supreme Court's Griffin decision.
Attorneys ask the federal court to reopen the Topeka case to test whether segregation's effects remained (Brown III).

misconception.myth: The case began when Oliver Brown alone sued after his daughter Linda was turned away from a nearby white school and forced to walk far to a Black school.
misconception.fact: The Topeka NAACP deliberately organized a class action with 13 parents on behalf of 20 children; Oliver Brown was recruited to join and named because he was the only man in the group, and the Supreme Court decided Kansas's case together with cases from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and the District of Columbia involving nearly 200 people.
misconception.why: Reducing Brown to one family's story hides the years of organized legal strategy and the many students, parents, teachers and lawyers, in the South and beyond it, who took risks to bring the cases.

title: California Gold Rush
summary: The mass migration to California set off when James Marshall found gold at John Sutter's sawmill on the American River on January 24, 1848; it drew some 300,000 people from across the world by the mid-1850s, sped California to statehood as a free state in 1850, enriched merchants more than most miners, and brought dispossession, forced labor and mass death to Native Californians and discriminatory taxes on foreign miners.

review.question: Why did the Gold Rush bring California into the Union so quickly, and why was its admission controversial?
review.answer: The rush raised California's non-Native population from about 14,000 in 1848 to more than 200,000 by 1852, enough to write a constitution in 1849 and seek statehood; because California would be a free state and part of it lay south of the Missouri Compromise line, its admission as a free state reopened the fight over slavery's expansion and was settled only as part of the Compromise of 1850.

review.question: How did the Gold Rush affect Native Californians?
review.answer: Miners took their land, water and food sources, mining ruined salmon runs, epidemics spread, and the 1850 Act for the Government and Protection of Indians let Native people, including children, be held as indentured laborers; the Native population fell from about 150,000 in the 1840s to under 30,000 by 1870, and in 2019 the state formally apologized for this violence and dispossession.

review.question: Who profited most from the Gold Rush, and why?
review.answer: Merchants and suppliers such as Samuel Brannan and Levi Strauss, because thousands of miners in remote camps had to buy tools, food and clothing at inflated prices, while most miners found little gold and some went bankrupt.

review.question: How did California's foreign miners' taxes work, and whom did they target?
review.answer: A 1850 law charged non-citizen miners $20 a month, aimed mainly at Latin American miners and used by white miners to drive them from rich claims; after its repeal a $4 monthly tax followed, and an 1852 law aimed at Chinese miners, who paid more than $5 million, about a quarter of state revenue, until it was voided in 1870.

timeline.event: James Marshall finds a gold nugget at the sawmill he is building for John Sutter on the South Fork of the American River at Coloma.
California's military commander visits the diggings and finds about 4,000 people collecting gold; Coloma alone has about 4,000 people.
President James K. Polk confirms the reports of gold to Congress and asks for a branch mint in California.
About 25,000 emigrants travel overland to California, the first great year of the rush.
California voters ratify a state constitution, paving the way for statehood.
The legislature imposes a $20-a-month license fee on foreign miners, aimed chiefly at Latin American miners; it is repealed the next year.
The first state legislature passes the Act for the Government and Protection of Indians, allowing Native people to be held as indentured laborers.
California is admitted as the 31st state, free of slavery, as part of the Compromise of 1850.
About 67,000 people arrive in California, 20,000 of them from China, the peak year; a new foreign miners' tax falls mainly on Chinese miners.
The first federal census of California counts about 308,000 residents.
California's Native population has fallen below 30,000; the foreign miners' tax is voided.
James Marshall dies at 75 after decades of setbacks, having once been stranded penniless.
Governor Gavin Newsom formally apologizes on behalf of the State of California to California Native peoples.

misconception.myth: The forty-niners struck it rich; the Gold Rush made ordinary miners wealthy.
misconception.fact: A few miners found fortunes, but most did not; many made modest profits at best, while others went bankrupt or died, and the surest fortunes went to merchants and speculators such as Samuel Brannan and Levi Strauss who sold goods to miners. Even the discoverer, James Marshall, was at one point stranded penniless.
misconception.why: Stories of lucky strikes travelled faster than accounts of hardship, and the "forty-niner" became a romantic symbol of quick wealth in the West.

title: Census and apportionment
aliases: Apportionment of the House of Representatives
summary: The constitutional rule that seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are divided among the states by population, using an "actual Enumeration" of the people taken every ten years; it has been carried out after every census since 1790 except that of 1920.

review.question: Why did the original apportionment formula give slaveholding states extra representation, and how did that change?
review.answer: Article I counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for apportionment though they could not vote, adding seats for slaveholding states; after emancipation the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) counted the whole number of persons, which would have fully counted freed people and so increased Southern power, which is why it added a never-enforced penalty for denying men the vote.

review.question: Why did Washington veto the first apportionment bill in 1792?
review.answer: He judged it unconstitutional because no single ratio produced its allotment and it gave eight states more than one representative per 30,000 people, the Constitution's limit.

review.question: How did the failure to reapportion after the 1920 census change the process?
review.answer: Rural members, fearing a loss of power to fast-growing cities, blocked reapportionment for a decade; the 1929 act responded by making apportionment automatic after each census with the House kept at 435 seats.

review.question: What is the difference between apportionment and redistricting?
review.answer: Apportionment divides the 435 House seats among the states by population; redistricting is each state's redrawing of district boundaries within its borders, using small-area counts the Census Bureau supplies.

timeline.event: The Constitutional Convention votes to tie representation and direct taxes to population, counting enslaved people at three-fifths.
U.S. marshals and their deputies begin the first federal census, which counts 3,929,214 people.
George Washington casts the first presidential veto, rejecting a 120-seat apportionment bill as unconstitutional.
Washington signs a replacement act giving the House 105 seats under Jefferson's method.
Congress begins fixing the size of the House before apportionment and adopts the Vinton (Hamilton) method.
The Fourteenth Amendment replaces the three-fifths formula with a count of the whole number of persons.
Congress fixes the House at 433 seats, plus one each for Arizona and New Mexico on statehood.
The census shows a shift to cities; Congress fails to reapportion for the only time.
The Reapportionment and Census Act makes apportionment automatic after the 1930 census and keeps 435 seats.
The Attorney General concludes that no American Indians remain 'not taxed' for census purposes.
Congress adopts the method of equal proportions for all future apportionments.
In Department of Commerce v. Montana the Supreme Court upholds the equal-proportions method.
The Census Bureau delivers 2020 apportionment counts; Texas gains two seats and seven states lose one.

misconception.myth: The Census Bureau decides how many House seats each state gets and draws the new congressional districts.
misconception.fact: The Bureau counts the population and applies a formula that Congress wrote into law (equal proportions, adopted in 1941); the states then redraw their own district lines using census redistricting data.
misconception.why: Because seat gains and losses are announced by the Census Bureau, the count, the formula and the separate state-run redistricting process are easily blurred together.

title: Cherokee Nation v. Georgia
aliases: The Cherokee Nation v. the State of Georgia
summary: The 1831 U.S. Supreme Court case in which the Cherokee Nation asked the Court to stop Georgia from enforcing its laws on Cherokee land; the Court dismissed the suit for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the Nation was not a foreign state under Article III but one of the "domestic dependent nations" whose relation to the United States resembled that of a ward to a guardian.

review.question: Why did the Supreme Court refuse to hear the Cherokee Nation's suit against Georgia?
review.answer: The Constitution lets the Court hear suits between a state and foreign states, and the majority held that the Cherokee Nation, though a distinct political society, was not a foreign state but a domestic dependent nation, partly because the commerce clause lists foreign nations, states and Indian tribes as separate categories; without jurisdiction it had to dismiss the case.

review.question: How did the 1831 dismissal help set up Worcester v. Georgia?
review.answer: Marshall suggested the land question might be decided in a proper case with proper parties, and when Georgia convicted missionaries such as Samuel Worcester under its license law, their appeal from a state court gave the Supreme Court jurisdiction to rule that Georgia's laws had no force in the Cherokee Nation.

review.question: Why is the case's guardian-and-ward language still important in federal Indian law?
review.answer: Marshall's description of the tribes' relation to the United States as resembling that of a ward to its guardian became a root of the federal trust responsibility, the duty the federal government owes tribes to protect their remaining lands and provide services.

timeline.event: The Cherokee Nation adopts a written constitution modeled on the U.S. Constitution.
Georgia declares the Cherokee government abolished and places Cherokee citizens under state law; gold is found on Cherokee land in the north Georgia mountains.
President Andrew Jackson signs the Indian Removal Act.
The Cherokee Nation's motion for an injunction against Georgia is set for hearing before the Supreme Court; Georgia does not appear.
The Court denies the injunction and dismisses the Cherokee Nation's bill for want of jurisdiction.
In Worcester v. Georgia the Court holds that Georgia's laws have no force within the Cherokee Nation.
A small Cherokee faction without authority under Cherokee law signs the Treaty of New Echota.
President Martin Van Buren orders General Winfield Scott to remove the remaining Cherokees, beginning the Trail of Tears.

misconception.myth: In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia the Supreme Court upheld Georgia's laws and ruled that the Cherokee Nation had no sovereignty.
misconception.fact: The Court never reached the merits; it dismissed the suit because it lacked jurisdiction, while describing the Cherokee Nation as a distinct political society capable of governing itself. A year later Worcester v. Georgia held Georgia's laws void inside the Nation.
misconception.why: Because the Cherokees lost the case and were later forcibly removed, the jurisdictional dismissal is easily remembered as a ruling on Georgia's power or a denial of Cherokee nationhood.

title: Civil rights movement
summary: The mass struggle, led and sustained above all by Black Americans, to end legal segregation and racial discrimination and secure equal citizenship and voting rights; its best-known phase ran from the mid-1950s to 1968 and produced the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

review.question: Why did violence against peaceful protesters in Birmingham and Selma help win federal civil rights laws?
review.answer: Televised attacks on marchers in Birmingham in May 1963 shocked the nation and were followed by Kennedy's civil rights bill, and the 1965 attack in Selma drew national attention that helped persuade Johnson and Congress to pass the Voting Rights Act.

review.question: How did the 1966 Chicago campaign challenge the idea that segregation was only a Southern problem?
review.answer: Chicago activists invited King and SCLC north to fight de facto segregation in housing, schools and employment; marchers met violent hostility in white neighborhoods, and city agencies later failed to carry out the open-housing agreement they had signed.

review.question: How do Jacquelyn Dowd Hall and Sundiata Cha-Jua and Clarence Lang disagree about the movement's time span?
review.answer: Hall argues for a "long" movement beginning in the late 1930s that linked racial and economic justice nationwide, while Cha-Jua and Lang argue that stretching it that far blurs chronology, place and the differences between civil rights and Black Power.

timeline.event: After A. Philip Randolph threatens a march on Washington, Executive Order 8802 bars discrimination in defense industries with government contracts.
Executive Order 9981 directs equal treatment and opportunity in the armed forces regardless of race.
The NAACP's legal campaign against segregated schools culminates in Brown v. Board of Education.
Rosa Parks is arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, setting off the Montgomery bus boycott.
More than sixty ministers meet at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta and form the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.
Four North Carolina A&T students sit in at a segregated Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro; sit-ins spread across the South.
Students found the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee at a conference at Shaw University organized by Ella Baker.
Thirteen Black and white Freedom Riders leave Washington, D.C., to test the desegregation of interstate bus travel.
More than 200,000 people join the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.
Mississippi Freedom Summer begins; James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner are murdered by Klansmen in Neshoba County.
President Lyndon B. Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
State troopers and local officers attack about 600 voting-rights marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama (Bloody Sunday).
Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Stokely Carmichael of SNCC makes Black Power a public slogan at a rally in Greenwood, Mississippi.
The Chicago Freedom Movement reaches an open-housing summit agreement with city officials and lenders.
Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee.
Johnson signs the Civil Rights Act of 1968, known as the Fair Housing Act.

misconception.myth: The civil rights movement was a Southern story, led from the top by Martin Luther King Jr., against a problem confined to the South.
misconception.fact: The movement was built by many organizations and local people, especially students and Black women such as Ella Baker, Diane Nash, Clara Luper and Gloria Richardson, and it confronted segregation in housing, schools and jobs in Northern cities too, as the 1966 Chicago campaign showed.
misconception.why: A story centered on one leader and one region makes the movement look finished and distant, hiding the grassroots organizing that powered it and the national scope of the discrimination it fought.

title: Colorado River
summary: The great river of the American Southwest, flowing about 1,450 miles from the Rocky Mountains of Colorado and Wyoming through the Grand Canyon toward the Gulf of California in Mexico; homeland of many Native nations, it is now divided among seven states, tribes and Mexico by the "Law of the River" and supplies water to nearly 40 million people.

review.question: Why did the 1922 Compact divide the river at Lee Ferry rather than state by state, and what did it promise each side?
review.answer: Herbert Hoover proposed splitting the basin into an Upper and a Lower half; the Compact gave each 7.5 million acre-feet a year (the Lower Basin could add 1 million more) and required the Upper Division not to deplete the flow at Lee Ferry below 75 million acre-feet over any ten years. The Lower Basin's share was divided among Arizona, California and Nevada later, by the 1928 Boulder Canyon Project Act.

review.question: How do tree-ring studies help explain the Colorado River's modern water shortages?
review.answer: They show the Compact was based on an unusually wet period (1905–1930), so the long-term flow (about 13.5 million acre-feet a year in one reconstruction) is far below the 16.5 million acre-feet promised to the two basins plus 1.5 million to Mexico.

review.question: How were Native nations' water rights treated in the Compact and later recognized?
review.answer: No tribe took part in the 1922 negotiations, and the Compact only said it did not affect U.S. obligations to tribes; in Arizona v. California (1963) the Supreme Court applied the 1908 Winters doctrine and held that five lower-river reservations had reserved enough water to irrigate their practicably irrigable land.

timeline.event: Hopi guides lead a party under García López de Cárdenas, part of Coronado's expedition, to the rim of the Grand Canyon.
The Domínguez–Escalante expedition fords the river at the Crossing of the Fathers, now beneath Lake Powell.
The federal government establishes the Colorado River Reservation for the Mohave and Chemehuevi peoples.
John Wesley Powell's expedition launches four boats at Green River, Wyoming; it leaves the Grand Canyon on August 28.
Representatives of seven states and the federal government sign the Colorado River Compact at Santa Fe, New Mexico.
The Boulder Canyon Project Act approves the Compact, authorizes Hoover Dam and divides the Lower Basin's share among Arizona, California and Nevada.
A water treaty with Mexico commits 1.5 million acre-feet a year of the river's flow to Mexico.
In Arizona v. California the Supreme Court settles the Lower Basin division and recognizes reserved water rights for five reservations.
A pulse flow under Minute 319 of the 1944 treaty begins; it eventually reaches the river's estuary in the Gulf of California.
The Bureau of Reclamation declares the first shortage in Lake Mead's history, cutting 2022 deliveries to Arizona, Nevada and Mexico.

misconception.myth: The 1922 Colorado River Compact divided a river whose long-term average flow was well known.
misconception.fact: Negotiators relied on only about 20 years of gauge records; a 1976 tree-ring reconstruction put the 1564–1961 average at about 13.5 million acre-feet a year and found 1905–1930 the wettest such period in 400 years, while the Compact and the 1944 treaty together assigned up to 17.5 million.
misconception.why: The Compact's fixed numbers look like measurements, but they rest on an unusually wet stretch of record, which is a root of today's shortages.

title: Constitutional Convention
summary: The meeting of delegates from twelve states in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787, that was called to revise the Articles of Confederation and instead drafted the United States Constitution.

review.question: Why did the convention end up writing a whole new constitution when Congress had asked only for revisions?
review.answer: Many delegates believed the Articles left the central government too weak; Randolph's Virginia Plan on May 29 proposed a new national legislature, executive and judiciary, and by mid-June the delegates had accepted that they were drafting a new frame of government rather than amending the old one.

review.question: How did the Great Compromise settle the quarrel between large and small states?
review.answer: It gave the House of Representatives seats in proportion to each state's population and gave every state equal representation in the Senate; it passed on July 16, 1787, by a single state's margin.

review.question: How did the convention's decisions strengthen slaveholding states?
review.answer: Counting three-fifths of enslaved people added to slave states' seats in the House and, through the electoral college, their weight in presidential elections; the convention also barred Congress from ending the Atlantic slave trade before 1808 and added a fugitive slave clause.

review.question: Why do historians disagree about whether the Constitution was a proslavery document?
review.answer: Paul Finkelman argues its many protections for slavery made it a proslavery bargain, while Sean Wilentz argues that by refusing to recognise property in people the framers left an opening later antislavery politicians used; critics of Wilentz note that his key Madison quotation may have been added to Madison's notes later.

timeline.event: The Confederation Congress calls a convention to meet in Philadelphia in May to revise the Articles of Confederation.
The convention's scheduled opening day; too few delegations are present, so members adjourn from day to day.
Seven states form a quorum and the delegates unanimously elect George Washington president of the convention.
Edmund Randolph presents the Virginia Plan, and the convention adopts a rule keeping its proceedings secret.
James Wilson and Charles Pinckney propose counting three-fifths of enslaved people for representation.
The convention adopts the three-fifths rule, six states to two with two divided.
The Great (Connecticut) Compromise passes by a margin of one state.
A bargain between New England and Deep South delegates protects the Atlantic slave trade until 1808.
Thirty-eight delegates sign thirty-nine names to the finished Constitution; three present delegates refuse.
Congress unanimously resolves to send the Constitution to the states for ratifying conventions.
Delaware becomes the first state to ratify.
New Hampshire becomes the ninth state to ratify, enough for the Constitution to take effect.

misconception.myth: The delegates were sent to Philadelphia to write a new constitution.
misconception.fact: Congress called the meeting only to revise the Articles of Confederation and report proposed alterations to Congress and the states; the delegates decided on their own, by mid-June 1787, to draft an entirely new frame of government, and their Constitution took effect once nine state conventions had ratified it.
misconception.why: Because the convention's product replaced the Articles completely and is commemorated on September 17, it is easy to assume a new constitution was the assignment from the start, which hides how bold, and how contested, the delegates' decision was.

title: Declaration of Independence
aliases: The unanimous Declaration of the thirteen united States of America
summary: The statement adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, announcing that the thirteen American colonies were free and independent states, setting out a philosophy of natural rights and government by consent, and listing grievances against King George III.

review.question: Why did Congress cut Jefferson's passage blaming the king for the slave trade?
review.answer: Jefferson recorded that it was struck to accommodate South Carolina and Georgia, which wanted the slave trade to continue, and that some Northern delegates were uneasy because Northern merchants had carried enslaved people; the deletion kept those delegations behind independence.

review.question: How did declaring independence help the American war effort abroad?
review.answer: France would consider a formal alliance only once the colonies declared independence, so the Declaration opened the way to recognition and to the 1778 Treaty of Alliance with France, followed by Dutch recognition in 1782 and British acknowledgement in the 1783 Treaty of Paris.

review.question: Why is July 4 not the day the Declaration was signed?
review.answer: July 4 was the day Congress approved the text; the signing copy was only ordered on July 19, and most delegates signed it on August 2, 1776, with others signing later.

review.question: How did later reformers use the Declaration's language?
review.answer: The women who met at Seneca Falls in 1848 modelled their Declaration of Sentiments on it, declaring that all men and women are created equal, and Frederick Douglass in 1852 measured the nation's celebration of independence against the slavery it still allowed.

timeline.event: Richard Henry Lee of Virginia moves in Congress that the colonies are, and ought to be, free and independent states.
The drafting committee presents Jefferson's draft, edited by Adams and Franklin, to Congress.
A first vote on Lee's resolution: nine colonies in favour, Pennsylvania and South Carolina opposed, Delaware deadlocked and New York abstaining.
Twelve colonies vote for independence, with New York abstaining.
Congress approves the revised text and orders it printed; John Dunlap prints about 200 broadsides.
John Nixon gives the first public reading in the State House Yard in Philadelphia.
Congress orders the text engrossed on parchment under a new title for members to sign.
John Hancock and most of the delegates sign the engrossed parchment.
Congress authorizes a printing that carries the signers' names for the first time.

misconception.myth: The delegates signed the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776.
misconception.fact: Congress approved the text on July 4, but it ordered a parchment copy for signing only on July 19; most delegates signed on August 2, 1776, a few signed later that year, and Thomas McKean signed sometime after January 1777.
misconception.why: Later recollections by Jefferson and Adams placed the signing on July 4, and the copies printed that week carried only the names of John Hancock and Charles Thomson, so the date of approval and the act of signing blurred together in popular memory.

title: Department of Homeland Security
aliases: United States Department of Homeland Security
summary: The Cabinet-level executive department created by the Homeland Security Act of 2002 after the September 11 attacks, which took effect on January 24, 2003, and combined 22 federal agencies, among them the Customs Service, the Coast Guard, the Secret Service, FEMA, the TSA and the functions of the abolished Immigration and Naturalization Service.

review.question: Why did the Bush administration move from a White House office to a full Cabinet department for homeland security?
review.answer: The Office of Homeland Security created in October 2001 coordinated agencies but many observers doubted it had the authority to overcome bureaucratic obstacles; with Congress already drafting a department bill, Bush reversed course in June 2002 and proposed a permanent department that would combine the agencies directly.

review.question: How did the creation of DHS change the federal government's handling of immigration?
review.answer: The act abolished the Justice Department's Immigration and Naturalization Service and split its work among three DHS agencies — Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services — separating enforcement from the processing of visas and naturalization.

review.question: Why did Congress reorganize FEMA in 2006?
review.answer: The response to Hurricane Katrina in August 2005 exposed gaps in federal emergency management, so the Post-Katrina Emergency Management Reform Act gave FEMA substantial new authority and a stronger preparedness mission within the department.

timeline.event: The Hart-Rudman Commission proposes a National Homeland Security Agency to consolidate nearly two dozen agencies.
Executive Order 13228 creates the White House Office of Homeland Security and the Homeland Security Council.
Senator Joseph Lieberman introduces S. 1534, an early bill for a homeland security department.
President George W. Bush, reversing his earlier position, proposes a Cabinet-level department in an address to the nation.
The House passes H.R. 5005, 295–132.
The Senate passes the amended bill, 90–9; the House agrees to it on November 22.
Bush signs the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-296).
The act takes effect and the department comes into existence.
FEMA and 21 other organizations formally join the department.
Secretary Michael Chertoff's Second Stage Review leads to a major internal reorganization.
Bush signs the Post-Katrina Emergency Management Reform Act, reorganizing FEMA after Hurricane Katrina.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Act creates CISA within the department.

misconception.myth: The Department of Homeland Security took over the FBI and the CIA when it was created.
misconception.fact: The FBI and CIA stayed outside the new department; the 2002 act transferred only the FBI's National Infrastructure Protection Center and allowed FBI and CIA analysts to be detailed to DHS, and President Bush considered folding in the FBI but decided against it.
misconception.why: The department was sold as the answer to the intelligence-sharing failures before 9/11, so many people assume it absorbed the main intelligence agencies; the later Director of National Intelligence and counterterrorism center were separate reforms.

title: Desegregation of Little Rock Central High School
summary: The 1957–58 confrontation in Little Rock, Arkansas, in which Governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to keep nine Black students out of all-white Central High School until President Dwight D. Eisenhower sent federal troops to enforce a federal court's desegregation order.

review.question: Why did President Eisenhower send federal troops to Little Rock even though he was reluctant to act as a civil rights champion?
review.answer: He framed the deployment as enforcing the orders of federal courts against mob obstruction, arguing that if the executive did not uphold court rulings the rule of law would collapse; he also worried that the crisis was damaging America's standing abroad during the Cold War.

review.question: How did the Little Rock crisis lead to Cooper v. Aaron, and what did the Court decide?
review.answer: After a year of turmoil the school board sought to suspend its desegregation plan; in September 1958 the Supreme Court unanimously refused, holding under the Supremacy Clause that state officials cannot nullify federal court orders based on Brown or war against the Constitution they swore to support.

review.question: Why do historians disagree about Governor Orval Faubus's motives?
review.answer: Before 1957 he was seen as a racial moderate who had hired Black state employees and supported Black colleges, so his biographer argues his stand was a political calculation to win re-election in 1958, while some observers insisted catering to segregationists was out of character for him; many voters rewarded him for appearing to stand up to the federal government.

timeline.event: The Supreme Court rules in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated public schools are unconstitutional.
The Little Rock School Board adopts Superintendent Virgil Blossom's gradual plan, beginning with token desegregation of Central High in 1957.
Federal judge Ronald Davies voids a state court injunction against integration and orders the district to proceed.
Governor Orval Faubus announces on television that he has called out the Arkansas National Guard.
Guardsmen turn the Black students away; fifteen-year-old Elizabeth Eckford walks alone past a jeering crowd.
Faubus and Eisenhower meet at Newport, Rhode Island, without reaching agreement.
Judge Davies orders Faubus and the Guard to stop interfering, and Faubus withdraws the troops.
The students enter Central, but a mob of more than 1,000 forms outside and they are taken out by lunchtime; Eisenhower issues Proclamation 3204.
Eisenhower signs Executive Order 10730, federalizing the Arkansas Guard and sending in the 101st Airborne Division.
Escorted by federal troops, the Little Rock Nine attend their first full day of classes.
The 101st Airborne returns to Fort Campbell, leaving federalized Guard units in charge for the rest of the year.
Minnijean Brown is expelled after retaliating against harassment.
Ernest Green becomes the first Black student to graduate from Central High.

misconception.myth: Once federal troops escorted the Little Rock Nine into Central High in September 1957, the school and the city's schools were desegregated and the crisis was over.
misconception.fact: Troops stayed all year while the Nine faced daily harassment and one of them was expelled; in September 1958 Faubus closed all four Little Rock high schools under a new state law, voters backed closure three to one, and the schools did not reopen until August 1959.
misconception.why: The famous images of paratroopers escorting the students compress a multi-year struggle into one moment of victory and hide how long and how deliberately segregationists resisted after the troops arrived.

title: Dred Scott v. Sandford
summary: The 1857 U.S. Supreme Court decision that rejected Dred Scott's claim to freedom, declared in Chief Justice Roger B. Taney's opinion that Black Americans could not be citizens of the United States, and struck down the Missouri Compromise's ban on slavery in federal territories.

review.question: Why did Dred Scott's case end up in federal court after he lost in the Missouri Supreme Court?
review.answer: Scott sued John F. A. Sanford, Irene Emerson's brother and the executor of John Emerson's estate, who was a citizen of New York; because the parties lived in different states, Scott could sue under the federal courts' diversity jurisdiction, which raised the question of whether he was a citizen at all.

review.question: How did the Court's ruling on citizenship let it avoid deciding Scott's case on the merits, and why did it go further anyway?
review.answer: Holding that Scott was not a citizen meant the federal courts lacked jurisdiction and the case had to be dismissed; but after re-argument the majority also ruled that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, partly because dissenting justices planned to argue that Congress had that power.

review.question: How did the decision deepen the sectional crisis before the Civil War?
review.answer: It made the Republican goal of keeping slavery out of the territories unconstitutional, which Republicans saw as proof of the Slave Power's reach, and it undercut Stephen Douglas's popular sovereignty, prompting his Freeport Doctrine, which alienated Southern Democrats and helped split the Democratic Party.

review.question: Which constitutional change reversed the decision's ruling on citizenship?
review.answer: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, whose first sentence made all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens, following the Civil Rights Act of 1866.

timeline.event: Dr. John Emerson, an army surgeon, takes the enslaved Dred Scott to Fort Armstrong in the free state of Illinois.
Emerson is transferred to Fort Snelling in the Wisconsin Territory, where the Missouri Compromise barred slavery; there Scott marries Harriet Robinson.
Dred and Harriet Scott file separate freedom suits against Irene Emerson in the St. Louis Circuit Court.
The first trial ends against the Scotts on a technicality, and their lawyer wins a new trial.
A St. Louis jury finds the Scotts free.
The Missouri Supreme Court reverses, rejecting the principle of once free, always free.
In the federal suit against John F. A. Sanford, Judge Robert W. Wells rules that Missouri law governs and finds for Sanford.
The U.S. Supreme Court hears the first oral argument; it orders re-argument, held in December 1856.
In his inaugural address, President James Buchanan says he will submit to the Court's coming decision.
The Court rules 7 to 2 against Scott, with Chief Justice Roger B. Taney delivering the opinion of the Court.
Taylor Blow emancipates Dred and Harriet Scott.
Dred Scott dies of tuberculosis in St. Louis.
Congress bans slavery in all western territories, undoing the decision's holding on territorial slavery.
The Fourteenth Amendment's citizenship clause makes all persons born in the United States citizens, overturning the decision's citizenship holding.

misconception.myth: Dred Scott v. Sandford was the first time the Supreme Court struck down an act of Congress.
misconception.fact: The first was Marbury v. Madison in 1803; Dred Scott was the first time since then that the Court invalidated a federal statute, the Missouri Compromise's restriction on slavery.
misconception.why: Remembering it as the second use of judicial review against Congress, after a 54-year gap, shows how unusual and consequential the Court's choice to rule on territorial slavery was.

title: Due process
summary: The constitutional guarantee, in the Fifth Amendment (binding the federal government) and the Fourteenth Amendment (binding the states), that no person may be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law: fair procedures such as notice and a hearing, and, as the courts have read it, some protection for fundamental rights as well.

review.question: Why does the Constitution contain two Due Process Clauses?
review.answer: The Fifth Amendment's clause was held in Barron v. Baltimore (1833) to bind only the federal government, so after the Civil War the Fourteenth Amendment (ratified 1868) added a parallel clause forbidding the states to deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law.

review.question: How does a court decide how much process is "due" when the government ends someone's benefits?
review.answer: Under Mathews v. Eldridge (1976) it balances three factors, the private interest affected, the risk of an erroneous deprivation under the procedures used, and the government's interest, against a baseline of notice and an opportunity to be heard.

review.question: Why is substantive due process more controversial than procedural due process or incorporation?
review.answer: Critics argue the clause's text guarantees lawful procedure, not limits on what laws may say, and note the doctrine's roots in Dred Scott and Lochner; defenders answer that more than a century of precedent and the Ninth Amendment support protecting unenumerated rights, and that the real question is how judges should identify them.

timeline.event: Magna Carta promises that free men will be judged by their peers or by the law of the land.
An English statute restating Magna Carta first uses the phrase "due process of law."
Sir Edward Coke's Second Institutes equates "law of the land" with "due process of law," shaping the founders' understanding.
Maryland's and Virginia's new constitutions adopt Magna Carta's "law of the land" protections.
Congress proposes twelve amendments, including the article containing the Due Process Clause.
Ratification of the Bill of Rights adds the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause to the Constitution.
New York becomes the first state to write "due process of law" into its own constitution.
Barron v. Baltimore holds that the Fifth Amendment and the rest of the Bill of Rights limit only the federal government.
In Dred Scott the Court suggests that freeing an enslaved man would deprive his owner of property without due process.
Ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment extends a due process guarantee against the states.
Lochner v. New York strikes down a workplace regulation on "freedom of contract" grounds.
West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish repudiates the Lochner approach to economic regulation.
Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank sets minimum requirements of notice, a hearing and an impartial tribunal.
Mathews v. Eldridge adopts a three-factor balancing test for the process due in civil proceedings.

misconception.myth: Due process is only about criminal trials.
misconception.fact: The clauses protect against any government deprivation of life, liberty, or property, including civil and administrative actions such as cutting off government benefits (Goldberg v. Kelly, 1970; Mathews v. Eldridge, 1976), and courts weigh how much process each situation requires.
