misconception.why: The most familiar procedural rights, such as indictment, jury trial and counsel, sit beside due process in the Fifth and Sixth Amendments, so people assume the clause belongs only to the courtroom.

title: Dust Bowl
summary: The drought and severe wind erosion that struck the Southern Great Plains in the 1930s, when dust storms stripped topsoil from plowed land in parts of Kansas, Colorado, New Mexico and the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, deepening the Great Depression and prompting federal soil-conservation programs.

review.question: Why did drought in the 1930s produce such severe dust storms on the Southern Plains?
review.answer: Between about 1909 and 1929 farmers had broken some 32 million acres of native sod, much of it for wheat; when drought killed the crops from 1931, bare plowed fields lost the grass roots that had held the soil, and high winds lifted it away.

review.question: How did the Dust Bowl change federal policy?
review.answer: Dust clouds reaching Washington in 1934 and 1935 helped Hugh Hammond Bennett persuade Congress to pass the Soil Conservation Act of 1935, which created the permanent Soil Conservation Service; it promoted terracing, strip cropping and grass seeding and led to locally run soil conservation districts.

review.question: Why do historians disagree about the causes of the Dust Bowl?
review.answer: Donald Worster argued that a market-driven plow-up of marginal grassland made it a human-made ecological disaster, while later researchers using county data and climate models stress that dust storms are natural in long Plains droughts, that the heaviest wheat areas were not always the worst hit, and that ocean temperatures drove the drought.

review.question: Were most migrants who went to California from the Dust Bowl itself?
review.answer: No. Of roughly half a million Southern Plains migrants, many were tenant farmers from Arkansas, Missouri, eastern Oklahoma and East Texas displaced by economic forces rather than drought.

timeline.event: Over the next two decades farmers break about 32 million acres of Great Plains sod, much of it for wheat.
Drought ruins the Southern Plains wheat crop in the autumn, leaving fields bare.
By late January winds are lifting loose soil into dust storms.
The Soil Erosion Service is set up in the Interior Department with Hugh Hammond Bennett as chief.
A great dust storm carries Plains soil over Washington, D.C., and out over the Atlantic.
A second March dust cloud darkens Washington as Congress holds hearings on soil conservation.
Black Sunday: a dust front sweeps from central Nebraska toward the Mexican border; a reporter's account names the Dust Bowl.
Roosevelt signs the Soil Conservation Act, creating the permanent Soil Conservation Service in the Agriculture Department.
In a fireside chat Roosevelt reports on his tour of nine drought states and outlines work relief and land-use plans.
The first soil conservation district is organized, in North Carolina's Brown Creek watershed.
With near-normal rain returning from 1938, the drought ends.

misconception.myth: The "Okies" who poured into California in the 1930s were mostly farm families blown out of the Dust Bowl.
misconception.fact: Dust Bowl refugees were only part of a migration of roughly half a million people from several Southern Plains states; many came from Arkansas, Missouri, eastern Oklahoma and East Texas, where tenant farmers were pushed off the land by falling prices, foreclosures and landlords using federal crop payments to mechanize and evict them.
misconception.why: John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath and Depression-era photographs fused the dust storms and the westward migration into one story, and Californians labelled all the newcomers "Okies".

title: E pluribus unum
summary: The Latin motto "E pluribus unum" ("Out of many, one"), first proposed for a national seal in August 1776 and adopted on the Great Seal of the United States in 1782, where it refers to the union of the states; federal law still requires it on U.S. coins, though it was never designated the national motto.

review.question: Why does the Great Seal's motto describe "many" becoming "one", and what did the "many" originally mean?
review.answer: In 1776 and 1782 the motto referred to the thirteen states joining in one union; Du Simitière's design ringed the shield with thirteen escutcheons for the states, and the official 1782 remarks say the motto alludes to the union of the states under Congress.

review.question: How did a motto from a London magazine end up on the seal, and why is it uncertain who chose it?
review.answer: The phrase was printed on the title page of the widely read Gentleman's Magazine, which educated colonists knew. It first appears in the seal record in Du Simitière's August 1776 design for the Franklin-Adams-Jefferson committee, but no document says who suggested it, so the State Department credits Du Simitière, Deutsch argued for Franklin, and the Jefferson Papers editors leave it open.

review.question: Why is it inaccurate to say "In God We Trust" replaced E pluribus unum as the national motto in 1956?
review.answer: E pluribus unum had never been designated the national motto by law. The 1956 act was the first to declare a national motto, and E pluribus unum remained on the Great Seal and is still required by law on the reverse of every U.S. coin.

timeline.event: Pierre Motteux's London Gentleman's Journal carries the motto, the earliest printing Deutsch traced; the Gentleman's Magazine later puts it on its title page.
The Continental Congress appoints Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and Thomas Jefferson as a committee to design a seal.
The committee reports a design drawn up with artist Pierre Eugène Du Simitière bearing the motto E PLURIBUS UNUM; Congress tables it.
A second committee, advised by Francis Hopkinson, adds the 13 stripes, 13 stars and olive branch but produces no accepted seal.
Congress hands the work of all three committees to its secretary, Charles Thomson, who puts the motto on a scroll in the eagle's beak.
The Confederation Congress adopts the Great Seal with the motto.
Franklin D. Roosevelt approves a one-dollar bill design showing both sides of the Great Seal, putting the motto on the back of the note.
An act of Congress declares 'In God we trust' the national motto; E pluribus unum stays on the seal and coins.
Congress reenacts the national-motto statute without changing its wording.

misconception.myth: E pluribus unum was the official national motto of the United States until 1956, when Congress replaced it with "In God We Trust."
misconception.fact: E pluribus unum has been the motto of the Great Seal since 1782 and is a required coin inscription, but no statute designated it the national motto; the 1956 act declaring "In God we trust" is the law that names one, and E pluribus unum stayed on the seal and coins.
misconception.why: The phrase appeared on the seal, coins and the dollar bill for so long that it was widely treated as the country's motto, and even an editor's note on the online edition of a 1923 scholarly study says it was replaced in 1956.

title: Equal protection
summary: The constitutional guarantee, in the Fourteenth Amendment's command that no state "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws," that government may not draw arbitrary or invidious distinctions among the people it governs.

review.question: Why did the framers of the Fourteenth Amendment write an equal protection guarantee into the Constitution rather than rely on ordinary legislation?
review.answer: They wanted to give civil rights measures such as the Civil Rights Act of 1866 a constitutional footing that a later simple majority in Congress could not repeal, so that the equal legal standing of formerly enslaved people could not be undone by shifting politics.

review.question: How can two laws that both classify people be judged so differently under the Equal Protection Clause?
review.answer: Courts apply different levels of review depending on the classification. Most laws need only a rational relationship to a legitimate interest, but a law that sorts people by race (a suspect classification) or burdens a fundamental right must survive strict scrutiny, meaning it must be narrowly tailored to a compelling government interest.

timeline.event: The House approves the proposed Fourteenth Amendment, 120-32, carrying the equal protection language.
Ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment writes the Equal Protection Clause into the Constitution.
The Slaughter-House Cases recognize formerly enslaved African Americans as the clause's primary intended beneficiaries while noting its words reach everyone.
Yick Wo v. Hopkins applies equal protection beyond race to discriminatory enforcement of an ordinance.
Brown v. Board of Education holds that segregated public schools violate equal protection.
Reed v. Reed applies heightened review to a sex-based classification for the first time.
Craig v. Boren sets the intermediate-scrutiny standard for sex classifications.
Obergefell v. Hodges holds that state bans on same-sex marriage violate the clause.

misconception.myth: The Equal Protection Clause forbids government from ever treating people differently.
misconception.fact: Governments classify people constantly, by age, income, or occupation, and most such lines stand if they are "rationally related to a legitimate state interest"; only suspect classifications such as race, or laws burdening fundamental rights, face the demanding test of strict scrutiny.
misconception.why: Equal protection requires equal treatment of those who are "similarly situated," not identical treatment of everyone, so the real question a court asks is which differences a law may lawfully draw on.

title: Fifteenth Amendment
aliases: Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
summary: The 1870 amendment to the U.S. Constitution that bars the United States and the states from denying or abridging citizens' right to vote "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude," and gives Congress power to enforce that ban; the last of the three Reconstruction Amendments.

review.question: Why could Southern states keep most Black men from voting for decades even though the Fifteenth Amendment was in force?
review.answer: The amendment only barred denial of the vote on account of race, color or previous servitude and left states free to set other qualifications, so states used poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses and discriminatory administration, while 1876 Supreme Court rulings such as United States v. Reese weakened federal enforcement.

review.question: How did the amendment divide the women's rights movement?
review.answer: Because it protected against racial but not sex discrimination, Lucy Stone and Frederick Douglass supported it as a first step while Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed any amendment that excluded women; the American Equal Rights Association broke up in 1869 and two rival suffrage organizations formed.

review.question: How is the Voting Rights Act of 1965 connected to the Fifteenth Amendment?
review.answer: The Act used the enforcement power in the amendment's Section 2; President Johnson asked Congress for a law that would make it impossible to thwart the amendment, and the Act abolished remaining barriers and authorized federal supervision of registration.

timeline.event: Congress enfranchises Black men in the District of Columbia and the territories and requires seceded states to guarantee Black male suffrage as a condition of readmission.
Representative George Boutwell proposes a suffrage amendment in the House.
After a conference committee narrows the text to racial discrimination, Congress gives final approval (House 144 to 44, Senate 39 to 13).
The American Equal Rights Association splits over the amendment's omission of women at its annual meeting.
The amendment is ratified by three-fourths of the states.
Black Baltimoreans hold a parade celebrating ratification.
United States v. Reese and United States v. Cruikshank narrow federal enforcement.
Southern states begin adopting grandfather clauses that exempt mostly white voters from literacy tests.
Guinn v. United States unanimously strikes down Oklahoma's grandfather clause.
Lane v. Wilson holds that the amendment reaches subtle as well as overt discrimination.
President Lyndon B. Johnson asks Congress for a law to make the amendment impossible to evade.
Rice v. Cayetano holds that the amendment protects all persons and that ancestry can serve as a proxy for race.
The Supreme Court strikes down a key federal oversight provision of the Voting Rights Act.

misconception.myth: The Fifteenth Amendment gave all Black Americans the right to vote in 1870.
misconception.fact: The amendment only forbade denying the vote because of race, color or previous servitude; it conferred no right of suffrage on anyone, did not cover sex, so Black women were still excluded, and left states free to impose poll taxes, literacy tests and other qualifications that Southern states used to disfranchise most Black men until federal enforcement under the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
misconception.why: Treating 1870 as the moment Black Americans won the vote hides nearly a century of disfranchisement and explains poorly why the civil rights movement still had to fight for the ballot in the 1960s.

title: Fourteenth Amendment
aliases: Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
summary: The 1868 amendment to the U.S. Constitution that made all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens and barred states from denying any person due process of law or the equal protection of the laws; it also reshaped representation, barred certain former officials who joined the rebellion from office, and settled Civil War debts.

review.question: What problems was the amendment meant to solve after the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery?
review.answer: Southern states were passing Black Codes to limit freed people's rights while white southerners terrorized them, and Dred Scott's rule still denied Black Americans citizenship; the amendment made all persons born or naturalized in the country citizens, barred states from denying due process or equal protection, and gave Congress power to enforce those guarantees.

review.question: How did the Slaughter-House Cases change what the amendment meant in practice?
review.answer: The Court held that the Privileges or Immunities Clause protected only rights of national citizenship, leaving most rights to the states and turning the clause into a practical nullity, so later protection of Bill of Rights guarantees against the states came instead through the Due Process Clause, case by case.

review.question: Why were former Confederate states required to ratify the amendment?
review.answer: White southerners rejected it almost unanimously in 1866 and 1867; after Northern voters backed Republicans in the 1866 elections, Congress made ratification a condition for restoring a state's representation, and Southern ratifications in 1868 completed the three-fourths.

review.question: Who was left out of the citizenship clause at first, and how did that change?
review.answer: Native people under tribal rather than U.S. authority were excluded, and Elk v. Wilkins (1884) held that Native Americans were not U.S. citizens even after leaving their nations; Congress made all Native Americans citizens only with the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924.

timeline.event: Congress creates the Joint Committee of Fifteen on Reconstruction.
Congress passes the Civil Rights Act of 1866.
The Senate passes the amendment, 33 to 11.
The House passes the amendment, 120 to 32.
The joint resolution is submitted to the states.
The Reconstruction Act places former Confederate states except Tennessee under military districts.
Louisiana and South Carolina ratify, completing the three-fourths needed.
Secretary of State William H. Seward certifies ratification by 28 states.
The Slaughter-House Cases narrow the Privileges or Immunities Clause.
Minor v. Happersett holds that citizenship does not carry a right to vote.
Elk v. Wilkins holds that Native Americans who had left their nations were still not U.S. citizens.
United States v. Wong Kim Ark applies birthright citizenship to a U.S.-born son of Chinese parents.
The Indian Citizenship Act makes Native Americans U.S. citizens.

misconception.myth: By making women citizens, the Fourteenth Amendment gave them the right to vote.
misconception.fact: Section 2 penalized states only for denying the vote to male citizens, and in Minor v. Happersett (1875) the Supreme Court held that citizenship did not carry the right to vote; women won a constitutional guarantee only with the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.
misconception.why: Assuming citizenship and voting rights always went together hides how long women, and Native Americans after the 1924 citizenship act, were citizens who could still be kept from the polls.

title: Frederick Douglass
summary: An abolitionist, orator, editor and public official (c. 1818–1895) who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the most prominent Black American voice of the nineteenth century, campaigning against slavery, for Black citizenship and voting rights, and for women's rights.

review.question: Why did publishing his Narrative in 1845 put Douglass in danger, and how was that danger resolved?
review.answer: The book named the people and places of his enslavement, exposing him as a fugitive who could be seized; he toured Britain and Ireland, where supporters raised $711.66 to buy his freedom from Hugh Auld, so he returned to the United States legally free in 1847.

review.question: How did Douglass's view of the Constitution change, and why does it matter?
review.answer: He first held William Lloyd Garrison's view that the Constitution was a proslavery compact, but between about 1848 and 1852 came to read it as an antislavery document; that let him work through politics and the law against slavery and broke his alliance with Garrison.

review.question: Why did Douglass support the Fifteenth Amendment even though it did not enfranchise women?
review.answer: He backed women's suffrage, but argued in 1869 that for Black Americans in the former slave states the vote was a matter of life and death, so Black men's voting rights could not wait for a separate women's amendment.

timeline.event: Born Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey in Talbot County, Maryland, according to a later ledger notation; he himself believed he was born about 1817.
Sent to Baltimore to live with Hugh and Sophia Auld, where he begins learning to read.
Hired out to Edward Covey, a so-called slave breaker, and fights back against his beatings.
Escapes to New York disguised as a sailor, using a free Black sailor's papers and a ticket paid for by Anna Murray.
Marries Anna Murray in New York; the couple settles in New Bedford, Massachusetts, as the Douglasses.
Hired as a lecturer by the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society.
Publishes Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass and begins a lecture tour of Britain and Ireland.
Returns legally free after supporters pay Hugh Auld $711.66; launches the North Star in Rochester, New York.
Seconds Elizabeth Cady Stanton's suffrage resolution at the Seneca Falls women's rights convention.
Delivers "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" at Corinthian Hall, Rochester.
Meets President Lincoln to protest unequal pay and treatment of Black soldiers.
At the American Equal Rights Association meeting, argues that Black men's voting rights are a matter of life and death.
Appointed U.S. marshal for the District of Columbia by President Hayes.
Appointed U.S. minister resident and consul general to Haiti, serving until 1891.
Dies at Cedar Hill, his Washington home, after attending a meeting of the National Council of Women.

misconception.myth: Douglass was born on February 14, 1818, a birthday recorded at the time.
misconception.fact: No record gives the day. Douglass believed he was born about 1817; a ledger kept by his enslaver Aaron Anthony notes February 1818, possibly added later, and Douglass chose February 14 to celebrate.
misconception.why: Enslaved people were routinely denied knowledge of their own birthdays, and the uncertainty is itself evidence of what slavery took from them.

title: Gatun Locks
summary: The three-step flight of paired lock chambers at the Atlantic end of the Panama Canal, built by the United States between 1909 and 1913, which uses gravity-fed water from Gatun Lake to raise and lower ships about 85 feet between the Caribbean Sea and the lake.

review.question: Why do the Gatun Locks need no pumps to raise a ship?
review.answer: Gatun Lake sits about 85 feet above sea level, so opening valves lets lake water flow down by gravity through 18-foot culverts and up through 100 floor holes per chamber, filling a chamber in about eight minutes; emptying it reverses the process.

review.question: Why does every transit through the Gatun Locks depend on Gatun Lake?
review.answer: The lake supplies the water that fills each chamber, roughly 26.7 million gallons per filling and about 52 million gallons of fresh water per ship, while the Gatun Dam that holds the lake also generated electricity for canal operations, including the gates.

review.question: Why did the United States begin, and then stop, a third set of locks near Gatun?
review.answer: By 1939 ships, especially warships, were growing too wide for the 110-foot chambers and officials feared one act of sabotage could close the canal, so Congress authorized larger locks; excavation ran from 1940 until Secretary of War Stimson ended it on May 23, 1942, as wartime money shifted elsewhere.

review.question: Who did much of the dangerous work of building the lock gates?
review.answer: Rivet gangs made up mostly of West Indian workers, who under the canal's segregated gold-and-silver-roll system did some of the riskiest jobs, drove more than six million rivets into the canal's hollow steel gates.

timeline.event: Workers pour the first concrete at the Gatun lock site.
Erection of the upper lock gates at Gatun gets under way.
Concreting of the canal's locks is completed.
The tug Gatun makes the first trial lockage, with valves worked by hand.
The Gamboa dike is destroyed, joining Gatun Lake with the Culebra Cut.
The Ancon makes the canal's first official transit.
Excavation begins for a wider third set of locks near the existing ones.
Secretary of War Henry Stimson terminates the Third Locks Project.
The inaugural transit of the expanded canal begins at the new Agua Clara Locks on the Atlantic side.

misconception.myth: Giant pumps lift ships up through the Panama Canal's locks.
misconception.fact: No pumps are used; valves let fresh water from Gatun Lake flow down by gravity through culverts in the lock walls and up through holes in the chamber floors, and to lower a ship the chamber is drained downward through the same culverts.
misconception.why: The scale of the lift suggests heavy machinery, but the system's real limit is the supply of lake water, about 52 million gallons for each ship that transits.

title: George Washington
summary: A Virginia planter, surveyor and soldier (1732–1799) who commanded the Continental Army in the American Revolutionary War, presided over the Constitutional Convention and served as the first president of the United States (1789–1797), setting many precedents of the office while enslaving hundreds of people at Mount Vernon.

review.question: Why did Washington's will free only 123 of the 317 enslaved people living at Mount Vernon in 1799?
review.answer: Only 123 belonged to him; 153 were "dower" slaves from the estate of Martha Washington's first husband, which neither spouse could legally free and which passed to the Custis grandchildren, and 40 more were rented from a neighbor.

review.question: How did the Western Confederacy's victory over Arthur St. Clair in 1791 change Washington's frontier policy?
review.answer: After more than 630 of St. Clair's roughly 930 soldiers were killed, Washington and Congress built a larger, professionally trained Legion of the United States under Anthony Wayne, which won at Fallen Timbers in 1794 and forced the 1795 Treaty of Greenville cessions.

review.question: Why do historians disagree about whether Washington stood above party politics?
review.answer: He warned in his Farewell Address against the spirit of party and never joined a party, yet he sided with Hamilton against Jefferson and, in Encyclopedia Virginia's account, led a Federalist faction that voters rejected in 1800.

timeline.event: Born at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia (February 11 under the Julian calendar then in use).
Surrenders Fort Necessity to French forces, a clash that helped open the Seven Years' War.
Takes his seat in the Virginia House of Burgesses, weeks after marrying Martha Dandridge Custis.
The Second Continental Congress appoints him commander in chief of the new Continental Army.
Crosses the Delaware on Christmas night and wins at Trenton, then at Princeton days later.
Lord Cornwallis surrenders the British army at Yorktown, Virginia.
Resigns his commission to Congress at Annapolis, Maryland.
Elected president of the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia.
Takes the oath as the first president at Federal Hall in New York City.
Western Confederacy warriors led by Little Turtle rout Arthur St. Clair's army on the Wabash.
Issues a proclamation of neutrality in the war between France and Britain.
His Farewell Address appears in a Philadelphia newspaper.
Leaves office after two terms.
Dies at Mount Vernon of an acute throat infection.
The 123 people Washington enslaved become free under his will, after Martha Washington signs a deed of manumission.

misconception.myth: George Washington wore wooden false teeth.
misconception.fact: Mount Vernon finds no wood in any of his dentures; they were made of human teeth, ivory, metal and probably cow and horse teeth, and staining could make them look like wood.
misconception.why: The myth hides a harder story, since some of the human teeth available to him may have come from enslaved people at Mount Vernon.

title: Gilded Age
summary: The period of U.S. history from roughly 1870 to 1900, named after Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner's 1873 satire, when railroads, factories, cities and immigration grew at unprecedented speed while wealth concentrated, labor conflict sharpened, and Black, Native, Chinese and working-class Americans faced disfranchisement, dispossession and exclusion.

review.question: Why did Twain and Warner's title become the name of a whole era?
review.answer: Their 1873 novel satirized postwar corruption, and "gilded" captured the contrast historians still see between dazzling new wealth and progress on the surface and deep inequality and corruption underneath.

review.question: How did rapid industrialization lead to the labor conflicts of the period?
review.answer: Railroads and large corporations grew fast while wealth concentrated at the top, wages stayed low and work was often seasonal; fewer workers could expect to become independent, so many joined unions such as the Knights of Labor, and more than 20,000 strikes and lockouts followed, often broken by private guards, militia or federal troops.

review.question: Why do some historians, such as Rebecca Edwards, argue that "Gilded Age" is a poor label?
review.answer: The name was meant as an indictment of the elite, so it focuses attention on robber barons and corrupt politicians and misses the grassroots ferment of the period, from farmers' alliances and unions to women's organizations and Black activism.

timeline.event: Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner publish The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today, a satire of postwar corruption that gives the era its name.
The Great Railroad Strike spreads from Baltimore to St. Louis; about 100 people die before federal troops end it.
Henry George publishes Progress and Poverty, a bestselling critique of inequality.
President Chester A. Arthur signs the Chinese Exclusion Act, barring Chinese laborers for ten years.
Congress passes the Pendleton Civil Service Act, two years after President James Garfield's assassination.
A bomb at a labor rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square kills seven policemen; four anarchists are later hanged.
Congress approves the Dawes Act, dividing reservation land held in common into individual allotments.
The Homestead strike is broken at Carnegie's Pennsylvania steel works; the People's Party adopts its Omaha Platform; Ida B. Wells publishes Southern Horrors.
Federal troops break the Pullman sympathy strike led by the American Railway Union, and Eugene Debs is jailed.
William McKinley, backed by business and the gold standard, defeats William Jennings Bryan for the presidency.
The Gold Standard Act effectively settles the currency debate; the census counts 76,212,168 people.

misconception.myth: Gilded Age politics was issueless and corrupt, and ordinary Americans tuned it out.
misconception.fact: Corruption and patronage were real, but voter participation in the 1880s and 1890s was the highest in American history, presidential elections were razor-close, and voters fought hard over tariffs, currency, Prohibition and schooling.
misconception.why: Taking the era's satirical label at face value hides how intensely Americans contested the direction of an industrializing country, and how those fights set up Populist and Progressive reform.

title: Great Depression
summary: The longest and deepest economic downturn in U.S. history, which began in August 1929, hit bottom in March 1933 and lasted until wartime demand restored full employment in 1941, throwing about a quarter of the labor force out of work, collapsing the banking system and reshaping the federal government's role through the New Deal.

review.question: Why do most economists argue the 1929 crash alone does not explain the Great Depression?
review.answer: The economy was already contracting from August 1929, and the deepest damage came later, when regional and national banking panics from 1930 to 1933 wiped out deposits, the money supply fell by nearly 30 percent, and the Federal Reserve failed to act as a lender of last resort.

review.question: How did the gold standard help spread and deepen the Depression?
review.answer: Because gold linked interest rates and prices across countries, U.S. tightening forced other gold-standard countries to deflate too; countries that left gold early, like Britain, began recovering sooner, while those that stayed on longest, like France, suffered longer.

review.question: How did Hoover's response differ from Roosevelt's?
review.answer: Hoover relied mainly on voluntary pledges from business and labor and private relief, adding the Reconstruction Finance Corporation's loans to banks and railroads in 1932; Roosevelt's New Deal used direct federal relief, jobs programs such as the WPA, banking reform and Social Security.

review.question: Why did the Depression and the New Deal affect Black, Mexican American and Native communities differently from others?
review.answer: Black workers faced unemployment near 50 percent by 1932 and were often left out of New Deal programs, such as Social Security's exclusion of domestic and farm workers; people of Mexican ancestry, many of them U.S. citizens, were pushed or forced to leave for Mexico; and the 1934 Indian Reorganization Act reversed allotment and encouraged tribal self-government.

timeline.event: The expansion of the 1920s ends and the economy begins to contract.
Black Thursday: the New York Stock Exchange loses 11 percent of its value.
Black Tuesday: more than 16 million shares change hands and over $14 billion in wealth is lost in a day.
Hoover signs the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, raising duties on farm and industrial imports to historic highs.
After Britain leaves the gold standard, the New York Fed raises its discount rate; 522 commercial banks close that month.
Federal troops drive the Bonus Army of unemployed World War I veterans out of their camps in Washington, D.C.
Franklin D. Roosevelt is inaugurated with nearly 25 percent of the labor force jobless, and soon declares a national bank holiday.
The Indian Reorganization Act ends the Dawes-era allotment policy and encourages tribal self-government.
Congress passes the Social Security Act, the Wagner Act and the relief appropriation that funds the Works Progress Administration.
After federal spending cuts, a sharp recession pushes unemployment up again and cuts industrial production by about a third.
The Fair Labor Standards Act sets a federal minimum wage and a 40-hour week, the last major New Deal law.
Wartime demand restores full employment, ending the Depression.

misconception.myth: The stock market crash of October 1929 caused the Great Depression.
misconception.fact: The downturn had already begun in August 1929, and production, prices and incomes were falling before the crash; the crash was one of a series of financial shocks, and the waves of bank failures and the shrinking money supply of 1930–33 did most to turn a recession into a depression.
misconception.why: Black Tuesday is a single, dramatic date, while bank panics, tight monetary policy and the gold standard worked over years and are harder to picture.

title: Great Railroad Strike of 1877
summary: A wave of strikes, protests and riots that began on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad at Martinsburg, West Virginia, on July 16, 1877, spread along the rail lines from Baltimore to Chicago and St. Louis, and was put down by state militias and federal troops, leaving about a hundred people dead.

review.question: Why did a wage cut on one railroad turn into a crisis that stretched from Baltimore to St. Louis?
review.answer: Railroad workers had already suffered years of depression and repeated wage cuts since 1873, so when the Baltimore and Ohio announced another ten percent cut, the walkout at Martinsburg spread along the connected trunk lines, drew in unemployed people and workers in other trades, and local police and militias could not or would not stop it.

review.question: How did the federal government become involved, and what limits did President Hayes set on that role?
review.answer: Governors who said they could not keep order formally asked for federal help, and Hayes issued proclamations and sent Army troops; he refused the Pennsylvania Railroad's request to act directly for the companies and did not use soldiers to run trains, describing his aim as restoring order, though the deployment set a precedent for later presidents.

review.question: What lessons did workers and employers each draw from the strike?
review.answer: Many workers concluded they needed lasting, organized unions, while businesses concluded they needed more political influence and government help, including better-prepared state forces to deal with future labor unrest.

timeline.event: The railroads' financial bubble bursts, beginning years of depression, layoffs and repeated wage cuts.
Railroad workers at Martinsburg, West Virginia, walk off the job over a ten percent wage cut on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad and stop trains.
Governor Henry M. Mathews asks for federal help, and President Rutherford B. Hayes proclaims that those obstructing the railroad must disperse by noon the next day.
Federal troops arrive at Martinsburg and end the violence there.
Hayes issues a similar proclamation for Maryland; in Pittsburgh, militia from Philadelphia fire into a crowd near the 28th Street crossing, killing about twenty people.
Fires in Pittsburgh destroy the Pennsylvania Railroad's Union Depot, more than thirty buildings and thousands of locomotives and cars.
Unrest in Chicago peaks over five days of walkouts, sympathy strikes and clashes with police, militia and U.S. Army troops.
By the end of July the strikes have largely been put down along the trunk lines.
By early 1880 the railroads have restored the wages they had cut.

misconception.myth: The 1877 strike was a planned national uprising, organized and directed by labor unions or radical leaders.
misconception.fact: The walkout began on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad and spread largely on its own along the rail lines; almost none of the strikers belonged to a union and no leaders or organization controlled the strike as a whole, although local groups such as a railroad firemen's organization in West Virginia and socialists in Chicago and St. Louis played real roles in particular places.
misconception.why: The strike's sudden national reach and the visible part socialists played in a few cities made it look coordinated, and treating it as a conspiracy obscures the wage cuts and hard times that drove ordinary workers and their neighbours into the streets.

title: Harriet Tubman
summary: A freedom seeker, Underground Railroad conductor, Union scout and nurse, and women's-suffrage advocate (c. 1822–1913) who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849, returned about 13 times to lead roughly 70 family members and friends to freedom, and helped lead the 1863 Combahee River raid that freed more than 700 enslaved people.

review.question: Why did Tubman return only to Maryland's Eastern Shore rather than travel all over the South?
review.answer: Her missions were to bring away family members and friends she knew and trusted; she knew that landscape from her years of labor in its marshes and woods, and unfamiliar places were far more dangerous.

review.question: How did the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 change where Tubman took the people she rescued?
review.answer: The 1850 law put any freedom seeker in the United States, even in the North, at risk of recapture, so she guided people beyond Philadelphia to St. Catharines, Ontario, in Canada.

review.question: Why did Tubman have to petition Congress for a pension, and what did she get?
review.answer: She had served the Union as a nurse, cook, scout and spy without formal enlistment or regular pay, and at first received only an $8-a-month widow's pension as Nelson Davis's widow; in 1899 Congress raised it to $20 a month for her service as a nurse.

timeline.event: Born Araminta "Minty" Ross, probably in February or early March, on Anthony Thompson's plantation at Peter's Neck, Dorchester County, Maryland.
Probably marries John Tubman, a free Black man, and takes the name Harriet.
After her enslaver Edward Brodess dies in March, she fears being sold, escapes alone in the late fall and reaches Philadelphia.
Congress passes the Fugitive Slave Act; Tubman makes her first rescue, of her niece Kessiah and Kessiah's two children.
Rescues her three remaining brothers from Dorchester County.
Brings her aging parents north after learning her father faces arrest.
Meets John Brown at St. Catharines, Ontario, and recruits support for his plans, though she does not join the 1859 Harpers Ferry raid.
Buys a house and seven acres near Auburn, New York, from Senator William H. Seward.
Last rescue mission to Maryland brings away seven people.
Arrives at Port Royal, South Carolina, to serve the Union Army as a scout, spy, cook and nurse.
Helps lead the Combahee River raid with Colonel James Montgomery, freeing more than 700 enslaved people.
Sarah Bradford publishes the first biography of Tubman; Tubman marries Civil War veteran Nelson Davis in Auburn.
Congress passes H.R. 4982, raising her pension to $20 a month in recognition of her service as an army nurse.
The AME Zion Church opens the Harriet Tubman Home for aged and poor African Americans on land she had transferred to it in 1903.
Dies of pneumonia in Auburn and is buried at Fort Hill Cemetery.

misconception.myth: Tubman made 19 trips into the South and rescued more than 300 people, with a $40,000 bounty on her head.
misconception.fact: Records and her own accounts show about 13 trips, all to Maryland's Eastern Shore, freeing about 70 people, while she gave directions to about 70 more who escaped on their own. The only documented reward was $100 each for her and two brothers in 1849, offered by slaveholders who did not know she was Tubman.
misconception.why: The larger numbers come from Sarah Bradford's 1868–69 biography and an 1867 letter supporting her pension claim; they stuck because they suited a legend, but they obscure how carefully she chose people she knew and trusted.

title: Hawaii
summary: The fiftieth U.S. state (admitted August 21, 1959), a volcanic island chain in the north Pacific settled by Polynesian voyagers centuries before European contact; an independent Native Hawaiian kingdom until a U.S.-backed overthrow in 1893, it was annexed by joint resolution in 1898 over petitions signed by more than half of Native Hawaiians and governed as a territory until statehood.

review.question: Why was Hawaiʻi annexed by a joint resolution of Congress rather than by treaty?
review.answer: A treaty needed a two-thirds Senate vote, and after more than 21,000 Native Hawaiians petitioned against annexation, only 46 senators would support the 1897 treaty. When the Spanish–American War revived interest in the islands, supporters used a joint resolution, which needed only simple majorities, and McKinley signed it on July 7, 1898.

review.question: How did the sugar plantation economy change who lived in Hawaiʻi?
review.answer: Planters recruited contract laborers from Japan, China, the Philippines, Portugal and elsewhere, while disease after Western contact sharply reduced the Native Hawaiian population. Native Hawaiians fell from 97 percent of the population in 1853 to 16 percent in 1923, when people of Japanese ancestry were the largest group.

review.question: Why did statehood take until 1959, and how was it tied to Alaska?
review.answer: Territorial requests for statehood began in 1903 and a 1937 congressional committee found Hawaiʻi qualified, but plantation interests, the Pearl Harbor attack and Senate inaction delayed it. Congress paired Hawaiʻi with Alaska; once Alaska was admitted in early 1959, Hawaiʻi's bill passed in March, voters accepted it in June, and it became the fiftieth state on August 21, 1959.

review.question: What does the 1993 Apology Resolution do, and what does it not do?
review.answer: It acknowledges that U.S. agents and citizens took part in the 1893 overthrow and apologizes for depriving Native Hawaiians of self-determination, but it states that it does not settle any claims against the United States.

timeline.event: By about 1000–1200 CE, according to recent carbon dating, Polynesian voyagers from the Marquesas have settled the islands; later voyagers come from the Society Islands.
British captain James Cook reaches the islands.
Kamehameha completes Puʻukoholā Heiau on Hawaiʻi Island during his wars of unification.
Kamehameha I unites the islands into one kingdom after Kauaʻi comes under his rule.
Kamehameha I dies; his son Liholiho (Kamehameha II) soon ends the kapu system.
A U.S.–Hawaiian treaty indirectly recognizes the kingdom's independence.
The United States and the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi sign a Treaty of Reciprocity.
White landowners and businessmen force King Kalākaua to sign a constitution that strips him of power.
A Committee of Safety, backed by U.S. Minister John L. Stevens and U.S. naval forces landed the day before, overthrows Queen Liliʻuokalani.
Members of Hui Aloha ʻĀina sign petitions against annexation; the drive gathers 21,269 Native Hawaiian signatures.
President McKinley signs the Newlands Resolution annexing Hawaiʻi by joint resolution, after an annexation treaty failed in the Senate.
The United States formally annexes Hawaiʻi.
Hawaiʻi becomes a U.S. territory with a single non-voting delegate in the House.
On the day of the Pearl Harbor attack, the territorial governor signs a declaration of martial law.
In Duncan v. Kahanamoku the Supreme Court voids military-tribunal convictions of civilians under martial law.
President Eisenhower signs the statehood act passed by Congress.
Eisenhower proclaims Hawaii the fiftieth state, after island voters accept statehood in a June referendum.
Voters approve a constitutional amendment making English and Hawaiian the state's official languages.
Congress apologizes for the U.S. role in the 1893 overthrow (Public Law 103-150).
The census counts 1,455,271 residents, 7.0 percent more than in 2010.

misconception.myth: Native Hawaiians accepted annexation, and Hawaiʻi joined the United States through a ratified treaty.
misconception.fact: More than 21,000 Native Hawaiians—over half of those counted in 1897—signed petitions against annexation, and the 1897 treaty died in the Senate with only 46 supporters; annexation came instead by a joint resolution that needed only simple majorities, signed July 7, 1898.
misconception.why: The petitions were long absent from Hawaiian history books and few people knew they existed until a scholar found them in the National Archives, while the 1959 statehood referendum is easily read back onto 1898.

title: Hayden Geological Survey of 1871
summary: A federally funded scientific expedition led by geologist Ferdinand V. Hayden from June to October 1871 that mapped, measured, sketched and photographed the Yellowstone region; its reports, specimens, maps and images, including William Henry Jackson's photographs and Thomas Moran's art, fed the campaign that produced the Yellowstone National Park Act of March 1, 1872.

review.question: Why did Hayden's survey carry a painter and a photographer as well as scientists?
review.answer: Hayden's instructions called for gathering as full material as possible to illustrate his report, so alongside botanists, a mineralogist, a topographer and others he brought photographer William Henry Jackson and artists Thomas Moran and Henry W. Elliott to give visual proof of features earlier explorers had only described.

review.question: How did the survey contribute to the creation of Yellowstone National Park?
review.answer: It corroborated the 1869 and 1870 accounts with scientific measurements, maps and specimens; Hayden then went to Washington to report, displayed specimens and images for members of Congress and published articles urging a park law, joining Nathaniel Langford and others in the lobbying that preceded the March 1, 1872 act.

review.question: Why do some historians doubt that Jackson's photographs were decisive?
review.answer: Howard Bossen found that the congressional record mentions the photographs only once, the House never discussed them, and the famous story of prints on every desk comes from a 1947 book with no contemporary support, so the images look like one strand of evidence among many rather than the deciding factor.

review.question: Why is the survey's legacy now viewed more critically?
review.answer: Hayden made demeaning statements about Native peoples, urging that they be made into farmers or destroyed if they resisted federal demands, and the park his survey helped create removed Indigenous people from lands they had used for at least 11,000 years.

timeline.event: A sundry civil act provides $40,000 to continue Hayden's survey of the territories.
The party of more than 30 men sets out in early June; the USGS dates its departure from Ogden, Utah, to June 8.
The survey reaches Fort Ellis near present-day Bozeman, Montana.
It enters the Yellowstone region, reaching Mammoth Hot Springs and then Tower Fall.
The party arrives at Yellowstone Lake, where members build the boat Annie to take depth soundings.
Exploration of the Lower, Midway and Upper Geyser Basins continues through this date.
Several earthquakes shake the camp at Steamboat Point on Yellowstone Lake.
The survey reaches Fort Bridger in southwestern Wyoming Territory.
Hayden formally ends the expedition.
Senator Pomeroy introduces S. 392 to set the Yellowstone region apart as a park.
Hayden dates his report on the season's work to Interior Secretary Delano.
The Yellowstone park bill becomes law, about ten weeks after its introduction.

misconception.myth: William Henry Jackson's photographs, laid on the desk of every member of Congress, persuaded Congress to create Yellowstone National Park.
misconception.fact: The Congressional Globe mentions the photographs only once, when Senator Pomeroy told colleagues on January 23, 1872, that they could see them; the House debate never mentions them, Hayden's report carried drawings rather than photographs, and the desk story first appears in a 1947 book by Jackson's son with no contemporary record to support it. The photographs were one part of a larger body of evidence alongside reports, specimens, art, lectures and personal lobbying.
misconception.why: Histories of photography from the late 1930s onward repeated the story, often without sources, because a single striking cause is easier to tell than a ten-week campaign by many advocates.

title: Hoover Dam
summary: A 726-foot concrete arch-gravity dam in Black Canyon of the Colorado River on the Arizona–Nevada border, built by the Six Companies consortium for the Bureau of Reclamation between 1931 and 1936; it created Lake Mead, supplies water and hydroelectric power across the Southwest, and was known officially as Boulder Dam from 1933 until Congress restored Herbert Hoover's name in 1947.

review.question: Why was the dam called Boulder Dam for fourteen years, and how was the Hoover name restored?
review.answer: Wilbur announced the Hoover name in 1930 to honor Hoover's role in the Colorado River Compact, but after Hoover's reputation fell during the Depression, Interior Secretary Harold Ickes ordered it renamed Boulder Dam in May 1933, arguing a structure should not be named for a sitting president and that it was already known by that name; a 1947 congressional resolution restored "Hoover Dam."

review.question: Why do counts of construction deaths at Hoover Dam differ (96 versus 112)?
review.answer: The official 96 counts only industrial fatalities at the site, such as drownings, blasts and falling rock; the larger figure adds deaths from before the dam was authorized, like the 1922 surveyors, and deaths from causes such as heat, pneumonia or heart trouble.

review.question: How did the dam's builders keep its enormous mass of concrete from cracking as it cured?
review.answer: They poured it as interlocking vertical columns rather than one block and embedded about 582 miles of steel pipe through which river water and then refrigerated water circulated to carry off the heat of curing, before grouting the joints.

review.question: How did racial discrimination shape who built the dam?
review.answer: After Las Vegas's Colored Citizens Labor and Protective Association protested in 1931 that none of the first thousand workers were Black, only 24 African Americans had been hired by 1933; they were barred from living in Boulder City, assigned to the hot Arizona gravel pits and bused in on segregated buses.

timeline.event: Reclamation surveyors J. G. Tierney and Harold Connelly drown in the Colorado River while studying possible dam sites.
Seven basin states sign the Colorado River Compact at Santa Fe.
President Coolidge signs the Boulder Canyon Project Act authorizing the dam.
At a ceremony opening work on the project, Interior Secretary Ray Lyman Wilbur announces the name Hoover Dam.
The construction contract is awarded to Six Companies on a bid of about $48.9 million.
Six Companies receives notice to proceed, the formal start of construction.
Workers strike after a pay cut for tunnel crews; the strike collapses and the cut stands.
The river is turned through the diversion tunnels around the dam site.
Interior Secretary Harold Ickes orders the structure renamed Boulder Dam.
The first concrete is placed.
The dam begins impounding water in Lake Mead.
The last concrete is placed.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicates the dam.
Reclamation formally accepts the completed dam from Six Companies.
The first generating unit, N-2, goes into full operation.
A congressional resolution makes the name Hoover Dam official.
The final original generating unit, N-8, goes online.
The Interior Department designates the dam a National Historic Landmark.

misconception.myth: Workers who died building Hoover Dam are entombed in its concrete.
misconception.fact: The Bureau of Reclamation states that no one is buried in the dam; concrete was placed in five-foot-high blocks that rose gradually as crews packed each layer, which made an unnoticed burial virtually impossible. The official toll counts 96 industrial deaths at the site.
misconception.why: The dam's sheer mass and its real death toll make the legend feel plausible, and confusion between the official 96 and a broader count of 112 deaths keeps the story of "missing" men alive.

title: Huffman Prairie Flying Field
summary: A former cow pasture east of Dayton, Ohio, now on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, where Wilbur and Orville Wright turned their 1903 Kitty Hawk machine into the first practical airplane in 1904–1905 and later ran the Wright Company's flying school (1910–1916).

review.question: Why did the Wrights need a catapult at Huffman Prairie when they had not needed one at Kitty Hawk?
review.answer: The Ohio pasture lacked the Outer Banks' steady strong winds and sand hills, so the brothers built a falling-weight derrick to get the heavier Flyer up to flying speed.

review.question: How did the experiments at Huffman Prairie change the Wrights' machine from a novelty into a practical airplane?
review.answer: Through repeated flights and crashes they enlarged and moved the elevator, enlarged the rudder and gave the pilot separate control of it, so that the 1905 Flyer III could bank, circle, fly figure-eights and stay aloft for more than half an hour.

review.question: Why did the Wrights stop flying after October 1905, just as they had succeeded?
review.answer: They feared that public demonstrations would let others copy their design before their patent was secure and before they had a buyer, so they took the Flyer apart and did not fly again for nearly three years.

timeline.event: Before a dozen invited reporters, the Wrights' new Flyer II fails to leave the ground because of engine trouble.
The brothers first use a weight-and-derrick catapult to launch the Flyer in the prairie's light winds.
The first complete circle by an airplane is flown over the pasture.
The season ends after 105 starts adding up to under an hour in the air.
Orville makes the first flight of the rebuilt Wright Flyer III.
A crash that throws Orville through the upper wing prompts a redesign of the controls.
Wilbur flies about 24 miles in some 39 minutes, a world record.
The Wright School of Aviation moves its training to Huffman Field.
The Wright Company stops using the field after training 119 students there.
The Army leases the land around the field for Wilbur Wright Field, a World War I training post.
Huffman Prairie Flying Field is designated a National Historic Landmark.
The Dayton Aviation Heritage Preservation Act makes the field part of a new national historical park.

misconception.myth: The Wright brothers had a finished, practical airplane once they flew at Kitty Hawk in 1903.
misconception.fact: The 1903 flights were brief, straight-line hops; the brothers learned to turn, circle, bank and stay up for half an hour only at Huffman Prairie in 1904–1905, with the redesigned Flyer III.
misconception.why: The single dramatic date of December 17, 1903, is easy to remember, while two seasons of unpublicized trial and error in an Ohio pasture drew little press attention.

title: Indian Removal Act
summary: The federal law signed by President Andrew Jackson on May 28, 1830, that authorized the president to exchange lands west of the Mississippi River for the homelands of Native nations in the East, and that became the legal basis for the forced removal of the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole and other nations in the 1830s and 1840s.

review.question: If the Indian Removal Act was written as a voluntary exchange of lands, how did it lead to the forced removal of the Cherokee Nation?
review.answer: The act let the president negotiate exchange treaties. When the Cherokee government under John Ross refused, federal agents concluded the Treaty of New Echota with a minority Treaty Party that had no authority to sign it; the Senate ratified it by a single vote, and in 1838 President Van Buren sent the army to round Cherokees into stockades and march them west.

review.question: Why did the Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia fail to stop removal?
review.answer: The Court held that Georgia's laws had no force in Cherokee territory, but neither Georgia nor President Jackson enforced the decision, so state pressure on Cherokee land continued.

review.question: Why do estimates of how many people were removed range from about 50,000 to about 88,000?
review.answer: The figures count different things — about 50,000 eastern Native people removed under Jackson's treaties, about 70,000 from the five southeastern nations over several decades, and about 88,000 including northern nations removed in the 1830s and 1840s.

timeline.event: Georgia cedes its western lands to the federal government, which promises in return to extinguish Indian land title within the state (the Compact of 1802).
After Andrew Jackson's forces defeat the Creeks at Horseshoe Bend, the Creeks surrender more than twenty million acres.
The Cherokee Nation adopts a written constitution; Georgia begins extending state jurisdiction over Cherokee territory.
Gold is found on Native lands in Georgia.
After passing the Senate 28 to 19 and the House 102 to 97, the Indian Removal Act is signed by President Jackson.
Jackson tells Congress that removal is nearing a 'happy consummation' and that two nations have agreed to terms.
The Supreme Court in Cherokee Nation v. Georgia calls the Cherokees a 'domestic dependent nation' and declines to hear their suit; Choctaw removal begins.
In Worcester v. Georgia the Court rules that Georgia's laws have no force in Cherokee territory; Georgia and the president do not enforce the ruling.
A minority Treaty Party signs the Treaty of New Echota without the authority of Principal Chief John Ross or the Cherokee government; the Second Seminole War begins the same year.
The Senate ratifies the New Echota treaty 31 to 15; most Muscogee (Creek) people are forced west.
Under orders from President Martin Van Buren, the army begins rounding up Cherokees into stockades.
The last Cherokee detachments reach Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma.
The reunited Cherokee Nation adopts a new constitution with its capital at Tahlequah.

misconception.myth: The Indian Removal Act itself ordered the army to drive Native nations out of the East.
misconception.fact: The act authorized the president to offer western lands in exchange for eastern homelands to nations that chose to make the exchange, and appropriated $500,000; the force came afterwards, through treaties obtained under heavy pressure — the Cherokee treaty was signed by a faction without the authority of the nation's government — and through troops sent to enforce them.
misconception.why: Knowing that the law was framed as voluntary exchange shows how coercion operated through treaties, state laws and enforcement decisions, and why the Cherokee and others fought removal in the courts and in Congress rather than simply in the field.

title: Japanese American incarceration during World War II
summary: The forced removal of people of Japanese ancestry from the U.S. West Coast under Executive Order 9066 and their imprisonment, without charges or trial, in War Relocation Authority camps and other sites from 1942 to 1946; about two-thirds of those held were U.S. citizens.

review.question: Why do the National Park Service and many historians prefer "incarceration" and "forced removal" to "internment" and "evacuation"?
review.answer: Internment is a law-of-war term for detaining enemy nationals, which the Justice Department and Army did separately to non-citizens; most people in the ten WRA camps were U.S. citizens held without charges, and "evacuation" wrongly suggests being moved out of danger.

review.question: How did the government justify the removal, and what does the evidence show?
review.answer: General DeWitt and President Roosevelt claimed military necessity, citing reports of signals and sabotage; those reports were unverified, the FBI's director mocked the Army's intelligence as hysterical, and no Japanese American was convicted of serious espionage or sabotage.

review.question: How did the Supreme Court's two December 1944 decisions differ?
review.answer: In Korematsu it upheld the exclusion order 6–3 as a military necessity, while in Ex parte Endo it ruled that the government could not keep detaining citizens it conceded were loyal; the exclusion orders were lifted effective January 2, 1945.

review.question: What did the redress movement achieve, and how?
review.answer: Japanese American organizations pressed Congress, which created a commission in 1980; its findings and recommendations led to the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, which apologized, paid $20,000 to each surviving incarcerated person (82,219 people in all) and funded public education.

timeline.event: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor; a presidential proclamation makes Japanese nationals in the U.S. liable to be detained as enemy aliens.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt signs Executive Order 9066, letting military commanders designate areas from which any person may be excluded.
Executive Order 9102 creates the War Relocation Authority (WRA) to run the camps.
Public Law 503 makes violating an exclusion order a federal crime.
The first Civilian Exclusion Order removes Japanese Americans from Bainbridge Island, Washington.
The Army activates the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, combining the 100th Battalion with mainland Nisei volunteers.
The WRA begins giving incarcerated adults the so-called loyalty questionnaire.
Tule Lake is designated a segregation center for people the government labeled disloyal.
The Supreme Court upholds exclusion in Korematsu v. United States but rules in Ex parte Endo that loyal citizens cannot be held.
The West Coast exclusion orders are lifted.
Tule Lake closes, the last of the ten WRA camps; the WRA is disbanded on June 30, 1946.
A federal court in San Francisco vacates Fred Korematsu's conviction, citing government misconduct.
President Ronald Reagan signs the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, with an apology and $20,000 for each surviving incarcerated person.

misconception.myth: Japanese Americans were removed and imprisoned because they were caught spying or committing sabotage, so the camps were a military necessity.
misconception.fact: No Japanese American was convicted of serious espionage or sabotage during the war; the rumours cited by the Army were unverified, and Congress later found the policy was driven by racial prejudice, war hysteria and a failure of political leadership.
misconception.why: The government justified the removal as military necessity at the time, the Supreme Court accepted that claim in 1944, and the word "evacuation" made forced removal sound like protection.

title: Jazz
summary: A form of music created by African American musicians in New Orleans around the turn of the twentieth century, blending blues, ragtime, brass-band and dance traditions with collective and solo improvisation, which spread across the United States and the world through recordings, migration and touring.

review.question: How did the segregation laws of the 1890s help shape early jazz in New Orleans?
review.answer: They stripped Creoles of color of their separate social status and pushed them together with uptown Black musicians, combining the Creoles' formal training and discipline with the improvised, blues-based playing of uptown bands.

review.question: Why is the story that jazz musicians left New Orleans because Storyville closed misleading?
review.answer: Many musicians, such as Jelly Roll Morton, the Original Creole Orchestra and Tom Brown's band, had left before the district closed in November 1917, and research on musicians who left between 1902 and 1922 shows they sought better pay, working conditions, racial equality and safety; King Oliver, for example, had been repeatedly arrested while playing.

review.question: How did bebop change the role of jazz compared with the swing era?
review.answer: Swing big bands played largely for dancing, while bebop, developed in Harlem after-hours sessions in the early 1940s, used small groups, fast tempos and improvised solos over chord changes, and was meant mainly for listening.

timeline.event: New Orleans begins sanctioning Sunday ring shouts by enslaved and free Black people at Place Congo (Congo Square), a practice allowed until 1856.
Around this time uptown cornetist Charles "Buddy" Bolden begins improvising on the blues and speeding up dance tunes, a style many early musicians later called the first jazz.
Pianist and composer Jelly Roll Morton begins touring outside New Orleans.
Tom Brown's band leaves New Orleans for Chicago.
The Original Dixieland Jazz Band makes the first commercial jazz recordings in New York City.
New Orleans closes its Storyville red-light district.
Kid Ory's band records in California, the first recording by a Black New Orleans jazz band; Louis Armstrong joins King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band in Chicago.
Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings (1925–1928) begin shifting jazz toward the improvising soloist.
Duke Ellington's band begins its engagement at Harlem's whites-only Cotton Club, with nightly radio broadcasts.
Thelonious Monk is house pianist at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem, where after-hours sessions help create bebop.
Dizzy Gillespie makes the first major-label bebop recording, for RCA's Bluebird label.
The State Department sends Dizzy Gillespie on the first of its Cold War jazz-ambassador tours.

misconception.myth: Jazz was born in the brothels of Storyville, and its musicians scattered north when the district was closed in 1917.
misconception.fact: Jazz grew out of New Orleans neighborhood life — brass bands, parades, dance halls, social clubs and street music — and Storyville was only one of many places musicians worked. Research by Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive curator Bruce Raeburn on musicians who left the city between 1902 and 1922 found that they went for better pay, working conditions, racial equality and safety, not because the district closed; several had left years before 1917.
misconception.why: The red-light story is colorful and easy to tell, but it hides the African American and Creole communities, institutions and traditions that actually produced the music, and the segregation and police harassment that drove many musicians away.

title: Jim Crow laws
summary: The state and local laws, backed by custom and violence, that enforced racial segregation and stripped Black Americans of voting rights, mainly in the South and border states, from the end of Reconstruction until federal laws and court rulings dismantled them in the 1950s and 1960s.

review.question: Why did historians argue for decades about when Jim Crow began?
review.answer: C. Vann Woodward held that legal segregation was not inevitable and arrived mainly in the 1890s after a more fluid period, while critics such as Joel Williamson and Howard Rabinowitz found segregation by custom, and in some places by law, already in place during Reconstruction; the dispute shapes whether Jim Crow is seen as a legacy of slavery or a new system built by later choices.

review.question: How did southern states keep Black citizens from voting despite the Fifteenth Amendment?
review.answer: They used poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, white primaries and new state constitutions such as Louisiana's of 1898 and Alabama's of 1901, enforced alongside economic intimidation and violence including lynching.

review.question: Which federal actions dismantled the Jim Crow system?
review.answer: Court rulings such as Brown v. Board of Education (1954), Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections (1966) and Loving v. Virginia (1967), together with the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Civil Rights Act of 1968.

timeline.event: Thomas Dartmouth Rice first performs the blackface minstrel routine "Jump Jim Crow," source of the later name for segregation.
Alabama adopts a Black Code controlling the labor and movement of freed people.
Tennessee's Chapter 130 permits discrimination in hotels, theaters, trains and streetcars.
Tennessee orders segregated railroad cars, a law often called the first Jim Crow law.
In the Civil Rights Cases the Supreme Court strikes down key parts of the Civil Rights Act of 1875.
Louisiana passes the Separate Car Act, one of nine state laws of 1887–1892 separating passengers by race.
Plessy v. Ferguson upholds state-mandated segregation under the separate but equal doctrine.
Louisiana's new constitution mandates segregated schools and restricts Black men's voting.
Alabama's constitution disfranchises Black voters, segregates schools and bars interracial marriage.
In Guinn v. United States the Supreme Court rules Oklahoma's grandfather clause violates the Fifteenth Amendment.
Brown v. Board of Education declares school segregation unconstitutional.
The Civil Rights Act outlaws segregation in businesses such as theaters, restaurants and hotels.
President Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act.
Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections holds Virginia's poll tax unconstitutional.
Loving v. Virginia unanimously strikes down a state ban on interracial marriage.
A new Civil Rights Act prohibits discrimination in housing.

misconception.myth: Jim Crow laws existed only in the former Confederate states.
misconception.fact: Most Jim Crow laws were passed in the South, but border states adopted them too, Oklahoma used a grandfather clause to bar Black voters until 1915, and Black Northerners met segregation in schools and public accommodations.
misconception.why: Treating segregation as a purely regional custom hides how widely racial discrimination operated and why the civil rights movement sought national laws to end it.

title: Lattimer massacre
summary: The killing of at least nineteen unarmed striking coal miners, nearly all Polish, Slovak and Lithuanian immigrants, by a Luzerne County sheriff's posse on the road to Lattimer, Pennsylvania, on September 10, 1897; the sheriff and his deputies were acquitted, and the killings drove thousands of anthracite miners into the United Mine Workers.

review.question: Why were the Lattimer marchers on strike, and why were immigrant miners especially vulnerable in 1897?
review.answer: They were protesting low wages, high prices for supplies the company sold them and abuses by company-town staff. As recent Polish, Slovak and Lithuanian immigrants, none of them citizens, they faced nativist hostility, a new state tax on employers of non-citizens, and a sheriff's posse drawn from Anglo-American townspeople and company agents.

review.question: How did a massacre that ended in acquittals end up strengthening the miners' union?
review.answer: The killings united the region's immigrant communities and disproved the idea that Slavic and Italian workers were docile; within four months more than 15,000 anthracite workers joined the United Mine Workers, which under John Mitchell led the 1900 and 1902 strikes that brought presidential intervention.

review.question: Why did the Lattimer massacre fade from national memory, and how was it revived?
review.answer: Scholars point to the victims' ethnicity, nativist attitudes, the site's rural remoteness and coal operators' interest in forgetting. Interest revived in the civil rights era, leading to a 1972 memorial dedicated with Cesar Chavez, centennial markers in 1997 and an archaeological survey in 2010.

timeline.event: Pennsylvania enacts the Campbell Act, a tax of three cents a day on coal operators for each non-citizen they employ.
Sheriff James Martin's deputies fire on about 400 marching strikers near Lattimer, killing nineteen and wounding dozens.
Martin and his deputies go on trial for murder at the Luzerne County Courthouse in Wilkes-Barre.
The jury acquits all the defendants.
A UMW-led anthracite strike of about 125,000 workers ends.
Miners return to work after the five-month anthracite strike of 1902.
A memorial boulder and state marker are dedicated at Lattimer; Cesar Chavez speaks.
The centennial is marked with new state markers and remarks in the Congressional Record.
University of Maryland archaeologists and local volunteers survey the massacre site with metal detectors.

misconception.myth: The "Lattimer riots" were a violent uprising by armed foreign miners that deputies had to put down.
misconception.fact: The marchers had agreed not to carry firearms or clubs, the state's historical marker and a National Park Service study describe them as unarmed, and over a dozen marchers were shot in the back while fleeing; exactly how the first shots came is still debated.
misconception.why: Early newspaper accounts came largely from the sheriff and coal-company sympathizers, the trial records have been lost, and nativist hostility toward Slavic immigrants made the "riot" label easy to accept, so some newspapers still used it in the 1930s.

title: Liberty Bell
summary: The cracked bronze bell, recast in Philadelphia in 1753 for the Pennsylvania State House (now Independence Hall), whose biblical inscription about proclaiming liberty led abolitionists to name it the "Liberty Bell" in 1835 and later movements to adopt it as a national symbol of freedom.

review.question: Why did abolitionists, rather than the Revolutionary generation, give the Liberty Bell its name?
review.answer: The inscription from Leviticus 25:10, about proclaiming liberty to all inhabitants, went largely unnoticed during the Revolution. In the 1830s antislavery activists saw the gap between those words and the enslavement of millions, and the Anti-Slavery Record of February 1835 called the State House bell "The Liberty Bell" and said its peals were a mockery while slavery lasted.

review.question: How did a Philadelphia bell become a national symbol between 1885 and 1918?
review.answer: It traveled by rail to seven fairs and expositions between 1885 and 1915, drawing huge crowds along the way, and during World War I the government used it in Liberty Loan drives that raised more than $17 billion. These tours and campaigns turned a local relic into a symbol recognized across the country.

review.question: Why is it uncertain whether the bell rang for the Declaration of Independence?
review.answer: No record shows the bell ringing on July 4 or July 8, 1776, and the steeple was in poor condition. The National Park Service says there is no evidence, while historian Gary Nash writes that it is believed to have rung at the July 8 public reading; the July 4 version is Lippard's fiction.

timeline.event: Superintendents of the Pennsylvania State House order a bell of about 2,000 pounds from London, with a verse from Leviticus as its inscription.
The bell, cast at the Whitechapel foundry, cracks on its first test strike soon after arriving in Philadelphia.
Philadelphia metalworkers John Pass and John Stow recast it; the bell face bears the date MDCCLIII.
The bell rings in protest as a ship carrying stamped paper for the Stamp Act approaches.
Fearing the British would melt it for munitions, Philadelphians hide it in Allentown's Zion Reformed Church; it returns in 1778.
The American Anti-Slavery Society's Anti-Slavery Record calls it 'The Liberty Bell', the earliest known use of the name.
Workers drill out a hairline crack before Washington's Birthday; a new fissure opens and the bell is silenced for good.
George Lippard's fictional story 'Ring, Grandfather, Ring' ties the bell to July 4, 1776.
The bell travels to the World's Industrial and Cotton Centennial Exposition in New Orleans, the first of seven trips.
The bell leaves on its last journey, a tour of more than 10,000 miles to the Panama-Pacific Exposition in San Francisco.
Pennsylvania suffragists first ring their replica Justice Bell at Independence Square after the Nineteenth Amendment.
The National Park Service takes custody of the bell and Independence Hall.
For the Bicentennial the bell moves from Independence Hall to a glass-and-brick pavilion a block away.
The bell moves to a new building at Sixth and Market Streets, beside the site where Washington held enslaved people in the 1790s.

misconception.myth: The Liberty Bell rang out on July 4, 1776, to announce the Declaration of Independence, and cracked doing so.
misconception.fact: The National Park Service finds no evidence the bell rang on July 4 or July 8, 1776; the July 4 story comes from George Lippard's 1847 fiction, and the crack that silenced the bell dates from the 1840s.
misconception.why: Lippard's tale was retold as fact in books and schoolrooms, and it gave a beloved object a dramatic founding moment that the record does not supply.

title: Louisiana Purchase
summary: The 1803 agreement in which the United States paid France $15 million for its claim to Louisiana, about 828,000 square miles west of the Mississippi River, roughly doubling the nation's size while leaving the land itself in the hands of the Native nations who lived there.

review.question: Why did Jefferson's envoys end up buying far more land than they were sent to get?
review.answer: They were authorized to pay up to $10 million for New Orleans and the Floridas, but Napoleon, whose army had been devastated in Saint-Domingue and who faced renewed war with Britain, offered all of Louisiana, so Livingston and Monroe exceeded their instructions and agreed to $15 million for the whole territory.

review.question: How did the purchase test Jefferson's own view of the Constitution, and how did he resolve it?
review.answer: Jefferson believed the Constitution made no provision for acquiring foreign territory and drafted an amendment, but his Cabinet argued it was unnecessary and Napoleon's deadline loomed, so he let the Senate ratify the treaty without one, comparing himself to a guardian investing a ward's money in adjacent land.

review.question: According to Robert Lee, what did the United States actually acquire from France, and why does that change the meaning of the $15 million price?
review.answer: It acquired France's claim of preemption — the exclusive right to obtain land from Native nations — rather than the land itself, so the real cost of the territory was paid later through many treaties and cessions backed by force, adding up to far more than $15 million.

timeline.event: A treaty with Spain (Pinckney's Treaty) lets Americans navigate the Mississippi and deposit goods at New Orleans for export.
France reacquires Louisiana from Spain.
Spain's King Charles IV signs the decree transferring Louisiana to France, and the Spanish official at New Orleans revokes Americans' right of deposit.
Jefferson sends James Monroe as minister extraordinary to join Robert Livingston in Paris, authorized to pay up to $10 million for New Orleans and the Floridas.
French foreign minister Talleyrand tells Livingston that France will sell all of Louisiana.
Livingston, Monroe and François Barbé-Marbois sign the treaty of cession and two financial conventions in Paris.
The purchase is officially announced in the United States.
