The Senate ratifies the treaty by a vote of 24 to 7.
Spain formally returns Louisiana to France.
France transfers Louisiana to the United States at New Orleans.
Congress creates the Territory of Orleans from the southern part of the purchase.
More than eighty enslaved people launch the German Coast uprising upriver from New Orleans.
Louisiana is admitted as a state; President James Madison signs the statehood law.
The Adams-Onís (Transcontinental) Treaty with Spain finally settles the purchase's disputed borders.

misconception.myth: In 1803 the United States bought the land of the Louisiana Territory from France for a few cents an acre.
misconception.fact: France sold what it had, a European claim to sovereignty that gave the United States the exclusive right to acquire land from the Native nations who held and lived on it; the United States then acquired that land over the following decades through hundreds of treaties, agreements and seizures, eventually paying Native nations about $2.6 billion in disbursements by one historian's count.
misconception.why: The famous price makes the purchase look like a single real-estate bargain and erases the Native nations whose lands were the real subject of later negotiation, pressure and war.

title: Minimum wage
aliases: Minimum wage in the United States
summary: The legal floor on hourly pay in the United States, first adopted by the states for women workers beginning with Massachusetts in 1912 and set nationally by the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, which fixed a federal minimum of 25 cents an hour; the federal rate has been $7.25 since July 24, 2009, while most states set higher rates of their own.

review.question: Why were the first American minimum wage laws limited to women and minors?
review.answer: Organizing women into unions was seen as difficult, so legislated standards were thought justified for them, while the AFL under Samuel Gompers opposed legal wage floors for men and wanted men's pay won through collective bargaining.

review.question: How did the Supreme Court's 1937 decision in West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish clear the way for a federal minimum wage?
review.answer: It upheld Washington's minimum wage law and overruled Adkins v. Children's Hospital, rejecting the idea that a constitutional freedom of contract barred wage laws; that turnaround improved the prospects of the federal bill Roosevelt sent to Congress two months later.

review.question: Why does the federal minimum wage not settle what most American workers must be paid?
review.answer: Employers must pay the highest applicable federal, state or local rate, and as of July 2026 thirty states and the District of Columbia set minimums above $7.25, so the federal rate binds mainly in states with no law or one at or below it.

review.question: How did the 1938 law's exemptions shape who benefited from it?
review.answer: It left out farmworkers, domestic workers, government employees, intrastate retail and much transportation; farmworkers were covered only after the 1966 amendments and domestic workers in 1974, and historian Phyllis Palmer links the exclusions to racial and gender inequalities.

timeline.event: Massachusetts enacts the first state minimum wage law; it takes effect on July 1, 1913.
Congress passes a minimum wage law for women and minors in the District of Columbia.
In Adkins v. Children's Hospital the Supreme Court voids the District of Columbia law; sixteen states then have minimum wage laws for women.
In West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish the Court upholds Washington's minimum wage law and overrules Adkins.
Franklin D. Roosevelt sends a wages-and-hours bill to Congress.
Roosevelt signs the Fair Labor Standards Act.
The first federal minimum wage, 25 cents an hour, takes effect.
In United States v. Darby the Court upholds Congress's power to set wage and hour standards.
The federal minimum reaches 40 cents an hour.
Amendments extending coverage to large retail and service enterprises take effect.
Under the 1966 amendments, farmworkers are covered by the federal minimum for the first time, at $1.00 an hour.
Domestic workers are brought under the law.
The federal minimum rises to $7.25 an hour, its rate since.

misconception.myth: The minimum wage began with Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938.
misconception.fact: The states came first. Massachusetts passed the first minimum wage law in 1912, and by the end of 1938 twenty-five states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico had minimum wage legislation. The 1938 federal law built on that state experiment, and at first it covered industries employing only about a fifth of the labor force.
misconception.why: The federal act was the first national floor and its 25-cent rate is a famous milestone, so the decades of earlier state laws, most of them limited to women and minors, drop out of the popular story.

title: Mississippi River
summary: North America's second-longest river, flowing about 2,340 miles from Lake Itasca in Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico and draining roughly 1.2 million square miles of the interior; a homeland and highway for Native nations, a prize of empires and the Civil War, and a heavily engineered shipping and flood-control system today.

review.question: Why is it inaccurate to call the Mississippi the longest river in the United States, and why do published lengths for it differ?
review.answer: The Missouri, which flows into it, is longer (2,540 miles against 2,340 in the USGS list, or about 100 miles longer by the Park Service's count); figures for the Mississippi itself range from about 2,300 to 2,350 miles because agencies measure a shifting channel differently.

review.question: Why did Union leaders consider capturing Vicksburg essential?
review.answer: The Confederacy had closed the Mississippi to Northern commerce; taking Vicksburg would reopen the river to Midwestern farm exports, split the South in two and cut a vital Confederate supply line.

review.question: How did the Great Flood of 1927 change federal flood-control policy, and who bore its heaviest costs?
review.answer: It showed that levees alone could not hold the river, so the 1928 Flood Control Act added spillways, floodways and diversion works; the heaviest costs fell on displaced residents, including many Black tenant farmers who were segregated in relief shelters and later left for northern cities.

timeline.event: The Mississippian culture flourishes in the river valley; its greatest center, Cahokia, rises near present-day St. Louis and lasts until about 1350.
Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto becomes one of the first Europeans to travel the river.
Louis Jolliet and the Jesuit Jacques Marquette travel the river for France.
Pinckney's Treaty with Spain opens the river to American ships and duty-free transport through New Orleans.
Confederate forces surrender Vicksburg, Mississippi, ending a campaign for control of the river.
During the Great Flood of 1927, engineers begin dynamiting the levee at Caernarvon, Louisiana, below New Orleans.
Congress passes the Flood Control Act, shifting federal policy from levees alone to spillways and floodways.
A major summer flood strikes the upper river basin.

misconception.myth: The Mississippi is the longest river in the United States.
misconception.fact: The U.S. Geological Survey lists the Missouri River, the Mississippi's largest tributary, at 2,540 miles against the Mississippi's 2,340, and the National Park Service also describes the Missouri as about 100 miles longer.
misconception.why: The Mississippi carries the larger flow and the larger name, and the two rivers are often added together as one system, so its length record gets assumed rather than checked.

title: Missouri Compromise
summary: The 1820 act of Congress, signed by President James Monroe on March 6, 1820, that let Missouri enter the Union without a ban on slavery, paired its admission with that of Maine as a free state, and prohibited slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of latitude 36°30′.

review.question: Why did Congress link Maine's statehood to Missouri's?
review.answer: Admitting Missouri as a slave state would have tipped the evenly divided Senate toward the slave states, so Senate leaders would advance Maine (a free state carved from Massachusetts) only if Missouri entered without the Tallmadge restriction; admitting both kept the balance at twelve and twelve.

review.question: How did the 36°30′ line work, and how was it undone?
review.answer: It barred slavery in the remaining Louisiana Purchase territory north of Missouri's southern border while leaving Missouri itself open to slavery; the Kansas-Nebraska Act repealed it in 1854, and in 1857 the Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision declared the compromise unconstitutional.

review.question: Why did a second compromise become necessary in 1821?
review.answer: Missouri's 1820 constitution directed the legislature to keep free Black people from entering the state, which some members of Congress said violated the rights of free Black people recognized as citizens in northern states; Clay's resolution admitted Missouri only after its legislature pledged in a public act that the disputed clauses would not be enforced.

review.question: Why did Jefferson call the settlement "a reprieve only"?
review.answer: He believed that a geographic line coinciding with a moral and political principle would never be erased and would deepen with each new dispute, threatening the Union.

timeline.event: Representative James Tallmadge Jr. of New York proposes amending the Missouri statehood bill to bar further slavery there; the House adopts it on sectional lines, but the Senate strikes it and the bill dies.
The Sixteenth Congress convenes; Senate leaders go on to tie Maine's statehood to Missouri's.
The House accepts the compromise, admitting Missouri without restriction and closing the territory north of 36°30′ to slavery.
President James Monroe signs the act.
Maine becomes the 23rd state.
Thomas Jefferson writes to John Holmes that the Missouri question struck him like a fire bell in the night.
Missouri adopts a constitution that protects slavery and directs the legislature to keep free Black people out of the state.
Under a second compromise brokered by Henry Clay, Missouri's legislature pledges that the disputed clauses will not be enforced.
Monroe proclaims Missouri the 24th state.
The Kansas-Nebraska Act repeals the 36°30′ restriction after 34 years.
In Dred Scott v. Sandford the Supreme Court declares the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional.

misconception.myth: Henry Clay drew up the Missouri Compromise and proposed its famous 36°30′ line.
misconception.fact: Senator Jesse B. Thomas of Illinois proposed the 36°30′ line; Speaker Henry Clay, working with President Monroe and Senate leaders, steered the package through the House and later brokered the 1821 second compromise over Missouri's constitution.
misconception.why: The Missouri fight launched Clay's lasting reputation as "the Great Compromiser," so later memory folded the work of Thomas, Monroe and others into his name.

title: Monroe Doctrine
summary: The foreign-policy principles President James Monroe set out in his annual message to Congress on December 2, 1823: that the Americas were closed to new European colonization, that European intervention in the independent states of the hemisphere would be seen as a threat to the United States, and that the United States would stay out of European affairs and existing European colonies.

review.question: Why did John Quincy Adams oppose issuing the declaration jointly with Britain?
review.answer: He argued a joint statement would make the United States look like it was following British policy and could limit future U.S. expansion, and he doubted Britain's commitment to the new Latin American republics, so the proposal became a unilateral U.S. declaration.

review.question: How could a weak United States make such a sweeping claim in 1823?
review.answer: Britain favored the policy, so the United States could in effect rely on the Royal Navy, and London secured a French promise not to help Spain recover its colonies.

review.question: How did the Roosevelt Corollary change the doctrine's meaning?
review.answer: The 1823 message warned Europeans against intervening in the Americas; Roosevelt's 1904 corollary claimed a right for the United States itself to intervene, leading to Marine deployments in Santo Domingo, Nicaragua and Haiti.

timeline.event: Russia claims the Pacific coast of North America north of the 51st parallel, extending its Alaska colony southward.
Monroe formally recognizes Argentina, Peru, Colombia, Chile and Mexico, newly independent of Spain.
British Foreign Minister George Canning proposes a joint U.S.-British declaration against European intervention in the Americas.
Persuaded by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams, Monroe decides on a unilateral U.S. statement instead.
Monroe announces the principles in his seventh annual message, at the opening of the 18th Congress.
The United States backs Mexican President Benito Juárez against the French-supported Emperor Maximilian.
Theodore Roosevelt's corollary claims an international police power for the United States in the hemisphere.
At the Montevideo Conference the Roosevelt administration backs a declaration that no state has the right to intervene in another's affairs.
John F. Kennedy invokes the doctrine during the Cuban Missile Crisis and imposes a quarantine on Cuba with OAS support.

misconception.myth: The Monroe Doctrine was a law or treaty that the United States enforced with its own military power from 1823 onward.
misconception.fact: It was a few paragraphs in a presidential message to Congress, not a statute or treaty. European powers paid it little attention, most governments doubted the United States could enforce it, and in practice Britain's Royal Navy kept other powers out; only in the late nineteenth century did U.S. power make enforcement realistic.
misconception.why: Later presidents from Polk to Theodore Roosevelt and Kennedy invoked the doctrine so forcefully that its twentieth-century weight is easily projected back onto 1823.

title: Montgomery bus boycott
summary: A 381-day mass protest, from December 5, 1955, to December 20, 1956, in which Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, refused to ride the city's segregated buses; it ended after federal courts struck down Alabama's bus segregation laws in Browder v. Gayle.

review.question: Why did the boycott continue after the federal district court ruled against bus segregation in June 1956?
review.answer: The city appealed and kept enforcing segregation, so King and the MIA urged boycotters to stay off the buses until the ruling was actually implemented; that happened only after the Supreme Court affirmed it in November and its order reached Montgomery on December 20, 1956.

review.question: How did tens of thousands of people get to work for more than a year without the buses?
review.answer: Many walked, sometimes miles a day, and after the city penalized Black taxi drivers who offered cheap fares, the MIA organized a volunteer carpool of roughly 300 cars with pick-up stations, modeled on the 1953 Baton Rouge boycott and funded by collections at church mass meetings.

review.question: Why was Rosa Parks not a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle?
review.answer: Her criminal case was still moving through the state courts, and Fred Gray wanted the federal court to face a single issue, the constitutionality of the bus segregation laws, so he filed on behalf of other women who had been mistreated on the buses.

timeline.event: The Women's Political Council meets Mayor W. A. Gayle to ask for changes in how Black riders are treated on city buses.
Council president Jo Ann Robinson writes to the mayor that many local groups have discussed a city-wide boycott.
Fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin is removed from a Montgomery bus and arrested for defying segregation.
Rosa Parks is arrested for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger.
About 90 percent of Black riders stay off the buses; the Montgomery Improvement Association forms and elects Martin Luther King Jr. president.
The MIA presents its demands: courtesy, first-come seating and Black drivers on mainly Black routes.
Segregationists bomb King's house.
Fred Gray and Charles D. Langford file Browder v. Gayle in federal court.
King is convicted under a 1921 anti-boycott law and fined $500 or 386 days in jail.
A three-judge federal court rules 2–1 that bus segregation is unconstitutional.
The U.S. Supreme Court affirms the district court's ruling.
The Supreme Court rejects city and state requests to reconsider.
The Court's order reaches Montgomery and the MIA votes to end the boycott.
Montgomery's buses operate on an integrated basis.

misconception.myth: Rosa Parks was a quiet seamstress who kept her seat only because she was tired after work, and the boycott arose spontaneously from her single act.
misconception.fact: Parks was a longtime NAACP member and secretary of the local branch who had attended a 1955 activism workshop at the Highlander Folk School, and she later said the only tiredness she felt was being tired of giving in; Black women in Montgomery had pressed the city over bus treatment since 1954, Claudette Colvin and Mary Louise Smith had been arrested earlier in 1955, and the Women's Political Council had discussed a boycott for more than a year.
misconception.why: The "tired seamstress" story turns an organized, community-wide campaign into an accident and hides the planning, risk and sacrifice of many people, especially Black women, that made it work.

title: Morrill Land-Grant College Act
summary: The federal law signed by President Abraham Lincoln on July 2, 1862, that gave each loyal state 30,000 acres of federal land or land scrip per member of Congress to endow colleges teaching agriculture and the mechanic arts, founding the land-grant university system — largely with land taken from Native nations.

review.question: Why could the Morrill Act pass in 1862 when a similar bill had failed in 1859?
review.answer: President Buchanan vetoed the 1859 bill on fiscal and constitutional grounds; after Southern states seceded, Morrill reintroduced it with added emphasis on military instruction and Lincoln signed it on July 2, 1862.

review.question: How did a law about colleges in the East depend on Native land in the West?
review.answer: States without enough federal land received scrip to claim and sell Western land, and Western states selected land within their borders; researchers traced about 10.7 million acres to cessions from nearly 250 tribes, bands and communities, for which the United States paid less than $400,000, often nothing.

review.question: How did the 1890 Morrill Act reshape the system the 1862 act began?
review.answer: It added annual federal funding and barred racial discrimination in admissions, but let states meet that rule with separate institutions "of like character," which produced the 19 historically Black 1890 Institutions in the segregated South.

timeline.event: Illinois College professor Jonathan Baldwin Turner proposes state industrial universities at a farmers' convention in Putnam County, Illinois.
Representative Justin Smith Morrill of Vermont introduces a national land-grant college bill.
President James Buchanan vetoes the bill passed by Congress, citing cost and constitutional limits on federal power.
Morrill reintroduces the bill after Southern states secede.
Lincoln signs the Morrill Act; states in rebellion are excluded from its grants.
The Hatch Act funds agricultural experiment stations at the land-grant colleges.
A second Morrill Act adds annual appropriations and leads to the founding of separate land-grant institutions for Black students in the segregated South.
The Smith-Lever Act creates the Cooperative Extension System.
The Equity in Educational Land-Grant Status Act makes tribal colleges and universities land-grant institutions.

misconception.myth: Land-grant universities are so called because the federal government gave them the land their campuses stand on.
misconception.fact: The act gave states land or scrip — vouchers for distant federal land — to sell; the proceeds became a permanent endowment that could not be spent on buildings, and most of that land had been taken from Native nations through cessions, many of them coerced.
misconception.why: The campus story hides where the money came from — New York's scrip, sold to fund Cornell, and Dakota land ceded in Minnesota endowed colleges far from the land itself.

title: Native Americans
aliases: Indigenous peoples of the United States
Native peoples of the United States
summary: The Indigenous peoples of the land that became the United States, whose ancestors lived in the Americas for well over ten thousand years before European contact; today they belong to hundreds of distinct nations, 575 of them federally recognized, and the 2020 census counted 9.7 million people who identified as American Indian or Alaska Native alone or in combination with another race.

review.question: Why do scholars' estimates of the Native population before 1492 differ so widely?
review.answer: Early counters like James Mooney and Alfred Kroeber used numbers recorded by Europeans after contact, which already reflected deaths from epidemics; later scholars such as Henry Dobyns scaled those numbers up on the assumption that disease had killed most people before counting began, so the result depends on how large one judges the epidemic losses to have been.

review.question: How did federal policy toward Native nations change between the 1950s and the 1970s?
review.answer: In the 1950s the government pursued termination of federal supervision over tribes and relocated Native people to cities; by 1970 President Nixon called forced termination unacceptable, and the 1975 Self-Determination Act let tribes run federal programs themselves, shifting policy toward tribal self-government.

review.question: Why did gaining citizenship in 1924 not guarantee Native Americans the vote?
review.answer: Voting remained governed by state law, and some states continued to bar Native Americans from voting until 1957.

review.question: Why does the census report two different counts of the American Indian and Alaska Native population?
review.answer: The "alone" figure (3.7 million in 2020) counts only people who chose that single race, while the "alone or in combination" figure (9.7 million) also includes people who reported it together with another race.

timeline.event: Cahokia, east of present-day St. Louis, undergoes a rapid political and social transformation; its population grows almost fivefold in a generation.
The United States begins making treaties with Native nations; the Senate ratifies 370 of them by 1871.
Congress ends treaty-making with Indian tribes.
The General Allotment (Dawes) Act breaks up tribal lands into individual allotments and opens land west of the Mississippi to non-Indian settlers.
The Indian Citizenship Act makes Native Americans born in the United States citizens; about 40 percent had not been citizens before.
The Indian Reorganization Act establishes modern tribal governments.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs sets up a Branch of Placement and Relocation to move Native people from reservations to cities.
Dennis Banks, Clyde Bellecourt and George Mitchell found the American Indian Movement in Minneapolis.
President Richard Nixon asks Congress to repudiate termination and adopt a policy of self-determination.
The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act lets tribes contract to run programs formerly run by the BIA and the Indian Health Service.
The 2020 census counts 3.7 million people who identify as American Indian and Alaska Native alone and 9.7 million alone or in combination.
The Interior Department's boarding school report identifies 417 federal Indian boarding schools and at least 973 children who died while attending them.

misconception.myth: Native Americans are a vanishing people who belong to the American past.
misconception.fact: The 2020 census counted 9.7 million people who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native alone or in combination, up from 5.2 million in 2010; the United States recognizes 575 tribal nations, and more than 70 percent of Native people live in urban or suburban areas.
misconception.why: Costumes, tipis and other stock images suggest that Native cultures exist only in the past, hiding the contemporary nations and communities that survived and continue to thrive.

title: New Orleans
summary: Louisiana's largest city, founded by the French in 1718 on a natural levee near the mouth of the Mississippi River on land Choctaw speakers call Bulbancha; a colonial capital, the nation's largest antebellum slave market, the birthplace of jazz, and a low-lying port whose levees failed during Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

review.question: Why did the French choose the site of New Orleans, and what Indigenous knowledge shaped that choice?
review.answer: Bienville was told to build a city near the Mississippi's mouth to keep British and Spanish rivals from moving up the river; Native people had told his brother Iberville's 1699 expedition of a ridge (now Esplanade Ridge) linking the river to Bayou St. John and Lake Pontchartrain, which made the spot strategically valuable.

review.question: Why did Jefferson want New Orleans, and how did that lead to the Louisiana Purchase?
review.answer: Its port was the outlet for produce from more than a third of the country, and Spain's refusal in 1802 to let Americans deposit goods there angered westerners; Jefferson told Livingston to buy the city, and the negotiations ended in the April 30, 1803 treaty for all of Louisiana.

review.question: How did events in New Orleans shape Reconstruction and the fight against segregation?
review.answer: The 1866 Mechanics' Institute massacre helped bring about Radical Reconstruction and stronger congressional action, including the Fourteenth Amendment's citizenship guarantees; in 1891 the city's Comité des Citoyens organized and funded the legal challenge to the Separate Car Law that became Plessy v. Ferguson.

review.question: Why did so much of the city flood in 2005 when its oldest districts stayed relatively high?
review.answer: Most of the city was built on drained swamp that has subsided since the early 1900s, creating a bowl below sea level; when levees separating the city from Lake Pontchartrain broke during Katrina, at least 80 percent of New Orleans flooded, while the original city on natural levees stood 5 to 10 feet above sea level.

timeline.event: Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville's French expedition learns from Native guides of a ridge linking the Mississippi to Bayou St. John and Lake Pontchartrain.
Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville founds La Nouvelle-Orléans near the river's mouth.
France makes New Orleans the capital of French Louisiana.
The U.S. flag is raised in New Orleans as Louisiana passes to the United States.
Andrew Jackson's forces defeat a British army below the city, after the Treaty of Ghent was signed but before it took effect.
The city's enslaved population peaks at 23,448, nearly a quarter of its residents.
White mobs, joined by police, kill nearly fifty people at the Mechanics' Institute during a convention seeking Black men's voting rights.
Creole of color activists announce the Comité des Citoyens to challenge Louisiana's Separate Car Law.
Cornetist Buddy Bolden forms his own band, an early landmark of New Orleans jazz.
After levee breaches during Hurricane Katrina, at least 80 percent of the city lies under floodwater.
The 2020 census counts 383,997 residents.

misconception.myth: All of New Orleans lies below sea level.
misconception.fact: A 2005 USGS statement to Congress put more than half of the city below sea level, some areas by as much as 10 feet, while the original city sat on natural river levees about 5 to 10 feet above sea level, and those old levees and sandy ridges remain above it.
misconception.why: Katrina's floodwaters covering most of the city made the "bowl" image memorable, but the oldest neighborhoods stand on the high ground the founders chose, and the low areas are largely drained swamp that has sunk since the early 1900s.

title: Obergefell v. Hodges
summary: The 2015 U.S. Supreme Court decision, decided 5–4, holding that the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses require every state to license marriages between two people of the same sex and to recognize such marriages lawfully performed in other states.

review.question: Why did the Court rely on both the Due Process Clause and the Equal Protection Clause rather than only one of them?
review.answer: The majority treated the right to marry as a fundamental liberty protected by due process and held that excluding same-sex couples from it also denied them equal treatment, reasoning that the two clauses are connected and each can inform the meaning of the other.

review.question: How did the dissenting justices' main objection differ from an argument about marriage policy itself?
review.answer: Chief Justice Roberts and the other dissenters argued chiefly about who should decide; they said the Constitution leaves the definition of marriage to voters and legislatures, so the Court had wrongly ended a democratic debate, whatever one thinks of same-sex marriage as policy.

review.question: Why did Congress pass the Respect for Marriage Act in 2022 even though Obergefell was still in force, and what does that law not do?
review.answer: The act replaced the Defense of Marriage Act's federal definition with one recognizing marriages valid where performed and barred states from denying recognition to other states' marriages because of the couple's sex or race; it does not require any state to issue marriage licenses itself, and it protects nonprofit religious organizations from having to provide services for weddings.

timeline.event: Congress passes the Defense of Marriage Act, defining marriage for federal purposes as between a man and a woman and letting states refuse to recognize other states' same-sex marriages.
Massachusetts's Supreme Judicial Court rules 4–3 in Goodridge v. Department of Public Health that the state's ban on same-sex marriage is unconstitutional.
Goodridge takes effect and Massachusetts becomes the first state where same-sex couples can marry.
United States v. Windsor requires the federal government to treat lawful same-sex marriages equally; dozens of federal courts then strike down state bans.
A divided Sixth Circuit panel upholds the bans in Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky and Tennessee, reversing the trial courts.
The Supreme Court agrees to hear the four consolidated cases.
The case is argued before the Supreme Court.
The Court rules 5–4 that states must license and recognize same-sex marriages, overruling Baker v. Nelson.
The Respect for Marriage Act is signed into law, repealing the Defense of Marriage Act's marriage definition and requiring interstate recognition of marriages.
The Supreme Court denies review in Davis v. Ermold, a former Kentucky clerk's petition that had asked it to revisit Obergefell.

misconception.myth: Same-sex marriage first became legal anywhere in the United States with the Obergefell decision in 2015.
misconception.fact: Same-sex couples had been marrying in Massachusetts since May 17, 2004; by June 2015 legislators or voters in eleven states and the District of Columbia had legalized it, and federal and state courts had struck down bans in many more, so Obergefell extended marriage to the remaining states that still barred it.
misconception.why: Remembering the decision as the starting point hides a decade of state court cases, legislative votes and ballot campaigns on both sides, and it overlooks that the Court's question was whether the states that still refused could keep doing so.

title: Okies
summary: The hundreds of thousands of migrants from Oklahoma, Arkansas, Texas and Missouri who moved to California and Arizona during the Great Depression, and the community and culture they built there; "Okie" began as a nickname for Oklahomans and became a slur for any poor Southwestern newcomer.

review.question: How did "Okie" change from a simple nickname into an insult?
review.answer: It began as a shortening of "Oklahoman", but in 1930s California reporters and residents applied it to every poor migrant from Oklahoma, Arkansas, Texas or Missouri, and it came to carry the sting of an ethnic slur, reinforced by the destitute image of the Joads in The Grapes of Wrath.

review.question: If the Dust Bowl was not the main cause, why did so many Oklahomans leave in the 1930s?
review.answer: More migrants left southeastern Oklahoma than the Panhandle Dust Bowl. They were pushed out by drought combined with a long agricultural depression, farm foreclosures, widespread tenancy, and mechanization and federal crop-reduction policies that idled land, and pulled by family ties and earlier migration to California.

review.question: How did the Okie migration lead to a Supreme Court ruling on the right to travel between states?
review.answer: California made it a crime to bring a poor nonresident into the state, and Fred Edwards was convicted for bringing his unemployed brother-in-law from Texas; in Edwards v. California (1941) the Court held that the law unconstitutionally burdened interstate commerce, and concurring justices said free movement was a right of national citizenship.

review.question: How did the migrants reshape California's culture?
review.answer: They built "Little Oklahomas" in the Central Valley, brought evangelical Protestantism (especially Baptist and Pentecostal churches) and a love of country music that shaped the state's country music scene, from Bob Wills to Merle Haggard.

timeline.event: Southwesterners begin moving west to California in significant numbers.
California's Indigent Act makes it a crime to bring a poor nonresident into the state.
The migration to California begins in earnest; that summer economist Paul Taylor reports on white migrant families in the farm districts.
Los Angeles police post a border patrol, the "bum blockade", to turn back poor arrivals; it is withdrawn under threat of lawsuits.
Migration peaks in 1937 and 1938; up to 37,000 migrants reach Arizona's cotton fields.
John Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath and Carey McWilliams's Factories in the Field are published; county prosecutors charge more than two dozen people under the Indigent Act.
Fred Edwards drives from California to Spur, Texas, to bring back his brother-in-law Frank Duncan, and is later convicted.
In Edwards v. California the Supreme Court strikes down the law, holding that states cannot bar poor migrants from other states.
Oklahoma governor Dewey Bartlett launches the OKIE campaign to turn the old insult into a badge of state pride.

misconception.myth: The Okies were mostly dirt farmers who all ended up picking crops in California's fields.
misconception.fact: At least half of the migrants had lived in towns or cities and worked blue-collar or white-collar jobs, and many went to California's cities, where they usually found work fairly quickly; at the Barstow junction about 38 percent headed for Los Angeles, while others went to the farm valleys.
misconception.why: The best-known images of the migration — Steinbeck's Joad family and Dorothea Lange's photographs of farm labor camps — focused on rural families in the fields, so the much larger urban side of the story faded from popular memory.

title: Panama Canal
summary: A lock canal across the Isthmus of Panama linking the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, built by the United States from 1904 and opened on August 15, 1914, largely by West Indian laborers under a segregated pay system; the U.S. controlled it and the surrounding Canal Zone until transferring the canal to Panama on December 31, 1999.

review.question: Why did Panama, rather than Colombia, sign the 1903 canal treaty with the United States?
review.answer: Colombia's congress rejected the Hay-Herrán Treaty over its financial terms; Panama then declared independence on November 3, 1903, with U.S. warships nearby, the United States recognized it within three days, and Panama's envoy Philippe Bunau-Varilla signed the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty on November 18.

review.question: How did the gold and silver rolls shape life for the canal's workers?
review.answer: Skilled white workers, mostly from the United States, were paid in gold on the gold roll and got better housing, dining and clubs; the mostly Black West Indian laborers on the silver roll were paid in local silver at about half the wage, lived in crowded camps, did the most dangerous work such as dynamiting, and died at far higher rates.

review.question: Why did the United States succeed in building a canal where the French effort had failed?
review.answer: The French were defeated by disease and bankruptcy after about 20,000 deaths; the Americans first ran a large sanitation campaign under William Gorgas that ended yellow fever in Panama City by 1905 and cut malaria deaths sharply, and they switched to a lock design, which Stevens argued could be finished about a decade sooner than a sea-level cut.

review.question: Why did the United States agree in 1977 to hand the canal to Panama?
review.answer: Many Panamanians had long questioned the 1903 treaty, which Bunau-Varilla negotiated without formal approval from Panama's government; after the 1964 flag riot both countries saw the need for a new agreement, and U.S. officials feared isolation abroad if talks failed, so the Torrijos-Carter Treaties scheduled the transfer for December 31, 1999, while a separate treaty kept the canal permanently neutral.

timeline.event: The United States and Britain sign the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty to limit rivalry over a proposed isthmian canal.
Ferdinand de Lesseps's French company begins excavating a canal in Panama, then part of Colombia.
The Hay-Pauncefote Treaty supersedes Clayton-Bulwer, letting the United States build and run its own canal.
The U.S. Senate votes to build the canal through Panama rather than Nicaragua.
Panama declares independence from Colombia while U.S. warships stand off Colón and Panama City.
The United States recognizes the Republic of Panama.
The Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty grants the United States a ten-mile-wide Canal Zone in perpetuity.
The United States formally takes over the French works and begins construction.
The last case of yellow fever in Panama City is reported.
The House follows the Senate in choosing a lock canal over a sea-level design.
Chief engineer John F. Stevens resigns and George Washington Goethals succeeds him.
The workforce peaks at 44,733 men on the job.
The cement boat Ancon makes the first official transit, opening the canal.
A riot over flying Panama's flag in the Canal Zone briefly breaks U.S.-Panamanian relations.
Jimmy Carter and Omar Torrijos sign the Panama Canal Treaty and the Neutrality Treaty.
The Senate approves the Neutrality Treaty, 68 to 32.
The Senate approves the Panama Canal Treaty by the same 68-to-32 margin.
The Panama Canal Zone ceases to exist.
The United States transfers the canal to Panama.

misconception.myth: Ships crossing the Panama Canal from the Atlantic to the Pacific sail westward.
misconception.fact: From its Atlantic end the canal runs south for about 10 miles and then east to the Pacific, so a ship heading for the Pacific finishes its transit to the east of where it started.
misconception.why: World maps fix the Atlantic on the east and the Pacific on the west, but the Isthmus of Panama bends in an S-shape, so the general picture of the Americas misleads about this crossing.

title: Panic of 1873
summary: A financial crisis that began when the railroad-financing bank Jay Cooke and Company failed on September 18, 1873, closed the New York Stock Exchange for ten days, and set off a depression that lasted until about 1879, ruining thousands of businesses, sinking the Freedman's Savings Bank and helping to turn national politics away from Reconstruction.

review.question: How did a stock market crash in Europe help cause a banking panic in the United States?
review.answer: After the Vienna crashes of 1873, European investors sold American securities, especially railroad bonds; that cut off the borrowing that overbuilt railroads depended on, many defaulted on their bank loans, and when Jay Cooke and Company, deeply invested in the Northern Pacific Railway, failed on September 18, depositors rushed to withdraw their money from banks across the country.

review.question: Why did the panic fall so hard on Black depositors of the Freedman's Savings Bank?
review.answer: After an 1870 charter change, the bank's trustees had put depositors' savings into railroads, real estate and risky loans; the panic made most of those investments worthless, runs drained its cash, and when it closed in June 1874 its deposits had no federal protection, so only about half of the depositors ever received anything, and they recovered roughly three-fifths of their balances.

review.question: Why do historians link the depression that followed the panic to the end of Reconstruction?
review.answer: The downturn pushed economic issues ahead of Reconstruction on the national agenda, eroded Northern willingness to keep intervening in the South, and helped Democrats win the House in 1874, while white Southern Democrats were regaining power state by state; historians differ on how much weight to give the economy versus Southern political violence.

timeline.event: A stock market crash in Vienna, Austria, the first of two that year, leads European investors to start selling American securities, especially railroad bonds.
Jay Cooke and Company, heavily invested in the Northern Pacific Railway, suspends payments and goes bankrupt.
The New York Stock Exchange closes for the first time in its history and stays shut for ten days.
The New York Clearing House suspends cash payments in New York.
The acute panic subsides by mid-October, but a long depression follows.
Frederick Douglass is elected president of the struggling Freedman's Savings and Trust Company; Congress passes a bill to issue more greenback currency, which President Grant vetoes.
The Freedman's Savings and Trust Company closes, days after Congress puts its assets under a three-member board.
The Specie Resumption Act commits the Treasury to retire greenbacks and return to gold-backed currency within four years.
Railroad wage cuts during the depression set off the Great Railroad Strike.
The depression begins to lift early in the year.

misconception.myth: The Panic of 1873 was a purely American crash that began on Wall Street when Jay Cooke's bank failed.
misconception.fact: Cooke's failure turned the strain into a U.S. panic, but stock market crashes in Vienna in May and September 1873 had already led European investors to dump American railroad bonds, cutting off the credit that overbuilt U.S. railroads needed.
misconception.why: Seeing the transatlantic origins shows how closely American railroads and banks already depended on European capital, and why a crash abroad could ruin firms, workers and depositors across the United States.

title: Pennsylvania
summary: A U.S. state on the Lenape (Delaware) homeland, chartered to the Quaker William Penn in 1681, where the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were written; the first state to pass an emancipation law (1780), the second to ratify the Constitution (December 12, 1787), and an industrial powerhouse of steel, coal, oil and railroads.

review.question: Why did Charles II grant Pennsylvania to William Penn, and how did Penn's Quaker beliefs shape the colony's government?
review.answer: The most plausible explanation is that the king owed Penn a large debt inherited from his father, Admiral Penn, and paid it in land. Penn's Frame of Government created an elected assembly, and the 1701 Charter of Privileges guaranteed worship to anyone who believed in one God, making Pennsylvania an early leader in separating religion from government, although Quakers were always a minority.

review.question: How did the Walking Purchase change the Lenape's place in Pennsylvania, and what did that lead to?
review.answer: Using an unsigned 1686 draft deed, proprietary agents had pre-scouted walkers cover more than 60 miles in a day and a half and angled the boundary to take perhaps over a million acres. Most Delawares in eastern Pennsylvania moved west to the Ohio Valley, traded with the French, and many sided with France in the Seven Years' War; the Lenape were later pushed on to Indiana, Kansas and Indian Territory.

review.question: Why did slavery linger in Pennsylvania for decades after the 1780 abolition law?
review.answer: The act freed no one at once; children born to enslaved mothers after it passed were bound as servants until age 28, and enslavers could keep registered people enslaved. The state recorded its last known enslaved person in the 1850s, and enslavers like President Washington rotated enslaved people in and out of Philadelphia to evade the residency rules.

review.question: How did Pennsylvania's resources make it the "Arsenal of America," and what labor conflicts came with that growth?
review.answer: Coal, oil (from 1859 near Titusville), more than 10,000 miles of railroad at its peak, and steel (60 percent of the nation's output in 1900) made it an industrial center that produced almost a third of U.S. steel in World War II. Growth brought violent conflicts such as the 1877 railroad strike in Pittsburgh, the 1892 Homestead Strike, and the 1897 Lattimer massacre of Slavic miners.

timeline.event: Swedes and Finns found New Sweden on the Delaware River, among Lenape communities already living on both banks.
Charles II grants William Penn the Charter of Pennsylvania, settling a debt owed to Penn's father.
Penn arrives on the Welcome; Philadelphia is laid out as the capital.
The provincial Assembly adopts the Great Law.
The Charter of Privileges guarantees worship to anyone who acknowledges one almighty God; it stays in force until 1776.
The Walking Purchase begins; proprietary agents use an unsigned 1686 draft deed to take perhaps over a million acres of Lenape land.
Mason and Dixon survey the boundary with Maryland.
Pennsylvania adopts its first state constitution, with a one-house Assembly and no governor.
The Assembly passes the Gradual Abolition Act, the first emancipation statute in the United States.
Pennsylvania becomes the second state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.
President Washington leads an army to suppress the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania.
The state capital moves to Harrisburg, after a stay in Lancaster from 1799.
A new state constitution disenfranchises free African Americans.
Commercial oil production begins near Titusville.
Union forces under Meade defeat Lee's invading army at Gettysburg.
The Homestead Strike ends in defeat for the steelworkers' union.
Pennsylvania produces 60 percent of U.S. steel.
The census counts 13,002,700 residents.

misconception.myth: Penn's "Great Treaty" with the Lenape under the elm at Shackamaxon was the one treaty never broken, so colonial Pennsylvania dealt honestly with Native people.
misconception.fact: No original written record of a 1682 treaty exists and historians debate whether and when it happened; and in 1737 Thomas Penn and agent James Logan used an unsigned draft deed in the Walking Purchase to take a vast tract of Lenape land, which a scholarly encyclopedia describes as defrauding the Delawares.
misconception.why: Voltaire's praise and Benjamin West's 1771–72 painting turned a possible meeting into a founding legend that still appears in textbooks, while the dispossession that followed is less visible in public memory.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
summary: The 1896 U.S. Supreme Court decision that upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers, giving constitutional approval to state-imposed racial segregation under what became known as the "separate but equal" doctrine.

review.question: Why did Homer Plessy board a whites-only car on a train that stayed inside Louisiana rather than an interstate train?
review.answer: Weeks earlier, in Abbott v. Hicks, the Louisiana Supreme Court had ruled that the Separate Car Act did not apply to interstate passengers, so the Comité des Citoyens needed an intrastate trip to test the law's constitutionality directly.

review.question: How did Justice Brown's majority answer the argument that forced separation stamped Black citizens as inferior?
review.answer: He said any such stigma did not come from the law itself but from how Black Americans chose to interpret it, and he treated segregation as a reasonable use of a state's police power that could take established customs into account.

review.question: Why is Plessy considered so consequential even though it concerned railroad cars?
review.answer: By holding that state-mandated separation did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment if accommodations were nominally equal, it gave legal cover to segregation in schools, transportation and public life for more than half a century, until Brown v. Board of Education rejected the doctrine in public education in 1954.

timeline.event: Louisiana's legislature passes the Separate Car Act (Act No. 111), requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers.
Eighteen New Orleans residents form the Comité des Citoyens to challenge the law in court.
Daniel Desdunes boards a whites-only car on an interstate train in a first test case.
In Abbott v. Hicks the Louisiana Supreme Court rules that the act does not apply to interstate passengers.
Homer Plessy is arrested after sitting in the whites-only coach of an East Louisiana Railroad train to Covington.
Judge John Howard Ferguson of the Orleans Parish Criminal Court rules against Plessy.
The Louisiana Supreme Court upholds Ferguson's ruling.
The U.S. Supreme Court affirms, 7 to 1, with Justice Henry Billings Brown writing and Justice John Marshall Harlan dissenting.
Plessy pleads guilty in New Orleans and pays a $25 fine.
Brown v. Board of Education rejects separate but equal in public education.
Louisiana Governor John Bel Edwards grants Plessy a posthumous pardon.

misconception.myth: The Supreme Court's majority opinion in Plessy announced the phrase "separate but equal."
misconception.fact: The majority opinion speaks of the statute's "equal but separate" accommodations; the words "separate but equal" appear in Justice Harlan's dissent, and the label for the doctrine became common afterward.
misconception.why: Knowing the exact wording shows that the Court was approving a state statute's own formula, and that the promise of equality was a legislative claim the majority accepted rather than tested.

title: Reynolds v. Sims
summary: The 1964 U.S. Supreme Court decision, written by Chief Justice Earl Warren, holding that the Equal Protection Clause requires the seats in both houses of a state legislature to be apportioned by population, applying the principle of one person, one vote to state lawmaking bodies.

review.question: How had rural Alabamians come to control the state legislature by the early 1960s?
review.answer: Although the 1901 constitution required reapportionment after each census, the legislature had not reapportioned since the 1900 census while nearly all of the state's growth came in urban areas; by the 1960 census about a quarter of the population lived in districts that could elect a majority of each house.

review.question: Why did the Court reject the argument that a state senate could be modeled on the U.S. Senate?
review.answer: It held that the federal arrangement grew out of a unique historical compromise among sovereign states, whereas counties and other political subdivisions are subordinate instruments of the state, so the federal analogy did not apply to state legislatures.

review.question: How did Reynolds build on Baker v. Carr?
review.answer: Baker (1962) held that apportionment challenges could be heard by federal courts; Reynolds supplied the substantive standard, requiring both houses to be apportioned so that districts were as nearly equal in population as practicable.

review.question: How did opponents of the ruling try to reverse it, and why did they fail?
review.answer: They proposed a constitutional amendment allowing one house of a state legislature to be apportioned using geography and political subdivisions as well as population; it won a 57 to 39 majority in the Senate on August 4, 1965, but fell short of the two-thirds a constitutional amendment requires.

timeline.event: Alabama's new constitution requires legislative seats to be reapportioned by population after each federal census; no statewide reapportionment follows the 1900 census.
Young Jefferson County lawyers file suit in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama, with M. O. Sims among the plaintiffs.
In Baker v. Carr the Supreme Court holds that challenges to legislative apportionment can be heard by federal courts.
Judges Frank M. Johnson and Richard T. Rives rule for the plaintiffs, and the court orders a temporary plan for the 1962 election.
In Gray v. Sanders the Court strikes down Georgia's county-unit system, declaring the principle of one person, one vote.
The Supreme Court hears oral argument in Reynolds v. Sims.
In Wesberry v. Sanders the Court requires congressional districts to be as equal in population as practicable.
The Court decides Reynolds 8 to 1 along with companion cases from New York, Maryland, Virginia, Delaware and Colorado.
A proposed constitutional amendment to let one legislative house be apportioned on factors besides population wins 57 to 39 in the Senate, short of two-thirds.
Avery v. Midland County extends the equal-population rule to elected local governments.
Mahan v. Howell upholds a state legislative map with a 16.4 percent total deviation, allowing more leeway than for congressional districts.
Evenwel v. Abbott holds that states may draw legislative districts using total population.

misconception.myth: Reynolds v. Sims coined the phrase "one person, one vote."
misconception.fact: The phrase entered the Supreme Court's case law a year earlier, in Gray v. Sanders (1963), which struck down Georgia's county-unit system for statewide elections; Reynolds applied that equality standard to the seats of both houses of state legislatures.
misconception.why: Because Reynolds reshaped every state legislature, it became the case most associated with the slogan, which blurs the sequence by which the Court built the doctrine from Baker to Gray, Wesberry and Reynolds.

title: Roosevelt Corollary
aliases: Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine
summary: The extension of the Monroe Doctrine that President Theodore Roosevelt announced in his annual message to Congress on December 6, 1904, claiming for the United States a right to intervene in Latin American and Caribbean nations that failed to keep order or pay foreign creditors, so that European powers would have no pretext to intervene themselves; it was officially abandoned in 1934.

review.question: Why did a crisis over Venezuela's debts prompt Roosevelt to rethink the Monroe Doctrine?
review.answer: The 1902 European blockade of Venezuela showed that European powers would use force to collect debts in the Americas; Roosevelt feared such actions could become invasions, so he claimed a U.S. right to step in first and make sure creditors were paid.

review.question: How did the corollary turn the Monroe Doctrine's meaning around?
review.answer: Monroe's 1823 doctrine was a largely passive warning to Europeans not to intervene in the hemisphere, while the corollary justified U.S. intervention, including later occupations of Haiti and the Dominican Republic.

review.question: How did the Dominican customs receivership show the corollary in practice?
review.answer: A U.S.-appointed receiver collected Dominican customs duties and applied them to receivership costs and a refinanced debt before passing the rest to the Dominican government, which could not raise its debt or change tariffs without U.S. agreement.

review.question: Why did Roosevelt use executive agreements in the Dominican case?
review.answer: Critics said his January 1905 agreement bypassed the Senate, and when Democratic opposition blocked a treaty, he put the receivership into effect by a modus vivendi until the Senate approved a convention in 1907.

timeline.event: James Monroe's annual message warns European powers against new colonization or intervention in the Americas.
British, German and Italian warships blockade Venezuela's ports after it defaults on debts to foreign bondholders.
Theodore Roosevelt announces the corollary in his annual message to Congress.
A U.S.-Dominican executive agreement gives the United States control of Dominican customhouses; critics say it bypasses the Senate.
With Senate action on a treaty blocked, Roosevelt puts a customs receivership into effect by a modus vivendi.
The United States and the Dominican Republic sign a convention at Santo Domingo making the receivership formal.
The U.S. Senate advises ratification of the Dominican convention.
Roosevelt proclaims the convention in force.
Undersecretary of State J. Reuben Clark's memorandum challenges the corollary on legal grounds.
At the Montevideo conference the United States pledges non-intervention in the hemisphere.
Franklin D. Roosevelt's Good Neighbor policy officially abandons the corollary.

misconception.myth: The Roosevelt Corollary was simply part of the Monroe Doctrine as announced in 1823.
misconception.fact: It was a separate statement made more than eighty years later, in Theodore Roosevelt's December 1904 message to Congress. The 1823 doctrine asked European powers to stay out of the hemisphere; the corollary claimed a right for the United States itself to intervene.
misconception.why: Roosevelt presented his policy as an extension of Monroe's, and the two are usually taught together, so the later claim of a U.S. police power is easily read back into 1823.

title: September 11 attacks
summary: The coordinated al Qaeda terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, in which 19 hijackers seized four U.S. airliners and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York City, the Pentagon in Virginia and a field in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.

review.question: Why did the 9/11 Commission call imagination the most important failure before the attacks?
review.answer: Officials had warnings about al Qaeda and earlier attacks such as the 1998 embassy bombings and the 2000 USS Cole attack, but no one treated the use of hijacked airliners as weapons as a real threat; the Commission found that U.S. measures between 1998 and 2001 never disturbed or delayed the plot.

review.question: How did the actions of the people aboard United 93 change the outcome of the attacks?
review.answer: After learning by phone of the other hijackings, the passengers and crew voted to fight back and forced the plane down in a Pennsylvania field about 20 minutes' flying time from Washington, so it never reached its probable target, the U.S. Capitol or the White House.

review.question: How did the attacks reshape the federal government at home?
review.answer: Within weeks the president created a White House Office of Homeland Security, Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act and created the TSA in 2001, and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 merged 22 agencies into a new Cabinet department; the 9/11 Commission's 2004 report then led to proposals such as a National Counterterrorism Center and a national intelligence director.

timeline.event: Al Qaeda leader Usama Bin Ladin approves the airliner plot conceived by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed (late 1998 or early 1999).
By early July all 19 hijackers, who had begun entering the country in January 2000, are inside the United States.

Hijacked airliners strike the World Trade Center's North Tower (8:46 a.m.) and South Tower (9:03 a.m.) and the Pentagon (9:37 a.m.); United 93 crashes in Pennsylvania at 10:03 a.m. after a passenger and crew revolt.
President George W. Bush signs the Authorization for Use of Military Force against those responsible.
Bush signs the USA PATRIOT Act, expanding surveillance and security powers.
U.S. air strikes against Taliban and al Qaeda targets in Afghanistan begin Operation Enduring Freedom.
The recovery effort at Ground Zero formally ends with the removal of the Last Column.
The Department of Homeland Security opens, combining parts or all of 22 federal agencies.
The bipartisan 9/11 Commission issues its final report and closes on August 21, 2004.
NIST issues its final report on the collapse of the Twin Towers.
The National September 11 Memorial opens to the public, a day after its dedication on the tenth anniversary.

misconception.myth: The Twin Towers were brought down by a planned controlled demolition using explosives or thermite rather than by the hijacked planes.
misconception.fact: The federal engineering investigation by NIST found that the impacts severed columns and stripped fireproofing, and that multi-floor fires weakened floors that pulled the perimeter columns inward until they failed; it found no corroborating evidence for explosives, and seismic signals came from falling debris after each collapse began.
misconception.why: The towers' sudden, total collapse was unprecedented and hard to grasp, and demolition stories replace a documented chain of failures and warnings with a hidden plot that the engineering and investigative record does not support.

title: Siege of Vicksburg
summary: The 47-day Union siege of the Confederate river fortress at Vicksburg, Mississippi, from May 18 to July 4, 1863, in which Ulysses S. Grant's army forced John C. Pemberton's garrison to surrender, giving the Union control of the Mississippi River and splitting the Confederacy.

review.question: Why did both sides consider Vicksburg so important?
review.answer: Confederate guns on its bluffs blocked Union traffic on the Mississippi, on which Midwestern farmers depended, and the city linked the eastern Confederacy to the supplies and men of Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas; taking it would reopen the river and split the South.

review.question: How did Grant finally get his army into position to besiege Vicksburg after months of failure?
review.answer: He crossed the river south of the city on April 30–May 1, 1863, won a string of battles inland through May 17 that drove Pemberton back into the city, and after two failed assaults on May 19 and 22 settled into a siege.

review.question: Why did Pemberton surrender on July 4 rather than fight his way out?
review.answer: After about six weeks of siege, hunger and disease had worn down his garrison; his commanders judged a breakout impossible, and Grant's offer to parole the men rather than imprison them was the best term available.

review.question: How did the fall of Vicksburg lead to Union control of the entire Mississippi?
review.answer: The garrison at Port Hudson, Louisiana, the last Confederate stronghold on the river, surrendered on July 9, 1863, after learning Vicksburg had fallen, opening the river from its source to New Orleans.

timeline.event: Union gunboats attack Vicksburg from upriver in the spring but eventually withdraw; Grant's first overland and river attempts follow that fall.
Grant's army crosses the Mississippi from Louisiana into Mississippi south of Vicksburg on the night of April 30–May 1.
Union victory at Port Gibson opens an inland campaign that wins at Raymond, Jackson, Champion Hill and the Big Black River by May 17.
Grant's Army of the Tennessee reaches the Confederate defenses of Vicksburg.
Sherman's corps assaults the Stockade Redan and is repulsed with about 1,000 Union casualties.
A second general assault on a three-mile front fails, and Grant settles into a siege.
Black Union regiments help repel a Confederate attack on the supply post at Milliken's Bend, Louisiana.
Union engineers explode 2,200 pounds of black powder under a Confederate redan on the Jackson Road; the crater fight gains no ground.
Pemberton and Grant meet between the lines; that night Grant offers to parole the garrison.
At 10 a.m. some 29,000 Confederates march out, stack their arms and surrender the city.
Port Hudson, Louisiana, surrenders after learning of Vicksburg's fall, opening the whole Mississippi to Union navigation.
Lincoln's public letter to James C. Conkling celebrates the reopened river and credits Black soldiers.
The last Union occupation troops, including U.S. Colored Troops, are withdrawn from Vicksburg.
The Mississippi African-American Monument is dedicated in Vicksburg National Military Park.

misconception.myth: Lincoln's line that the Father of Waters again flowed "unvexed to the sea" was his spontaneous reaction to the news from Vicksburg.
misconception.fact: The sentence appears in a public letter he wrote to James C. Conkling on August 26, 1863, nearly two months after the surrender, in a passage that also credits soldiers from many regions and Black troops.
misconception.why: Detaching the line from the letter loses Lincoln's purpose, which was to defend emancipation and Black enlistment to Northern critics by pointing to victories like Vicksburg.

title: Slavery in the United States
aliases: Chattel slavery in the United States
summary: The system of hereditary, race-based chattel slavery that held people of African descent, and in the colonial era many Native Americans, as property in the English colonies and the United States from the early 1600s until the Thirteenth Amendment abolished it in 1865.

review.question: Why did Virginia's 1662 law matter so much for slavery's growth?
review.answer: It made a child's status follow the mother's rather than the father's, so every child of an enslaved woman was born enslaved; slavery became hereditary and could grow through births rather than only through imports.

review.question: How did the enslaved population grow from about 700,000 in 1790 to nearly 4 million in 1860 even though importing enslaved people was banned from 1808?
review.answer: Because children of enslaved mothers were born enslaved, the population grew through births, and the domestic slave trade then moved about a million people from the Upper South to the cotton-growing Deep South.

review.question: How did slavery reach into the free states before the Civil War?
review.answer: The Constitution's fugitive slave clause required people escaping bondage to be returned, and the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 used federal commissioners without juries to send about 1,000 Black Americans South, provoking resistance in northern communities.

timeline.event: The English privateer White Lion lands about twenty captive Africans at Point Comfort, Virginia, and sells them for food.
Virginia's General Assembly rules that a child is enslaved or free according to the mother's status, making slavery hereditary.
A Virginia law classes enslaved people as real estate.
Pennsylvania passes a gradual emancipation law.
The federal ban on importing enslaved people takes effect.
Slavery ends in New York under its 1817 law.
Nat Turner's rebellion begins in Southampton County, Virginia.
Congress passes a Fugitive Slave Act that denies accused people a jury trial.
The census counts 3,953,760 enslaved people, the peak and the last census to count them.
General Order No. 3 announces freedom in Galveston, Texas, the origin of Juneteenth.
The Thirteenth Amendment is ratified, abolishing slavery nationwide.
New Jersey's governor signs a state constitutional amendment ending slavery there.

misconception.myth: Slavery was a purely Southern institution that the North never practised.
misconception.fact: Slavery was legal in the North too; enslaved people were 30 percent of Kings County (Brooklyn) residents in 1790, New York's final emancipation came only in 1827, and about 16 people in New Jersey were still legally enslaved in December 1865.
misconception.why: Treating slavery as only Southern hides how gradual and incomplete northern emancipation was, and how northern banks and merchants profited from the cotton economy.

title: Sojourner Truth
summary: An abolitionist, preacher and women's-rights advocate (c. 1797–1883) who was born enslaved in Ulster County, New York, freed herself in 1826, won a New York court case in 1828 to recover her son from slavery in Alabama, and from 1843 travelled as Sojourner Truth, speaking against slavery and for the rights of women and freed people.

review.question: Why do historians treat Marius Robinson's 1851 account of the Akron speech as more reliable than Frances Gage's 1863 version?
review.answer: Robinson published his within weeks of the convention and is believed to have reviewed it with Truth, while Gage wrote twelve years later without Truth's review and put a Northern-born, Dutch-speaking woman's words into Southern dialect.

review.question: How did New York law help Truth recover her son Peter in 1828?
review.answer: New York's gradual-emancipation laws forbade selling an enslaved New Yorker out of state in a way that denied the person the benefits of those laws, so his sale to Alabama was illegal and she could sue for his return, which she won.

review.question: How did Truth fund her work during the Civil War years?
review.answer: She sold copies of her Narrative and cartes de visite of herself at lectures and by mail, registering a copyright in the photographs in 1864 so that the income came to her.

timeline.event: Born Isabella Baumfree, about this year, to James and Elizabeth Baumfree, enslaved in Ulster County, New York.
Bought by John Dumont of West Park, New York, after being sold three times as a child.
Dumont breaks his promise to free her; she leaves with her infant daughter Sophia and is taken in by the Van Wagenen family.
New York's emancipation law takes effect.
Wins People v. Solomon Gedney in New York's courts, recovering her son Peter, who had been illegally sold to Alabama.
Takes the name Sojourner Truth and begins travelling to preach and speak against slavery.
The Narrative of Sojourner Truth, dictated to Olive Gilbert, is published.
Speaks at the Woman's Rights Convention in Akron, Ohio.
Marius Robinson's account of her Akron speech appears in the Anti-Slavery Bugle.
Moves to Harmonia, Michigan, near Battle Creek.
Frances Dana Gage publishes her dialect version of the Akron speech in The Independent.
Her copyright claim for cartes de visite titled "I sell the Shadow to Support the Substance" is recorded.
Meets President Abraham Lincoln at the White House while working for the National Freedman's Relief Association.
Campaigns for federal land grants to formerly enslaved people and meets President Ulysses S. Grant.
Dies at her home in Battle Creek, Michigan, and is buried in Oak Hill Cemetery.

misconception.myth: At Akron in 1851 Sojourner Truth gave a speech in Southern dialect, repeating "Ain't I a woman?" and telling how she had borne thirteen children, most sold into slavery.
misconception.fact: The refrain, the dialect and the thirteen children come from Frances Dana Gage's version published in 1863, twelve years later. Marius Robinson's account, printed within weeks of the convention, has no such refrain; Truth, raised in New York speaking Dutch, never lived in the South, and she had five children.
misconception.why: Gage's dramatic version was reprinted widely, entered later editions of Truth's own Narrative and became the text schoolbooks quote, so the more reliable 1851 record was long overlooked.

title: Supreme Court of the United States
summary: The highest court of the federal judiciary, created by Article III of the Constitution and organized by the Judiciary Act of 1789; it decides cases arising under the Constitution and federal law, mostly on appeal, and since Marbury v. Madison (1803) has claimed the power to strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution.

review.question: Why can Congress change the number of Supreme Court justices without amending the Constitution?
review.answer: Article III creates "one supreme Court" but says nothing about its size, so the number is set by statute; the Judiciary Act of 1789 set six, and later laws moved it between five (never in effect) and ten before an 1869 act fixed it at nine.

review.question: How did Marbury v. Madison expand the Court's role in the system of checks and balances?
review.answer: Chief Justice John Marshall held that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 conflicted with the Constitution and that courts must follow the Constitution when a statute conflicts with it, the first time the Court declared an act of Congress unconstitutional and the basis of judicial review.

review.question: Why did Franklin D. Roosevelt's 1937 plan to enlarge the Court fail?
review.answer: Many saw it as a threat to judicial independence; a bipartisan Senate Judiciary Committee majority urged its emphatic rejection, the Court began upholding New Deal-era laws such as the minimum-wage law in West Coast Hotel v. Parrish, Justice Van Devanter retired, and the Senate defeated the plan on July 22, 1937.

review.question: How does most of the Court's work reach it, and how selective is it?
review.answer: Most cases arrive as petitions for a writ of certiorari asking the Court to review a lower-court decision; four justices must agree to take a case, and of up to about ten thousand requests a year the Court accepts fewer than 2 percent.

timeline.event: The Judiciary Act of 1789 organizes the Court with a chief justice and five associate justices.
The Court first convenes in the Exchange Building in New York City, a day late because some justices could not arrive in time.
The Court issues its first opinion, in West v. Barnes.
The Court follows the capital from Philadelphia to Washington and is lent space in the Capitol.
In Marbury v. Madison the Court for the first time declares an act of Congress unconstitutional.
Congress adds a seventh seat.
Congress adds two more seats, bringing the Court to nine.
Chief Justice Roger B. Taney announces the Dred Scott decision.
A tenth seat is authorized during the Civil War.
Congress reduces the authorized seats to seven, to be reached as vacancies occur.
Congress fixes the Court at nine justices, where it has remained.
Chief Justice Charles Evans Hughes lays the cornerstone of the Supreme Court Building.
The Court moves into its own building in its 146th year.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt asks Congress for up to six additional justices.
The Court upholds a Washington State minimum-wage law for women in West Coast Hotel v. Parrish.
Roosevelt's plan to enlarge the Court is defeated in the Senate.
Thurgood Marshall is sworn in as the first African American justice.
Sandra Day O'Connor is sworn in as the first woman justice.

misconception.myth: The Constitution requires the Supreme Court to have nine justices.
misconception.fact: Article III creates "one supreme Court" but sets no size; the Judiciary Act of 1789 gave it six justices, Congress changed the authorized number several times, and the figure of nine dates only from an 1869 statute.
misconception.why: Because nine has stood for more than 150 years, an ordinary act of Congress is easily mistaken for a constitutional rule.

title: Thanksgiving
summary: A national holiday of the United States, observed on the fourth Thursday of November, that grew out of colonial and presidential days of thanksgiving, became an annual national observance with Abraham Lincoln's 1863 proclamation, and was fixed in federal law in 1941; its popular link to the 1621 Plymouth harvest gathering is remembered very differently by many Native people.

review.question: Why did the Wampanoag ally with the Plymouth colonists in 1621, according to the Smithsonian's account?
review.answer: Epidemics between 1616 and 1619 had killed up to 90 percent of New England's Native population, and the weakened Wampanoag also needed help against the rival Narragansett, so they agreed to a mutual-defense treaty; the alliance was driven by diplomacy more than friendship.

review.question: How did Thanksgiving become a fixed annual national holiday rather than an occasional proclamation?
review.answer: Sarah Josepha Hale campaigned for decades for a national day; Lincoln's 1863 proclamation set the last Thursday of November, and presidents kept proclaiming the day until Roosevelt's 1939 change caused confusion, after which Congress in 1941 fixed it by law on the fourth Thursday of November.

review.question: Why did Congress choose the "fourth" rather than the "last" Thursday of November in 1941?
review.answer: The Senate amended the House resolution so that the date would stay consistent in years when November has five Thursdays, the problem that had prompted the 1939 change.

timeline.event: Epidemics brought by Europeans begin sweeping coastal New England; by 1619 they have killed up to 90 percent of the region's Native people.
Wampanoag leader Ousamequin (Massasoit) and about 90 men join the Plymouth colonists for a three-day harvest gathering, probably in late September or early October.
At Congress's request, George Washington proclaims Thursday, November 26, 1789, a day of public thanksgiving and prayer.
Sarah Josepha Hale, editing the Ladies' Magazine in Boston, begins writing in favor of a national Thanksgiving.
Abraham Lincoln proclaims the last Thursday of November a national day of thanksgiving, after a letter from Hale dated September 28.
Congress makes Thanksgiving a holiday in the District of Columbia, leaving its date to the President.
Franklin D. Roosevelt moves Thanksgiving to the second-to-last Thursday of November; states split over which date to observe.
Roosevelt signs H.J. Res. 41, fixing Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday of November from 1942.
Frank James (Wamsutta), an Aquinnah Wampanoag, speaks on Cole's Hill in Plymouth on Thanksgiving Day, beginning the annual National Day of Mourning.

misconception.myth: Americans have celebrated Thanksgiving every year since the Pilgrims and their friendly Indian neighbors held the "first Thanksgiving" in 1621.
misconception.fact: The 1621 event was a three-day harvest gathering that also reinforced a new diplomatic alliance between the Wampanoag and the English; neither surviving English account calls it a thanksgiving. The national holiday descends from later official proclamations, above all Lincoln's in 1863, and the familiar story of a friendly shared meal took hold only in the mid-1800s.
misconception.why: The storybook version leaves out the Wampanoag's own reasons for the alliance, the epidemics that had devastated their communities, and the colonization and violence that followed — which is why many Native people mark the day as one of mourning.

title: The West
summary: The western part of the United States, defined by the Census Bureau as a 13-state region of Mountain and Pacific divisions; a largely arid land of Native homelands and former Mexican territory that the United States conquered and settled in the nineteenth century, where the federal government still owns much of the land, and whose meaning historians have long debated.

review.question: Why did Frederick Jackson Turner treat 1890 as a turning point, and how did Patricia Nelson Limerick challenge his view?
