review.answer: Turner took the 1890 census's finding that there was no longer a frontier line as the end of the westward advance that he believed had shaped American individualism and democracy; Limerick rejected the "closing frontier" model and described the West instead as a place of continuing conquest over land, resources and peoples, and wrote Native, Mexican, Chinese, Black and women's histories into the story.

review.question: Why did John Wesley Powell argue that the 160-acre homestead did not suit much of the West?
review.answer: Beyond about the 100th meridian, average rainfall is less than twenty inches a year, too little for most crops, so Powell recommended irrigation-based farming and ranching rather than small dry farms on the eastern model.

review.question: How did the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo shape the West, and what promise was weakened before ratification?
review.answer: Mexico ceded 55 percent of its territory, including present-day California, Nevada, Utah, New Mexico, most of Arizona and Colorado, for $15 million; the Senate struck Article X, which guaranteed protection of Mexican land grants, though Article VIII still promised to respect Mexicans' property.

review.question: Why does the federal government own so much more land in the West than in the East?
review.answer: The Congressional Research Service points partly to early treaties, land settlement laws and settlement patterns, along with the reservation of western parks and other reserves from 1872 on, and since 1976 federal law has generally kept the remaining public domain in federal hands; by 2024 about 46 percent of the 11 contiguous western states and 61 percent of Alaska was federal.

timeline.event: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo is signed; Mexico cedes 55 percent of its territory, including present-day California, Nevada and Utah.
Congress passes the Homestead Act, offering 160-acre claims to settlers who live on and improve the land for five years.
The U.S. Army begins forcing Navajo people on the Long Walk to Bosque Redondo, where they are held until 1866.
Colorado militia under John Chivington kill about 200 Cheyenne men, women and children at Sand Creek.
The Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads meet in Utah, completing the first transcontinental line.
Yellowstone is established, beginning the reservation of western lands as parks.
George Armstrong Custer and 268 of his men are killed at the Little Bighorn.
Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West show begins touring, spreading a romantic image of the West.
The Dawes General Allotment Act divides reservation land into individual allotments and opens the 'surplus' to settlers.
U.S. troops kill between 150 and 300 Lakota men, women and children at Wounded Knee.
Frederick Jackson Turner presents his frontier thesis to the American Historical Association in Chicago.
The Federal Land Policy and Management Act declares that remaining public-domain land will generally stay in federal ownership.
The last remaining homestead entries are eliminated.
Patricia Nelson Limerick publishes The Legacy of Conquest.
The 2020 census counts 78,588,572 people in the West region.

misconception.myth: The West was an empty wilderness of free land waiting for American settlers.
misconception.fact: Native nations controlled most of the continent west of the Mississippi deep into the nineteenth century, and the Mexican Cession brought Mexican citizens whose property the 1848 treaty promised to respect; the land became available to settlers through wars, treaties, removal and allotment.
misconception.why: Turner's emphasis on free land, dime novels and Wild West shows told the story from the settlers' side, leaving out the peoples whose homelands were taken.

title: Theodore Roosevelt
summary: The 26th president of the United States (1901–1909), a New York Republican who took office at 42 after William McKinley's assassination, regulated big business under his "Square Deal," protected about 230 million acres of public land, won the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize, and ran for president again in 1912 as a Progressive.

review.question: How did Roosevelt end the 1902 anthracite coal strike, and how did that episode give his domestic program its name?
review.answer: When the mine owners refused to negotiate, he threatened to have troops seize and run the mines as a federal operation; both sides then agreed to accept the recommendations of a commission. He called the settlement a "square deal," and the phrase became the name of his whole domestic program.

review.question: Why is it inaccurate to say that Roosevelt founded the National Park Service, even though he shaped the park system?
review.answer: The National Park Service was created in 1916, seven years after he left office. He shaped the system by helping create 23 of the 35 sites the agency inherited and by proclaiming 18 national monuments under the 1906 Antiquities Act.

review.question: Why do historians describe Roosevelt's record on race as divided or mixed?
review.answer: He invited Booker T. Washington to dine at the White House and appointed some Black Southerners to office, yet he discharged 167 Black soldiers after the Brownsville shooting without a trial, did little to stop Black disfranchisement, and, as Gary Gerstle argues, combined a civic nationalism open to European immigrants with a racial nationalism that excluded nonwhite Americans.

timeline.event: Born at 28 East 20th Street in New York City.
Graduates from Harvard College.
Wins a seat in the New York State Assembly.
First travels to the Dakota Badlands, where he later ranches.
His mother and his first wife, Alice, die in the same house on the same day.
Appointed to the U.S. Civil Service Commission by President Benjamin Harrison.
Resigns from the Civil Service Commission and becomes a New York City police commissioner.
Leads the Rough Riders in the fighting for the San Juan Heights in Cuba, alongside Black regulars of the 9th and 10th Cavalry.
Sworn in as president at 42 after the assassination of William McKinley.
Dines with Booker T. Washington at the White House, provoking a storm of criticism from white Southerners.
Brings coal operators and miners' leaders to the White House and pushes them into arbitration to end the anthracite coal strike.
The Supreme Court upholds the government's antitrust suit against the Northern Securities Company; Roosevelt wins a full term in a landslide.
Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his role in ending the Russo-Japanese War.
Signs the Antiquities Act, which he then uses to proclaim 18 national monuments.
A shooting in Brownsville, Texas, is blamed on Black soldiers of the 25th Infantry; Roosevelt later discharges 167 of them without honor or trial.
Leaves the presidency after keeping a pledge not to seek another term.
Leads the new Progressive ("Bull Moose") Party after losing the Republican nomination to William Howard Taft.
Shot in Milwaukee before a speech; his folded speech and spectacle case slow the bullet.
Explores an uncharted river in Brazil.
Dies at Oyster Bay, New York.

misconception.myth: Theodore Roosevelt created the National Park Service.
misconception.fact: The National Park Service was established in 1916, seven years after Roosevelt left office. What he did do was help create 23 of the 35 sites the new agency inherited, proclaim 18 national monuments under the Antiquities Act, and create the U.S. Forest Service in 1905.
misconception.why: Crediting him with the agency blurs the difference between the parks and monuments he set aside and the bureau that later managed them, and hides the separate national-forest system he built.

title: Third Locks Project
summary: A U.S. program, authorized by Congress on August 11, 1939, to build a third and larger set of locks for the Panama Canal near the existing Gatun, Pedro Miguel and Miraflores locks for defense and commerce; excavation began in 1940 and the Secretary of War halted it in May 1942.

review.question: Why did Congress authorize a third set of locks for the Panama Canal in 1939?
review.answer: Ships, especially warships, were growing too wide for the 110-foot lock chambers, and officials feared one act of sabotage could cripple the existing locks, so with war looming they backed larger, separately sited locks to improve both defense and commercial capacity.

review.question: Why did President Roosevelt sign the 1939 law while objecting to part of it?
review.answer: He wanted the third locks for the security of the canal and the hemisphere, but the law required new skilled and supervisory construction hires to be U.S. citizens, which he said conflicted with the 1936 treaty pledge of equal job opportunity for Panamanians, so he promised to seek an amendment.

review.question: Why was the project stopped in 1942?
review.answer: After Pearl Harbor naval priorities shifted from battleships to aircraft carriers, the Montana-class battleships the locks were sized for were suspended, wartime money and materials were needed elsewhere, and Army commanders argued new locks would add another air-attack target; Secretary of War Stimson halted the work on May 23, 1942.

review.question: How did the abandoned 1940s work affect the canal's 21st-century expansion?
review.answer: On the Atlantic side, Panama built its new, larger lock chambers on the original third-locks excavation, which sped construction; on the Pacific side the locks were placed elsewhere and the old cut was filled in.

timeline.event: The canal report later adopted as the plan for the work (House Document No. 210) is dated.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt signs H.R. 5129, capping the cost at $277 million, and objects to its citizenship hiring rule.
The State Department sends Roosevelt's statement to the U.S. ambassador to share with Panama's government.
The State Department tells Panama that a funding bill will again lack equal hiring for Panamanians, with an amending bill promised.
Excavation begins, with dredging at the Pacific end of the channel to the new Miraflores lock site.
Dry excavation begins in the Gatun sector.
Secretary of War Henry Stimson halts the project after nearly 13 million cubic yards have been removed.
The Navy cancels the Montana-class battleships whose width the new locks were meant to accommodate.
Panama breaks ground on its own Third Set of Locks Project, reusing the Atlantic-side excavations.
Panama's expanded canal opens with new locks on both coasts.

misconception.myth: The third set of Panama Canal locks that opened in 2016 was an idea first pursued in the 2000s.
misconception.fact: The United States authorized a third set of larger locks in 1939 and dug for nearly two years before halting the work in 1942; Panama's expansion later built its Atlantic-side locks on that original excavation.
misconception.why: The 1940s work stopped before any lock was built, so it left only dormant channels rather than a landmark, and it is easily overlooked in accounts of the modern expansion.

title: Thirteenth Amendment
aliases: Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
summary: The 1865 amendment to the U.S. Constitution that abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime, and gave Congress power to enforce that ban.

review.question: Why did Lincoln and Congress believe a constitutional amendment was needed even after the Emancipation Proclamation?
review.answer: The proclamation rested on Lincoln's war powers and applied only to areas in rebellion, not to loyal border states; its legal force after the war was doubtful, so an amendment was the only secure way to end slavery everywhere.

review.question: How did the 1864 election and the end of the war help the amendment pass and be ratified?
review.answer: After the House first failed to reach two-thirds, Lincoln's reelection campaign put the amendment on the Republican platform and a lame-duck session passed it in January 1865; later, President Andrew Johnson required Southern states seeking readmission to abolish slavery, and Georgia's ratification in December 1865 completed the three-fourths.

review.question: Why is the amendment's exception "as a punishment for crime" significant?
review.answer: Southern states used criminal convictions to lease mostly Black prisoners to private companies, as Georgia did from 1868 to 1908, and scholars still debate whether the framers meant the clause to permit that kind of forced labor.

timeline.event: Congress passes the Corwin Amendment, which would have shielded slavery in the states; it is never ratified.
The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect, but only in areas in rebellion.
The Senate Judiciary Committee under Lyman Trumbull reports the amendment to the full Senate.
The Senate passes the amendment, 38 to 6.
The House passes the amendment, 119 to 56, after earlier votes fell short.
Lincoln approves the joint resolution sending the amendment to the states.
Georgia becomes the 27th state to ratify, completing the three-fourths needed.
Secretary of State William H. Seward proclaims the amendment ratified.

misconception.myth: The Emancipation Proclamation ended slavery throughout the United States.
misconception.fact: The 1863 proclamation applied only to areas in rebellion and left slavery legal in loyal border states; slavery ended nationwide only with the Thirteenth Amendment, which freed people still enslaved in Delaware and Kentucky in December 1865.
misconception.why: Confusing a wartime executive order with a constitutional amendment hides why abolitionists, Congress and Lincoln fought for an amendment, and how close slavery came to surviving the war.

title: Thomas Jefferson
summary: A Virginia planter, lawyer and founder (1743–1826) who drafted the Declaration of Independence, wrote Virginia's statute for religious freedom, served as secretary of state and vice president, and was the third president of the United States (1801–1809), while holding more than 600 people in slavery over his lifetime.

review.question: Why did the House of Representatives, not the voters or the electors, decide the presidential election of 1800?
review.answer: Electors then cast two undifferentiated votes, so Jefferson and his running mate Aaron Burr tied at 73 electoral votes each; the Federalist-controlled House deadlocked for 35 ballots before choosing Jefferson on the 36th, on February 17, 1801.

review.question: How did the Louisiana Purchase test Jefferson's own reading of the Constitution?
review.answer: Jefferson doubted that the Constitution gave the president power to acquire territory and considered an amendment, but public support and the land's value led him to set aside his strict reading, a choice that helped build the principle of implied federal powers.

review.question: How did Jefferson's 1803 letter to William Henry Harrison propose to obtain Native land?
review.answer: He proposed government trading houses that would draw Native leaders into debt, which they would pay off by ceding land, and he expected Native nations either to be absorbed as citizens or to move west of the Mississippi.

timeline.event: Born at Shadwell plantation in western Virginia.
Admitted to the Virginia bar.
Enters the Virginia House of Burgesses, where he serves until 1774.
As a delegate to the Second Continental Congress, drafts the Declaration of Independence.
His wife, Martha Wayles Jefferson, dies after childbirth.
Begins about four years as American minister to France.
Virginia's General Assembly adopts his bill for religious freedom, first drafted in 1777.
Becomes secretary of state under George Washington; resigns in 1793.
Becomes vice president under John Adams after finishing second in the 1796 electoral vote.
The House of Representatives elects him president on its 36th ballot, breaking a 73-73 electoral tie with Aaron Burr.
The United States buys Louisiana from France for $15 million.
In a private letter to William Henry Harrison, lays out a plan to acquire Native lands through trade debts.
Signs the act banning the importation of enslaved people, effective January 1, 1808.
Congress passes his Embargo Act, barring American ships from leaving U.S. ports.
Signs the Non-Intercourse Act replacing the embargo, three days before leaving office.
Dies at Monticello, fifty years after the Declaration's approval.

misconception.myth: Thomas Jefferson wrote that the government is best which governs least.
misconception.fact: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation finds no such line in his writings; the earliest known printing of the wording is John L. O'Sullivan's 1837 introduction to the Democratic Review, and the earliest known attribution to Jefferson dates only from 1853.
misconception.why: The phrase was long associated with the political heirs of Jefferson's Democratic-Republican party, so it drifted onto the party's founder, and a familiar name makes a slogan sound authoritative.

title: Treaty of Paris (1783)
summary: The peace treaty between Great Britain and the United States, signed in Paris on September 3, 1783, that ended the American Revolutionary War, recognized the independence of the thirteen states, and set boundaries reaching west to the Mississippi River without any terms for the Native nations whose lands lay inside them.

review.question: Why did the American commissioners sign preliminary terms with Britain in November 1782 that could not take effect at once?
review.answer: The United States was allied with France, so the preliminary articles were written to take effect only after Britain and France agreed their own peace terms; France and Britain signed their preliminaries on January 20, 1783, and the definitive treaty followed on September 3.

review.question: How did Article 7 of the treaty, which barred the British from carrying away enslaved people, end up being applied in New York?
review.answer: Sir Guy Carleton read it as not covering Black people who had already joined the British, so they could not be returned as property; about 3,000 in New York received passes recorded in the Book of Negroes, and upwards of 9,000 people of African descent left with the British from New York and other ports.

review.question: Why did the treaty leave the Haudenosaunee and other Native nations to negotiate separately with the United States?
review.answer: The treaty was between Britain and the United States only and contained no negotiated terms for Britain's Native allies, so each nation had to make its own peace, as the Six Nations did under pressure at Fort Stanwix in 1784.

review.question: How did disputes over the treaty's debt and western-post terms help make the case for a stronger national government?
review.answer: Virginia closed its courts to British creditors because Britain had broken the treaty, and British garrisons stayed at Detroit, Niagara and other posts inside U.S. borders; Federalists argued that only a Congress able to tax and raise an army could force Britain to leave.

timeline.event: Formal peace negotiations open in Paris between British envoys and the American commissioners Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay.
The British and American commissioners sign preliminary articles of peace, to take effect only once Britain and France agree terms.
Britain and France sign their own preliminary articles, and an armistice is declared.
David Hartley and the three American commissioners sign the definitive treaty at the Hôtel de York in Paris; Britain's treaties with France and Spain are signed at Versailles the same day.
The Confederation Congress, meeting in Annapolis, ratifies the treaty.
With no terms for Britain's Native allies in the treaty, U.S. commissioners dictate a separate peace to the Six Nations at Fort Stanwix.

misconception.myth: In the Treaty of Paris, the Native nations east of the Mississippi gave up their lands to the United States.
misconception.fact: The treaty was made between Britain and the United States alone, signed only by their commissioners, and contained no terms at all for Britain's Native allies; Britain signed away only its own claims, and each nation was left to make its own peace with the United States, which at Fort Stanwix in 1784 treated four of the Six Nations as defeated enemies. A Native confederacy north of the Ohio went on to defeat U.S. armies in 1790 and 1791.
misconception.why: The treaty's boundary lines put the whole region between the Appalachians and the Mississippi inside the United States on paper, which makes it easy to read a European diplomatic agreement as if it settled who actually held and governed the land.

title: Tribal sovereignty
aliases: Tribal sovereignty in the United States
summary: The principle that Native nations are self-governing political communities whose authority over their members and territory predates the United States; federal law recognizes this inherent sovereignty and a government-to-government relationship with the 575 federally recognized tribes, while holding that Congress can limit it.

review.question: Why did the Supreme Court in Worcester v. Georgia hold that Georgia's laws could not reach the Cherokee Nation?
review.answer: Chief Justice John Marshall reasoned that Indian nations had always been distinct, independent political communities whose relations with the United States ran through treaties and federal law, so the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community occupying its own territory where state law had no force, and the Georgia statute used to convict Samuel Worcester was void.

review.question: How is tribal sovereignty both inherent and limited under federal law?
review.answer: The Court treats tribal powers as inherent, existing before and apart from the United States, yet it has also held that Congress has broad (plenary but not absolute) power over Indian affairs and can restrict tribal authority, as when courts held tribes lack criminal jurisdiction over non-Indians without congressional authorization.

review.question: How did termination policy in the 1950s and 1960s run against the principle of tribal sovereignty?
review.answer: Termination sought to end federal recognition and trust protection of tribes and shifted reservation jurisdiction to states; Congress began 60 termination proceedings and more than three million acres of tribal land were lost before the policy was repudiated in 1970 in favor of self-determination.

timeline.event: The United States signs its first treaty with a Native nation, the Lenape (Delaware); both sides treat early treaties as diplomatic agreements between sovereigns.
In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia the Supreme Court calls tribes "domestic dependent nations" and declines to hear the Cherokee suit.
In Worcester v. Georgia the Court holds that Georgia law has no force within the Cherokee Nation.
Congress forbids further treaty-making with tribes; more than 370 ratified treaties remain law.
United States v. Kagama upholds federal criminal laws on reservations as a power to protect dependent peoples.
House Concurrent Resolution 108 announces the policy of terminating federal supervision of tribes.
Public Law 280 shifts criminal and civil jurisdiction on most reservations in five states to state authorities.
The Nixon administration repudiates termination and turns federal policy toward tribal self-determination.
United States v. Wheeler describes tribal powers as inherent; Oliphant v. Suquamish Indian Tribe denies tribes criminal jurisdiction over non-Indians.
California v. Cabazon Band of Mission Indians holds that state regulation of on-reservation bingo would infringe tribal government.
McGirt v. Oklahoma holds that only Congress, by clear statement, can disestablish a reservation.

misconception.myth: Tribal sovereignty is a privilege the federal government granted to Native Americans as a racial group.
misconception.fact: Federal law treats tribal self-government as inherent, held before the United States existed and acknowledged in treaties and the Constitution rather than created by them; tribal status is political, attaching to nations and their citizens, not to race.
misconception.why: Because Congress can limit tribal powers and federal agencies administer many tribal programs, sovereignty is easy to mistake for a federal gift, and because tribal citizens are Native people, a political status is easy to mistake for a racial one.

title: United States
summary: A federal republic in North America made up of fifty states and the District of Columbia, with five inhabited territories and 575 federally recognized tribal nations within its borders; it declared independence from Great Britain on July 4, 1776, took its name in 1776, won recognition in the Treaty of Paris of 1783, and has been governed under the Constitution since 1789.

review.question: How did the United States grow from thirteen states on the Atlantic seaboard into a country reaching the Arctic and the Pacific, and who paid the cost?
review.answer: The 1783 Treaty of Paris set its western boundary at the Mississippi River; the Louisiana Purchase (1803) added about 530 million acres, and Alaska was bought from Russia in 1867; Alaska and Hawaii became states in 1959. The land was Native homeland, and expansion came at Native nations' expense; under the 1830 Indian Removal Act nearly 50,000 eastern Indians were relocated, and about 4,000 of 16,000 Cherokees died on the Trail of Tears.

review.question: Why does the Constitution apply differently in Puerto Rico or Guam than in a state?
review.answer: They are unincorporated territories, insular areas that are not part of any state or the federal district, where Congress has decided that only selected parts of the Constitution apply. Puerto Rico and the Northern Mariana Islands are also commonwealths with a more developed relationship set out in written agreements.

review.question: Why does the Declaration of Independence speak of the "united States of America" with a lowercase "united," and when did the name become official?
review.answer: In mid-1776 the states saw themselves as separate states acting together. Congress ordered "United States" to replace "United Colonies" in official documents on September 9, 1776, and the Articles of Confederation's first article made "The United States of America" the confederacy's formal name.

review.question: How do Native nations fit into the U.S. political system today?
review.answer: The 575 federally recognized tribes hold inherent rights of self-government (tribal sovereignty) and a government-to-government relationship with the United States, alongside the federal government, the fifty states, the District of Columbia and the territories.

timeline.event: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, enters a period of rapid growth; at its peak it is the largest settlement north of Mexico.
The mapmaker Martin Waldseemüller labels the Western Hemisphere's landmasses "America" after Amerigo Vespucci.
The Second Continental Congress votes for independence by adopting the Lee Resolution.
Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence.
Congress orders that "United States" replace "United Colonies" in official documents.
Congress adopts the Articles of Confederation, whose first article names the confederacy "The United States of America."
Maryland's ratification puts the Articles of Confederation into force.
The Treaty of Paris recognizes U.S. independence, with a western boundary at the Mississippi River.
The present-day Constitution goes into effect, replacing the Articles.
The Residence Act fixes the permanent seat of government on the Potomac River; Congress moves to Washington in 1800.
The United States buys the Louisiana territory, about 530 million acres, from France for $15 million.
President Andrew Jackson signs the Indian Removal Act.
Cherokees are forcibly removed to Indian Territory in 1838–39; about 4,000 of 16,000 die on the Trail of Tears.
The Thirteenth Amendment is ratified, abolishing slavery except as punishment for crime.
Alaska, bought from Russia for $7.2 million, is formally transferred to the United States.
Queen Liliuokalani writes to the House objecting to the U.S. claim of ownership over Hawaii.
Alaska becomes a state.
Hawaii becomes the fiftieth state.
The census counts 331,449,281 residents, up 7.4 percent from 2010.

misconception.myth: When Europeans arrived, the land that became the United States was a thinly peopled, untouched wilderness.
misconception.fact: Millions of Indigenous people lived in the Americas before 1492; they farmed corn, beans and squash, burned underbrush to shape forests, and built towns such as Cahokia, which may have held 10,000–20,000 people (some estimates run to 30,000) around 1050–1150.
misconception.why: Picturing an empty continent erases the Native nations whose homelands became the United States, and whose 575 federally recognized governments still keep a government-to-government relationship with it.

title: United States Congress
summary: The legislative branch of the U.S. federal government, created by Article I of the Constitution: a two-chamber body made up of the House of Representatives, apportioned among the states by population, and the Senate, with two members per state, which first met in 1789.

review.question: Why does Congress have two chambers with different bases of representation?
review.answer: The framers created a bicameral legislature in July 1787 in which House seats are apportioned among the states by population while every state has two senators, balancing the interests of populous and small states.

review.question: How did the Seventeenth Amendment change the Senate, and why was it adopted?
review.answer: It replaced election of senators by state legislatures with election by the people; legislative selection had produced long deadlocks (45 in 20 states between 1891 and 1905), vacant seats and bribery cases, and many states had already moved to popular choice through primaries before the amendment was ratified in 1913.

review.question: How did the original Constitution's formula for apportioning House seats involve slavery?
review.answer: Article I counted the whole number of free persons, excluded "Indians not taxed," and added three-fifths of "all other Persons," meaning enslaved people, who could not vote, still added to the representation of the states that held them.

review.question: Why was the First Congress unable to start work on March 4, 1789?
review.answer: Too few members had arrived in New York; only 8 of 22 senators and 13 of 59 representatives were present, so neither chamber had a quorum until April 1 (House) and April 6 (Senate).

timeline.event: Delegates at the Constitutional Convention agree on a two-chamber legislature with equal state representation in the Senate.
The First Federal Congress is scheduled to convene at Federal Hall in New York City, but neither chamber has a quorum.
The House of Representatives achieves the first quorum.
The Senate achieves its first quorum and the electoral votes for president are counted.
Representative James Madison proposes constitutional amendments on the House floor.
Congress begins a ten-year residence in Philadelphia.
The Senate moves into the unfinished Capitol in Washington, D.C.
British troops set fire to the Capitol during the War of 1812.
Hiram Revels is sworn in as the first African American senator.
A federal law fixes the House at 433 seats, plus one each for Arizona and New Mexico on statehood.
The Seventeenth Amendment, providing for popular election of senators, is ratified.
The Senate adopts its first cloture rule to limit filibusters.
Hattie Caraway becomes the first woman elected to the Senate.
The Legislative Reorganization Act reforms the committee system.

misconception.myth: The Constitution fixes the House of Representatives at 435 members.
misconception.fact: The Constitution set only the House's first size (65 members) and a minimum of one representative per state; Congress set the number by law, enlarging the House after most censuses, fixing it at 433 plus two in 1911 and capping it at 435 from 1929, apart from a temporary 437 after Alaska and Hawaii joined.
misconception.why: Because 435 has not changed for about a century, it is easy to mistake an ordinary statute that Congress could amend for a constitutional rule.

title: United States Constitution
aliases: Constitution of the United States of America
summary: The supreme law of the United States, a four-page charter signed in Philadelphia on September 17, 1787, and ratified in 1788 that created the federal government of three separate branches, divided power between the nation and the states, and has been amended twenty-seven times.

review.question: How does the Constitution try to keep any one part of the government from becoming too powerful?
review.answer: It separates legislative, executive and judicial power among Congress, the president and the courts, gives each checks on the others such as the veto, veto override, Senate confirmation, impeachment and judicial review, and divides power between the national government and the states.

review.question: Why did several states ratify only after being promised amendments, and what came of that promise?
review.answer: Anti-Federalists feared a strong central government could threaten individual liberties and demanded a bill of rights; the First Congress proposed twelve amendments in September 1789, and ten were ratified on December 15, 1791, as the Bill of Rights.

review.question: How did the original Constitution protect slavery without using the word "slave"?
review.answer: It used euphemisms such as other persons and persons held to service or labor; it counted three-fifths of enslaved people for representation and taxes, barred Congress from banning their importation before 1808, and required the return of people who escaped slavery into another state.

review.question: How did Charles Beard's interpretation of the Constitution differ from that of later ideological historians?
review.answer: Beard argued in 1913 that the framers and ratifiers acted mainly to protect their economic interests, while historians such as Bernard Bailyn and Gordon Wood argued that political ideas, especially republicanism, better explain the framing; later scholarship has largely undermined Beard's account.

timeline.event: A quorum of seven states is finally present and the Federal Convention opens in the Pennsylvania State House.
Delegates sign the finished four-page Constitution in Philadelphia.
Delaware becomes the first state to ratify.
New Hampshire becomes the ninth state to ratify, enough for the Constitution to take effect.
The date the framers set for the new Congress to convene.
The Senate achieves its first quorum.
The First Congress proposes twelve amendments to the states.
Rhode Island becomes the thirteenth and last original state to ratify.
Ten of the twelve proposed amendments are ratified as the Bill of Rights.
A pay amendment proposed in 1789 is ratified as the Twenty-seventh Amendment.

misconception.myth: The Constitution declares that "all men are created equal."
misconception.fact: That phrase comes from the Declaration of Independence. The original Constitution contained no such promise and instead counted three-fifths of enslaved people for apportionment; an equality guarantee entered the text only with the Fourteenth Amendment after the Civil War.
misconception.why: Running the two founding documents together hides how the 1787 text accommodated slavery and how much the Reconstruction amendments changed it.

title: Voting Rights Act of 1965
summary: The federal statute, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on August 6, 1965, that enforced the Fifteenth Amendment by banning racial discrimination in voting nationwide, outlawing literacy tests, and placing jurisdictions with a record of disenfranchisement under federal registration and "preclearance" oversight.

review.question: Why did Congress single out certain states and counties for preclearance instead of relying only on lawsuits?
review.answer: Case-by-case litigation was slow and easily evaded, so Section 4 used a formula (a voting test or device in 1964 plus registration or turnout under 50 percent) to identify places with a record of disenfranchisement, and Section 5 required them to get federal approval before changing voting rules; the Supreme Court said this shifted the "advantage of time and inertia" from those discriminating to their victims.

review.question: How did the Selma campaign help produce the Act?
review.answer: Violence against peaceful marchers, especially on Bloody Sunday in March 1965, drew national outrage; Johnson sent voting rights proposals to Congress within days and later credited the events at Selma with prompting federal action, though he had already been considering reform after the 1964 election.

review.question: How did Shelby County v. Holder change the Act without striking down Section 5 itself?
review.answer: The Court held that the Section 4(b) coverage formula relied on decades-old data, so no jurisdiction could be required to seek preclearance until Congress wrote a new formula, which it has not done.

review.question: What did the 1982 amendment to Section 2 change, and why?
review.answer: After Mobile v. Bolden (1980) required proof of discriminatory purpose in vote-dilution cases, Congress amended Section 2 so a violation could be shown without proving intent.

timeline.event: Voting rights activist Jimmie Lee Jackson dies of a gunshot wound inflicted by a white man in Alabama, prompting calls for a march from Selma to Montgomery.
On "Bloody Sunday," law enforcement officers attack about 600 marchers leaving Selma for Montgomery.
President Johnson outlines his voting rights proposals in a televised address to a joint session of Congress.
Some 25,000 marchers led by Martin Luther King Jr. reach Montgomery under federal protection.
The Senate passes S. 1564, 77 to 19, a day after invoking cloture 70 to 30 to end a filibuster.
The House passes H.R. 6400, 333 to 85.
Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act at the Capitol, a day after Congress completed final passage.
In South Carolina v. Katzenbach the Supreme Court upholds the Act's constitutionality.
Congress extends Section 5 preclearance for five years.
Congress extends preclearance for seven years and adds protections for language-minority citizens.
Congress renews the special provisions for 25 years and amends Section 2 so plaintiffs need not prove discriminatory purpose, responding to Mobile v. Bolden (1980).

Congress renews the special provisions for 25 more years in the Fannie Lou Hamer, Rosa Parks, Coretta Scott King, Cesar E. Chavez, Barbara Jordan, William Velazquez and Dr. Hector Garcia reauthorization act.
In Shelby County v. Holder the Supreme Court, 5 to 4, holds the Section 4(b) coverage formula unconstitutional, halting preclearance.
In Louisiana v. Callais the Supreme Court, 6 to 3, holds that Section 2 imposes liability in redistricting only where evidence supports a strong inference of intentional discrimination.

misconception.myth: Black Americans' right to vote rests on the Voting Rights Act and will expire unless Congress renews the Act.
misconception.fact: The bans on racial discrimination in voting in the Fifteenth Amendment and in the Act's core provisions, such as Section 2, are permanent; only the "special provisions" for certain jurisdictions, such as Section 5 preclearance and federal examiners and observers, were written with expiration dates and periodically renewed.
misconception.why: The rumor, which the Justice Department publicly called false, confuses temporary remedies with the underlying constitutional right, and it can distract from the real debates over how the Act's remedies should work.

title: War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)
summary: The twenty-year U.S.-led war in Afghanistan, launched on October 7, 2001, after the September 11 attacks to destroy al Qaeda's base and topple the Taliban government that sheltered it, which ended with the Taliban's return to power and the final U.S. withdrawal from Kabul on August 30, 2021.

review.question: Why did the United States go to war in Afghanistan in 2001?
review.answer: After the September 11 attacks Congress authorized force against those who planned them and anyone who harbored them; al Qaeda was based in Afghanistan under Taliban protection, so U.S. strikes began on October 7, 2001, to destroy al Qaeda's base and drive the Taliban from power.

review.question: How did the war in Iraq affect the war in Afghanistan?
review.answer: From 2003 U.S. attention and resources shifted to Iraq, where about 150,000–170,000 U.S. troops served against about 20,000 in Afghanistan; officials later said Afghanistan was under-managed in those years as the Taliban regrouped and violence rose from about 2005–2006.

review.question: How did the 2020 Doha agreement contribute to the events of August 2021?
review.answer: It committed the United States to withdraw all forces within 14 months without conditioning that on reduced Taliban violence; Congressional researchers reported it demoralized Afghan forces, and the later departure of contractors who maintained aircraft and supplied air support helped the Afghan military collapse as the Taliban took Kabul on August 15, 2021.

timeline.event: Congress's Authorization for Use of Military Force against those responsible for the September 11 attacks, and those who harbored them, is approved.
U.S. air strikes begin against Taliban military installations and al Qaeda training camps.
Hamid Karzai's southern opposition forces and U.S. Marines take Kandahar after the Taliban abandon Kabul and the north.
NATO assumes command of the UN-mandated International Security Assistance Force (ISAF).
In a speech at West Point, President Obama approves a surge of 33,000 more U.S. troops, with withdrawals to begin in July 2011.
Navy SEALs kill Osama bin Laden at a compound near Abbottabad, Pakistan.
Afghan forces begin taking over security responsibility from international troops.
ISAF's combat mission having ended in late 2014, NATO's smaller train-and-advise Resolute Support mission begins.
The United States and the Taliban sign the Agreement for Bringing Peace to Afghanistan in Doha, Qatar, setting a 14-month withdrawal timeline.
President Biden announces a final withdrawal to begin May 1, later setting August 31 as the end of the military mission.
The Taliban enter Kabul and President Ashraf Ghani flees the country.
A suicide bombing claimed by the Islamic State affiliate at a Kabul airport gate kills 13 U.S. service members and dozens of Afghans.
The last U.S. forces leave Kabul, ending the U.S. military and diplomatic withdrawal.

misconception.myth: Afghanistan's army collapsed in 2021 simply because its soldiers would not fight.
misconception.fact: At least 66,000 Afghan troops were killed in the war (SIGAR, 2021), and Congressional researchers traced the collapse to structural causes — corruption that left soldiers unpaid or unfed, dependence on departing U.S. contractors for maintenance, intelligence and air support, overstretched rural outposts, and demoralization after the 2020 U.S.-Taliban agreement.
misconception.why: The speed of the Taliban's August 2021 advance made a single explanation tempting, but it hides two decades of heavy Afghan losses and the design choices that left the force unable to sustain itself once foreign support ended.

title: Winged Figures of the Republic
summary: A pair of 30-foot bronze winged figures by the Norwegian-born sculptor Oskar J. W. Hansen, set on black diorite bases beside a 142-foot flagpole in a terrazzo plaza on the Nevada end of Hoover Dam, whose inlaid star map fixes the sky at the moment Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated the dam on September 30, 1935.

review.question: How does the star map let a future viewer work out when Hoover Dam was dedicated?
review.answer: Hansen laid out the positions of celestial bodies as they stood at the dam's dedication on September 30, 1935, and set them within a Circle of Precession showing the slow wobble of Earth's axis known as the Platonic Year, so the sky's arrangement fixes the moment even without a written date.

review.question: Why do some catalogues date the figures to 1935 when the plaza was finished in 1938?
review.answer: The Smithsonian's sculpture inventory ties the work to the dam's 1935 dedication, which the star map commemorates, but Reclamation photographs show Hansen still overseeing fabrication of the star map in April 1938, and the plaza was completed that year.

review.question: How did the builders set the heavy bronze figures on their polished bases without scratching them?
review.answer: The diorite bases were placed on blocks of ice and guided into position as the ice melted, avoiding scars to the polished stone and floor.

review.question: Why did Hansen describe the figures in terms of vigilance, and what is wrong with crediting that idea to Jefferson?
review.answer: Hansen said the figures stood for the eternal vigilance that is the price of liberty, casting them as sentries of the Republic; Monticello finds no evidence Jefferson ever said this, tracing it instead to John Philpot Curran.

timeline.event: President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicates the dam, then called Boulder Dam; Hansen's star map later records the sky at this moment.
The monument plaza on the Nevada side is completed.
A Reclamation photograph shows Hansen checking fabrication of the Circle of Precession for the terrazzo star map.
Hansen is photographed at the figures with Carl J. Hambro, president of the Norwegian Parliament.
The terrazzo floor receives its first repairs.
Hansen supervises a rebuilding of the terrazzo floor.
Visitor access to the plaza closes during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Reclamation contractors begin a full restoration; the figures are sandblasted and repatinated and the old star map is demolished to install drainage.
Preservationists launch a Save the Star Map campaign after the terrazzo work stalls.

misconception.myth: Thomas Jefferson coined the phrase "eternal vigilance is the price of liberty," which Hansen invoked to explain his statues.
misconception.fact: Monticello's research staff have found no evidence that Jefferson said or wrote it; the idea traces to John Philpot Curran, and the modern wording circulated in American newspapers without his name, first credited to Jefferson in print in 1834.
misconception.why: Patriotic maxims tend to migrate to the most famous founder, and a phrase carved into civic memory, as at Hoover Dam, rarely carries its real source with it.

title: Women's suffrage movement
aliases: Women's suffrage movement in the United States
summary: The seven-decade campaign to win American women the right to vote, which began with the women's rights conventions of the late 1840s, split and reunited over the Reconstruction amendments, won the vote state by state in the West, and secured the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, though many women of color stayed disfranchised for decades afterward.

review.question: Why did the women's suffrage movement split in 1869, and how did the two wings differ?
review.answer: The proposed Fifteenth Amendment barred racial discrimination in voting but not sex discrimination; Lucy Stone backed it and formed the American Woman Suffrage Association to win the vote state by state, while Stanton and Anthony opposed it, used racist arguments against Black men voting, and formed the National Woman Suffrage Association to seek a federal amendment.

review.question: How did NAWSA's and the National Woman's Party's different strategies combine to win the Nineteenth Amendment?
review.answer: Catt's 1916 Winning Plan concentrated NAWSA's resources on promising state campaigns, lobbying Congress and preparing for ratification, while Alice Paul's National Woman's Party kept pressure on President Wilson through parades, White House picketing, arrests and hunger strikes; together they built the pressure that brought Wilson's support in 1918 and passage by Congress in 1919.

review.question: Why did many women remain unable to vote after 1920?
review.answer: The amendment only banned sex discrimination, so other barriers still applied; Native American women were mostly not citizens until 1924, Chinese immigrant women could not become citizens under exclusion laws, and Southern states used the same discriminatory laws, intimidation and violence against Black women that they used against Black men.

timeline.event: The two-day women's rights convention at Seneca Falls, New York, opens and drafts the Declaration of Sentiments, which demands the vote.
Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony help form the American Equal Rights Association to seek suffrage for Black Americans and women alike.
The movement splits over the Fifteenth Amendment into the National and American Woman Suffrage Associations; Wyoming Territory enfranchises women.
Susan B. Anthony is arrested for voting in Rochester, New York, and Sojourner Truth is turned away from the polls in Battle Creek, Michigan.
Senator Aaron Sargent of California introduces the woman suffrage amendment in the Senate.
The Senate takes its first vote on the amendment and defeats it, 16 to 34.
The rival associations merge as the National American Woman Suffrage Association; Wyoming enters the Union with women's suffrage.
Colorado becomes the first state to adopt a state amendment enfranchising women.
Black clubwomen including Mary Church Terrell, Ida B. Wells-Barnett and Harriet Tubman form the National Association of Colored Women.
Alice Paul's suffrage procession in Washington, held the day before Woodrow Wilson's inauguration, is attacked by hostile crowds.
Carrie Chapman Catt unveils NAWSA's Winning Plan at its Atlantic City convention.
The National Woman's Party's Silent Sentinels begin picketing the White House.
New York adopts woman suffrage.
President Wilson addresses the Senate to urge passage of the amendment, which fails the next day.
The House of Representatives passes the amendment.
The Senate passes the amendment 56 to 25, sending it to the states.
Wisconsin becomes the first state to ratify.
Tennessee becomes the thirty-sixth state to ratify, completing ratification.
Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby certifies the Nineteenth Amendment.

misconception.myth: The Nineteenth Amendment gave all American women the right to vote in 1920.
misconception.fact: The amendment barred denying the vote on account of sex, but most Native American women were not citizens until 1924, Chinese immigrant women were barred from citizenship by exclusion laws, and Black women in the Jim Crow South faced the same disfranchisement and violence that kept Black men from the polls.
misconception.why: Treating 1920 as the finish line erases decades of further struggle by women of color and hides how race, citizenship and state law continued to decide who could vote.

title: Wright brothers' first flight
aliases: First flight of the Wright Flyer
summary: The four powered, controlled flights that Wilbur and Orville Wright of Dayton, Ohio, made in their engine-driven Flyer from the dunes at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903 — the first sustained flights of a heavier-than-air machine under a pilot's control.

review.question: Why did two Ohio bicycle makers test their aircraft on the North Carolina Outer Banks?
review.answer: They wanted steady winds, hills, soft sand and few trees; of the weather stations they wrote to, only Kitty Hawk replied, and its weatherman Bill Tate offered to host them.

review.question: How did the flight of December 17, 1903, differ from earlier hops and glides by other experimenters?
review.answer: Others had glided or lifted off briefly, but the Wrights' Flyer took off under its own engine power and flew in sustained flight under the pilot's complete control — the first such demonstration of a heavier-than-air machine.

review.question: Why did the 1903 Flyer spend twenty years outside the Smithsonian?
review.answer: After Langley's death the Smithsonian displayed his rebuilt Aerodrome as the first airplane capable of sustained flight, based on modified 1914 tests by Glenn Curtiss; Orville sent the Flyer to London in protest and it returned only after the Smithsonian published a correction in 1942, arriving in 1948.

timeline.event: The Wrights begin testing gliders on the Outer Banks near Kitty Hawk, whose weather station had answered their inquiry about steady winds and open sand.
Wilbur glides 622 feet in 21 seconds, setting American distance and time records for gliders.
The brothers file their patent application for a "Flying-Machine".
Samuel Langley's Smithsonian-backed Great Aerodrome crashes on its second launch attempt.
Wilbur wins a coin toss for the first try, but the Flyer stalls and noses into the sand.
Four powered flights from Kill Devil Hills; Orville flies 120 feet in 12 seconds, Wilbur 852 feet in 59 seconds.
The Wrights move their experiments to Huffman Prairie near Dayton with a sturdier new machine.
U.S. Patent 821,393 for the Wrights' flying machine is granted.
President Calvin Coolidge signs the act creating the Kill Devil Hill National Memorial.
Amid a feud with the Smithsonian, Orville ships the 1903 Flyer to the Science Museum in London.
The Flyer is installed at the Smithsonian, 45 years to the day after it flew.

misconception.myth: The Wright brothers first flew in the town of Kitty Hawk.
misconception.fact: The flights took off from the sand dunes at Kill Devil Hills, about four miles south of the village of Kitty Hawk; the brothers walked to Kitty Hawk afterwards to send the telegram announcing their success.
misconception.why: Kitty Hawk was the nearest village — its weather station first invited the brothers and their telegram was sent from there — so its name travelled with the news.

title: Wright Company School of Aviation
summary: The flight-training school run by Orville and Wilbur Wright's Wright Company from 1910 to 1916, which began in Montgomery, Alabama, settled at Huffman Prairie near Dayton, Ohio, and trained 119 pilots there, including some of the U.S. Army's first aviators.

review.question: Why did the Wrights start their school in Montgomery rather than in Dayton, and why did it move back so soon?
review.answer: Dayton's winter weather was poor for flying, and Montgomery offered less rain and suitable winds; but engine trouble, weather and the need to prepare for exhibition tours in June led Wilbur to close the camp in May 1910 and move training to Huffman Field.

review.question: How did the school help shape American military aviation?
review.answer: Army officers such as Henry H. Arnold and Thomas Milling learned to fly there in 1911 and then helped start the Army's first permanent flight school at College Park, Maryland; Arnold later commanded the Army Air Corps.

review.question: How did the school serve the Wright Company's business as well as teaching?
review.answer: It shared a hangar with the company's test flying and exhibition team, produced pilots for the exhibition circuit, and marketed the Wrights' airplanes to civilian and military buyers.

timeline.event: Wilbur Wright picks Frank Kohn's plantation near Montgomery, Alabama, for spring flight training.
Orville makes Montgomery's first powered flight; training of the first students follows.
The school moves its permanent operations to Huffman Field (Simms Station) east of Dayton.
Walter Brookins flies solo for about 12 minutes, the Montgomery camp's only graduate.
Army lieutenants Henry H. Arnold and Thomas DeW. Milling and Lt. John Rodgers arrive in Dayton for lessons.
Arthur L. Welsh, the school's first Dayton-trained pilot and later an instructor, is killed in a crash at College Park, Maryland.
Orville Wright sells the Wright Company to New York financiers.
The flying school at Huffman Field closes after training 119 students since May 1910.

misconception.myth: The Wright brothers' flying school began in Dayton, Ohio.
misconception.fact: Its first classes met in Montgomery, Alabama, in March–May 1910, on land that later became Maxwell Air Force Base; only then did the school settle at Huffman Prairie near Dayton.
misconception.why: The school is remembered through Dayton and its aviation park, while the short, troubled Alabama camp produced a single graduate and is mostly recalled locally.

title: Yellowstone National Park
summary: The first national park in the United States, set aside by an act of Congress signed by President Ulysses S. Grant on March 1, 1872; it covers about 2.2 million acres, mostly in northwestern Wyoming with slivers in Montana and Idaho, protects more than 10,000 hydrothermal features atop an active volcanic caldera, and lies on lands that 27 Native nations have used for more than 11,000 years.

review.question: Why did Congress create Yellowstone as a park rather than let it be settled like other western public land?
review.answer: Expeditions in 1869–1871, especially Hayden's survey with Moran's paintings and Jackson's photographs, publicized its wonders, and promoters including Nathaniel Langford and the railroad financier Jay Cooke, who expected tourist traffic, lobbied for a law withdrawing it from settlement, occupancy or sale and placing it under the Secretary of the Interior.

review.question: How did the U.S. Army come to run the park, and what changed after the 1894 Ed Howell arrest?
review.answer: Congress refused to fund civilian administration, so the Army took charge in August 1886; when soldiers caught Howell poaching bison in 1894, the publicity led Congress within about two months to pass the National Park Protection Act, which banned hunting in the park and gave its rules teeth.

review.question: How did the park's creation affect the Native peoples who used the area?
review.answer: The military was already moving tribes onto reservations, and after 1872 early superintendents discouraged Native people from hunting or gathering in the park; the Tukudika (Sheep Eaters) were dispersed to the Wind River and Fort Hall reservations, and the myth that Indians feared the geysers helped justify their exclusion.

review.question: Why do historians now treat the 1870 Madison Junction campfire story as legend?
review.answer: The account of Cornelius Hedges proposing a national park around the campfire was published by Langford only in 1905, expedition diaries recorded nothing of the kind, and the park grew out of many social, scientific, economic and aesthetic forces rather than one evening's conversation.

timeline.event: John Colter becomes the first known European American to visit the area of present-day Yellowstone.
The Washburn–Langford–Doane Expedition explores the plateau and names Old Faithful.
Ferdinand Hayden's government survey, with painter Thomas Moran and photographer William Henry Jackson, documents the region.
Park bills S. 392 and H.R. 764 are introduced in the Senate and House.
The Senate passes S. 392.
The House passes S. 392 by a vote of 115 to 65.
President Ulysses S. Grant signs the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act.
About 800 Nez Perce (Nimiipuu) people fleeing the U.S. Army enter the park and cross it in 13 days.
The U.S. Army takes charge of the park after Congress declines to fund its civilian administration.
After soldiers arrest the bison poacher Ed Howell, Congress passes the National Park Protection Act (Lacey Act) banning hunting in the park.
Park managers buy 21 bison from private owners to rebuild a wild herd that had fallen to about two dozen animals.
The new National Park Service takes over management and the Army leaves.
Yellowstone becomes the first U.S. site on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Wildfires burn about 36 percent of the park.
The first of 31 gray wolves captured in Canada are brought into the park, restoring a species killed off by 1926.

misconception.myth: Native Americans were afraid of Yellowstone's geysers and hot springs and avoided the area.
misconception.fact: More than 1,900 archeological sites have been found in the park even though only about 3 percent has been surveyed; people hunted, gathered, quarried obsidian and used thermal waters there for more than 11,000 years, and Kiowa, Crow and Shoshone traditions describe its thermal features as places of benevolent spirits and origin stories.
misconception.why: Early park administrators promoted the story to market a tourist destination emptied of its original inhabitants and to justify keeping Native people out; a secondhand line in William Clark's journals and later scholarship repeated it.
